However, we acknowledge that our ebullition evidence is a gross observation, as the pathway has been reported in several lakes in cold months (Walter, Zimov, Chanton, Verbyla, & Chapin, 2006; Wik, Crill, Bastviken, Danielsson, & Norbäck, 2011). In our study, we exclusively sampled on 1 day each month, which is not sufficient to accurately estimate this emission pathway. In the future, higher temporal resolution of sampling (by diurnal sampling, sampling several days per month and spatial analysis) is required to reduce uncertainties in CH₄ ebullition from aquatic ecosystems, as previously recommended by Wik, Thornton, et al. (2016). However, other methods used in the literature contain large uncertainties; DelSontro et al. (2011) indicated that the acoustic technology has large coefficients of variation that exceed 100%, while the classic randomised bubble trap method is highly biased and underestimates results (Walter Anthony & Anthony, 2013). Newer gas analysers and the combination with established techniques may help to determine CH₄ diffusion and ebullition in freshwater ecosystems. Zhao et al. (2015) suggested such a method as a tool for assessing diffusion and ebullition, while Grasset et al. (2016) was one of the first studies to include ebullition data from these newer gas analysers. In the context of CO₂, Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle can be classified as an acidic lake, in which CO₂ is the major inorganic carbon species (Cole & Prairie, 2009) and where the availability of allochthonous and autochthonous inorganic carbon is in some ecosystems a very important driver of CO₂ emissions to the atmosphere (Tank et al., 2018; Tranvik et al., 2009; Weyhenmeyer et al., 2015). During turnover events, with the exception of spring in the SW basin, peaks of CO₂ fluxes were detected jointly with high CO₂ stored in the water column. The surplus CO₂ for both basins likely did not completely originate from surficial (0–20 cm, data not shown) sediments (1.0 ± 0.5 g C/m², mean ± SD_y, pooled basins average), as stored quantities were one order of magnitude lower than the mass of CO₂ emitted (13.0 ± 4.6 g C/m², mean ± SD_y, pooled basins average) and dissolved in the water column (9.3 ± 4.3 g C/m², mean ± SD_y, pooled basins average). This suggests inputs of CO₂ directly from external sources of inorganic carbon and indirectly from mineralisation of internal or external DOC (Brothers et al., 2014; Engel et al., 2018; Maberly et al., 2013; Tank et al., 2018; Tranvik et al., 2009; Weyhenmeyer et al., 2015). The reduction in DOC in the NE basin potentially accounted for the 41% reduction in total annual CO₂ emissions. Moreover, CH₄ emissions decreased to a similar extent (53%), but cannot, as previously discussed, be adequately explained by the reduced availability of DOC to the pelagic community. Ducharme-Riel, Vachon, Del Giorgio, and Prairie (2015) remarked on the complexity of lake dynamics since interaction between physical and biological factors regulates CO₂ dynamics. Sources of CO₂ and contributions by different sources need to be elucidated (Drake et al., 2018; Engel et al., 2018; Tank et al., 2018). It is important to note that we could not observe any CO₂ ebullition with the new gas analyser used in this study, but we acknowledge that our device was not sensitive enough to confirm CO₂ in bubbles for several reasons: (a) CO₂ is highly soluble in water, and therefore, bubbles trapped in sediments might have had low CO₂ concentration; (b) the remaining CO₂ concentration in gas bubbles could have been re-dissolved through the water column before bubbles were emitted to the atmosphere (McGinnis et al., 2011); (c) there was a high CO₂ concentration inside the chamber (atmospheric concentration, ca. 380 ppm) at the initial time of sampling (to observe CO₂ bubbles it would be necessary to exceed this threshold). Similarly, the analyses of Casper et al. (2000) and Sepulveda-Jauregui et al. (2015) determined that only 1% of CO₂ was emitted by ebullition and 99% by diffusion in small shallow lakes. Together, our results may help to identify the environmental factors that regulate carbon emissions in small lakes. In freshwater systems, temperature controls the biological activity across food webs, the length of stratification periods and gas solubility. High temperatures amplified CH₄ emissions (Sepulveda-Jauregui et al., 2018), which led to markedly higher amounts of CH₄ stored and emitted from the basins in the hotter summer of 2014 with a clear correlation between CH₄ emissions and temperature. Similar responses to regional temperature have been shown in ponds, in small shallow, and medium-sized lakes (Bartosiewicz, Laurion, & Macintyre, 2015; Bartosiewicz et al., 2016; Encinas Fernández et al., 2014; Liikanen, Huttunen, Valli, & Martikainen, 2002; Miettinen et al., 2015; Natchimuthu et al., 2014; Room et al., 2014) and in enclosure experiments (Audet et al., 2017; Yvon-Durocher et al., 2017), suggesting that in predicted warming scenarios, an increase in carbon greenhouse gas emissions can be expected in lake ecosystems regardless of DOC inputs and their biogeochemical effects in the water column (e.g., in stratification, temperature regimes, pH, microbial metabolism and CO₂ dynamics). Despite the long-term division of Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle that created two very different stable ecosystems with regard to carbon supply, the CH₄ and to some extent CO₂, emissions to the atmosphere were mainly determined by DOC-independent environmental conditions, as suggested by direct correlations between gas flux and temperature and between pH and dissolved gases. However, pH is an indirect factor associated with DOC correlation with dissolved gas concentrations. Therefore, the correlation between pH and dissolved CH₄ and CO₂ in the SW basin implied that DOC can play an important role in greenhouse gas emissions (Drake et al., 2018). In the case of CH₄, previous studies on methanogenesis in sediments of this acidic bog lake showed that the pathways to form CH₄ were similar to those in pH-neutral lakes (Conrad et al., 2010). Therefore, the reduction in DOC inputs to aquatic ecosystems would benefit several ecological and environmental issues, but in the context of CH₄ and CO₂ emission to the atmosphere from small lakes, the lake size and warming are probably the key factors for determining CH₄ and CO₂ emissions (Holgerson & Raymond, 2016; Kankaala, Huotari, Tulonen, & Ojala, 2013; Room et al., 2014; Sepulveda-Jauregui et al., 2018; Yvon-Durocher et al., 2017). 4.2 | O₂ dynamics governing carbon greenhouse gas storage and emission Higher CH₄ emission periods coincided with the presence of extensive anoxic hypolimnia (in summer and fall). In contrast, low CH₄ emission periods were observed when the water column was oxygenated (in winter and early spring). We suggest that the presence of O₂ in the surficial sediment layers led to a decrease in methanogenic activity by inhibition because it is a strictly anaerobic process. Also, aerobic CH₄ oxidation likely occurred in the superficial sediment layers, further reducing the amount of CH₄ released to the water column. The reciprocal gradient between dissolved O₂ and CH₄ present during the stratification period suggested that CH₄ oxidation in the water column may have regulated diffusive CH₄ emission in stratification periods, but had little effect during mixing periods, as previously reported for lakes (Bartosiewicz et al., 2016; Casper et al., 2005; Encinas Fernández et al., 2014; Kankaala et al., 2006; Martinez-Cruz et al., 2015; Ricao Canelhas et al., 2016; Utsumi et al., 1998). The correlation analyses of dissolved gases (CH₄, CO₂ and O₂) showed that CH₄ and CO₂ are stored in anoxic layers and that they are indicators of high net heterotrophy (Borges et al., 2015; Sepulveda-Jauregui et al., 2015). The weaker correlation between CO₂ and O₂ (when compared to CH₄ and O₂) was consistent with previous reports of dissolved CO₂ patterns in acidic lakes (e.g., Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle) that are being strongly influenced by catchments rich in organic and inorganic carbon (Holgerson & Raymond, 2016; Tranvik et al., 2009; Weyhenmeyer et al., 2015). However, the reciprocal correlation between dissolved O₂ and CH₄ or CO₂ suggests that dissolved O₂ in the water column is an important indicator of CH₄ and CO₂ storage. Total carbon storage (calculated from dissolved CH₄ and CO₂ concentrations) followed dissolved O₂ changes over the seasons (Figure 7), with higher CH₄ and CO₂ emissions occurring when anoxic conditions predominated (maximum of 71 ± 13%, mean ± SD_y, pooled basins average). This may have been the result of higher microbial activity in the summer compared to colder periods of mixing; the reduction in the aerobic zone of the water column may have led to a decrease in aerobic methane oxidation activity. For more than 2 months during the winter, the water column was well oxygenated in both basins, and when temperature increased in spring, O₂ was quickly consumed in the newly established hypolimnia. Bartosiewicz et al. (2016) and Encinas Fernández et al. (2014) also found dissolved O₂ in the water column to be an indicator of CH₄ and CO₂ dynamics in summer. Moreover, Sabrekov et al. (2017) pointed out that O₂ patterns were among the major factors that controlled the dynamics of CH₄ and CO₂ in Siberian lakes, based on regional model development. Therefore, dissolved O₂ can be used as a tracer of biological activity associated with temperature and stratification changes during the seasons. Interestingly, we did not find any relationship between dissolved CH₄ or CO₂ and T or pH, when data from both basins were grouped. Instead, we found a positive correlation between pH and CO₂ and CH₄ concentrations when solely assessed in the water column of the SW basin. This correlation may indicate a higher microbial activity in all trophic levels (from primary production to heterotrophy) and not an intrinsic effect of recalcitrant DOC in the sediments (indicated by the low pH in the SW basin) on CH₄ and CO₂. Moreover, only the western basins of Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle receive inflow from an adjacent peat bog (Burkert et al., 2004; Koschel, 1995), which may supply CH₄ and CO₂ and explain the positive correlation between pH and both gases. Such external sources have been suggested as an important source of both gases for freshwater ecosystems (Garcia-Tigreros Kodovska et al., 2016; Tank et al., 2018; Weyhenmeyer et al., 2015). FIGURE 7 Per cent of carbon stored (sum of CH₄–C and CO₂–C) in the anoxic (grey) and oxic (white) water layers in the water column during the time of the study in both basins of Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle beginning in August 2014 and ending in July 2015 5 | CONCLUDING REMARKS In the artificially divided Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle, the reduction in DOC inputs over 30 years to one of the studied basins was not the factor dominating CH4 and CO2 dynamics. Instead, seasonal changes in ambient temperature, O2 and stratification periods determined the relative contribution of cumulative carbon greenhouse gas emissions. Despite significant differences in pH and DOC developed between the two basins, CH4 and CO2 emissions were in the same order of magnitude over the year. The latter result shows the knowledge gap regarding the mineralisation processes of DOC in small acidic lakes. Therefore, the effect of DOC inputs to these types of lakes, including on CH4 and CO2 emissions, is still unclear. Further studies in various types of lakes are needed in order to better identify the effects of DOC on small and shallow lakes, which are a key component in global carbon greenhouse gas emissions. STANDARD PAPER Assessment of methane and carbon dioxide emissions in two sub-basins of a small acidic bog lake artificially divided 30 years ago Armando Sepulveda-Jauregui1,2,3 | Karla Martinez-Cruz1,2 | Maximilian Lau4 | Peter Casper1 1Department of Experimental Limnology, Leibniz-Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries, Stechlin, Germany 2Department of Sciences and Natural Resources, University of Magallanes, Punta Arenas, Chile 3Center for Climate and Resilience Research (CR)2, University of Chile, Santiago, Chile 4Department of Chemical Analytics and Biogeochemistry, Leibniz-Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries, Berlin, Germany Correspondence Peter Casper, Department of Experimental Limnology, Leibniz-Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries, Stechlin, Germany. Email: pc@igb-berlin.de Funding information Leibniz-Gemeinschaft, Grant/Award Number: Aqualink/SAW 2012-IGB 4167, TemBi/SAW-2011-IGB-2; Consejo Nacional de Ciencia y Tecnología, Grant/Award Number: International Postdoctoral Fellowship/232083, PhD Fellowship/330197/233369; Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft, Grant/Award Number: Nr LA 4177/1-1 Abstract 1. Although lakes are important sources of methane (CH4) and carbon dioxide (CO2) to the atmosphere contributing to global warming, their CH4 and CO2 emissions are rarely assessed. In particular, increasing inputs of terrestrial dissolved organic carbon (DOC) may affect gas dynamics and alter seasonal changes in gas production. 2. Here, we analysed variations in CH4 and CO2 dynamics in sub-basins of an acidic bog lake, which was artificially divided into four quarters three decades ago, leading to divergence in water chemistry and biology. In the divided lake, only the south-west basin (SW) received DOC inputs from an adjacent peat bog, while the north-east basin (NE) was hydrologically disconnected. A year-long determination of CH4 and CO2 production and emission patterns in the two contrasting basins exposed the indirect mechanisms by which DOC supply exercised control on greenhouse gas dynamics in this shallow lake. 3. In both basins, dissolved CH4 was negatively correlated with dissolved oxygen (O2) through the water column, suggesting that aerobic methanotrophy is an important regulator of CH4 emissions in this lake. In contrast, the amount of CO2 stored in oxic and anoxic layers was not significantly different between the basins, suggesting that O2 is not the most important driver of dissolved CO2. 4. Estimated total CH4 and CO2 emissions were 2.1 and 1.7 times lower in the NE basin than in the SW basin, with major CH4 and CO2 emissions occurring during the fall turnover. The differences in CH4 and CO2 emissions suggest that the hydro-physical properties, namely seasonal temperature, the duration of stratification and O2 availability, are the main drivers of CH4 and CO2 emissions to the atmosphere from small shallow lakes under the influence of DOC inputs under global warming pressure. KEYWORDS carbon storage, dissolved greenhouse gases, humic substances, limnology, year-round experiment 1 | INTRODUCTION Even though lakes cover a small proportion of the global land masses (ca. 4%), they are considered a major component in the global carbon cycle (Cole et al., 2007), emitting significant amounts of methane (CH4) and carbon dioxide (CO2) to the atmosphere (Holgerson & Raymond, 2016; Saunois et al., 2016). From those ecosystems, small lakes with surface areas <1 km2 comprise the major proportion of lakes (Cael & Seekell, 2016; Verpoorter, Kutser, Seekell, & Tranvik, 2014). With respect to the amount of the Earth's surface that they cover, small lakes emit disproportionately high amounts of CH4 and CO2, and their projected contribution to global warming is still under investigation (Audet et al., 2017; Downing, 2010; Holgerson & Raymond, 2016; Wik, Varner, Walter Anthony, Macintyre, & Bastviken, 2016; Yvon-Durocher, Hulatt, Woodward, & Trimmer, 2017). Because small lakes are commonly shallow, the sediments and water column interact strongly with the air temperature (Bar-tosiewicz, Laurion, Clayer, & Maranger, 2016; Heslop et al., 2015). Therefore, carbon mineralisation from allochthonous and autochthonous sources increases in warmer seasons, resulting in higher production of CH4 and CO2 (Gudasz, Sobek, Bastviken, Koehler, & Tranvik, 2015; Schulz, Matsuyama, & Conrad, 1997; Sobek, Tranvik, & Cole, 2005). Although CH4 and CO2 productions are temperature dependent in lakes, their emission pathways are not identical. CH4 is mainly produced in anoxic sediments, with a lower amount derived from terrestrial inputs (Paytan et al., 2015; Stanley et al., 2016) and oxic layers (DelSontro, del Giorgio, & Prairie, 2017); it is released primarily by ebullition and, to a lesser extent, by diffusion (Casper, Maberly, Hall, & Finlay, 2000; DelSontro, Boutet, St-Pierre, Del Giorgio, & Prairie, 2016; Wik, Varner, et al., 2016). CO2 is produced along the water column and in sediments (biologically and abiotically), or is derived from terrestrial inputs, and is released primarily by diffusion due to its high solubility (24 times more soluble than CH4) (Battin et al., 2009; Casper et al., 2000; Engel et al., 2018; Maberly, Barker, Stott, & De Ville, 2013; Tank, Fellman, Hood, & Kritzberg, 2018; Weyhenmeyer et al., 2015). The delivery of fresh dissolved organic carbon (DOC) from the catchment is among the key drivers that have been shown to increase the magnitude of CH4 and CO2 emissions (Drake, Raymond, & Spencer, 2018), especially from small lakes (Chmiel et al., 2016; Gonzalez-Valencia et al., 2014; West, Creamer, & Jones, 2015). However, DOC can comprise different proportions of fresh (ready bio-labile) and more recalcitrant fractions, the latter being older in age, highly aromatic (and thus coloured) and regularly referred to as “humic-like” (Raeke, Lechtenfeld, Wagner, Herzsprung, & Reemtsma, 2016). Small lakes that receive large quantities of recalcitrant DOC generally feature the following: reduced metabolism, lower pH and O2 availability, altered contaminant toxicity, lowered light penetration, longer stratification periods and disfavoured food for fish and benthic communities (Brothers et al., 2014; Hessen & Tranvik, 1998; Wetzel, 2001; Williamson, Morris, Pace, & Olson, 1999). It has been regularly reported that, in small lakes with high DOC load, respiration dominates over primary production, resulting in CO2 supersaturation (Cole & Prairie, 2009; Kortelainen et al., 2006; Tranvik et al., 2009) and attenuated CH4 production (Casper, 1992a, 1992b; Casper, Chan, Furtado, & Adams, 2003). Alternatively, parts of the loaded DOC can be incorporated into higher trophic levels, photochemically degraded or absorbed to mineral surfaces (Brothers et al., 2014; Riedel, Zak, Biester, & Dittmar, 2013; Vachon, Lapierre, & del Giorgio, 2016). The cumulative effects of DOC on carbon greenhouse gas emissions from lakes are therefore highly complex and under ongoing debate (Casper et al., 2003; Kankaala, Taipale, Nykanen, & Jones, 2007; López Bellido, Tulonen, Kankaala, & Ojala, 2013; Miettinen et al., 2015; Peura et al., 2014). The current and projected increase in delivery of terrestrial carbon to freshwater ecosystems and the accompanying socio-ecological challenges (e.g., drinking water and fishery services) are some of the most pressing topics in limnology (Clark et al., 2010; Drake et al., 2018; Tank et al., 2018). One topic with several uncertainties is how the ecosystems will recover after the reduction and/or blocking of DOC inputs from the catchment. One method used for assessing this question is the use of experimental enclosures in the ecosystems; they can achieve a realistic manipulation of the ecosystem (Giling et al., 2017) to obtain insights into the functioning of lake metabolism at the ecosystem level, such as CH4 and CO2 cycling (Audet et al., 2017; Bogard et al., 2014; Casper, 1992a, 1992b; Casper et al., 2003, 2005; Davidson et al., 2015; Yvon-Durocher et al., 2017). Audet et al. (2017) and Davidson et al. (2015, 2018) found that biotic interactions influenced greenhouse gas emissions more strongly than warming effects, while Yvon-Durocher et al. (2017) showed that long-term effects of warming increased CH4 and CO2 emissions derived from the change in microorganism metabolism and ecosystem dynamics. In Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle, an acidic lake rich in DOC, CH4 and CO2 dynamics have been examined in sediments. Similar methanogenic communities and dissolved gases were found in contrasting basins (Casper, 1992a, 1992b; Casper et al., 2003, 2005). In this study, we assessed the balance between CO2 and CH4 accumulated and emitted in two contrasting basins in a long-running whole-lake experiment. In 1986, experimental Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle was first divided into two basins by a plastic curtain (Kasprzak, 1993), and later, in 1989, it was subdivided into four basins (Figure 1). The two western basins receive allochthonous DOC inputs from an adjacent peat bog (Sachse, Babenzien, Ginzel, Gelbrecht, & Steinberg, 2001), keeping the pH at 4.4. Meanwhile, the two eastern basins have remained unaffected by DOC inputs from the adjacent peat bog, favouring a pH increase up to 6.5. Besides this pH increase, biomass and biological activity across all trophic levels in the eastern basins were higher compared to those in the western basins (Hehmann, Krienitz, & Koschel, 2001). Our aim was to evaluate how long-lasting (nearly 30 years) modification of DOC input to a small lake alters its CH4 and CO2 dynamics. The experimental whole-lake enclosure allowed the manipulation of nonartificial DOC inputs for almost 30 years, which provided a unique opportunity to assess the effect of DOC reduction on carbon greenhouse gas emission in lakes. Independent from intersystem variations in climatic or land-use conditions, this work closely examined whether reduced DOC inputs could be a means for greenhouse gas mitigation in lakes. 2 | METHODS 2.1 | Study site and sampling strategy Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle is a small naturally acidic bog lake, located in a forested area in the Mecklenburg-Brandenburg Lake District in north-eastern Germany at an altitude of 59 m a.s.l. and about 100 km north of Germany's capital Berlin. The landscape, consisting of end moraine, outwash plain and glacial spillways, formed during the Weichsel glacial period (Burkert, Ginzel, Babenzien, & Koschel, 2004). At present, water supplies are provided by ground water and precipitation (Casper & Koschel, 1995). Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle was divided by plastic curtains in 1986 into two basins (east and west), and into four compartments by a second east–west separation in 1990. Initially, the division was conducted to enable whole-lake experiments in food-web manipulation (Kasprzak, 1993; Koschel, 1995). Over the decades of division, research in Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle has covered several other topics: plankton studies (Glöckner et al., 2000; Hehmann et al., 2001; Macek, Simek, & Bittl, 2001), microorganisms and microbial activity (Grossart et al., 2008; Kanaparthi, Pommerenke, Casper, & Dumont, 2013; Simek et al., 1998), basic limnology and geographical settings (Burkert et al., 2004; Kasprzak, 1993; Koschel, 1995; Richter, 1997; Succow & Jeschke, 1986), and CH4 and CO2 cycle (Casper et al., 2003; Chan, Wolf, Hepperle, & Casper, 2002; Conrad, Claus, & Casper, 2010), among others. The two most contrasting basins, namely south-west basin (SW) (characterised by a low pH of 4.4 and DOC of 37.3 mg/L) and the north-east basin (NE) (with a pH of 6.5 and DOC of 16.4 mg/L), were selected for this study (Figure 1). The main limnological characteristics of the original lake, NE and SW basins are summarised in Table 1. The catchment areas draining the eastern basins provided mainly inflow, while the catchment area adjacent to the western basins was only outflow (Figure 1). Generally, Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle is stratified during the summer stagnation period, and anoxic hypolimnia are usually found in all basins from May to September or October (Casper et al., 2003). Both basins were sampled monthly over 1 year from August 2014 to July 2015. Water samples for these analyses were collected in September 2014, January 2015 and June 2015. Sulphate was analysed using ion chromatography (electrical conductivity detector; Dionex Corp., Sunnyvale CA, USA), NO3– and SRP were analysed spectrophotometrically by flow injection analysis (FIAstar 5000, Foss Analytical, Hilleroed, Denmark), and DOC was measured using a total carbon analyser (Shimadzu TOC-Vcsh, Shimadzu, Kyoto, Japan). 2.3 | Dissolved CH4 and CO2 in the water column Monthly water samples were collected at 0.5-m depth intervals using a 2-L-Limnos sampler to measure dissolved CH4 and CO2 concentrations. We subsampled from the port of the Limnos sampler with a 60-ml syringe and gently transferred the sample into 20-ml headspace vials until the water overflowed (performed in duplicate). We then sealed the vials with silicone/PTFE stoppers and magnetic crimp caps. In the laboratory, a headspace was created by displacing water with He (99.999%; Air Liquide, Düsseldorf, Germany) using a two-way needle system. Approximately 40% of the water was replaced, and volumes of sample and headspace were calculated by weight. (2012) using the NIST database (Linstrom & Mallard, 2014). 2.4 | CH4 and CO2 storage estimation CH4 and CO2 stored in the water column were determined using the vertical profiles of CH4 and CO2 concentrations. For each month, we estimated the total mass of CH4 and CO2 stored in the basins by calculating the gas concentration and water volume of the respective layer. The volume of each layer was determined using a hypsometric curve (Supporting Information Figure S1). Linear regressions of total CH4 and CO2 content in the water columns over time were used to estimate stored/removed CH4 and CO2 through the seasons. Total masses of CH4 and CO2 removed (emitted or consumed) during the turnover were obtained from the difference in amounts of CH4 and CO2 stored in the water column before and after turnover using the slope determined in the regression analysis. 2.5 | Greenhouse gas flux measurement CH4 and CO2 fluxes were measured using the static chamber technique in a recirculation mode coupled to a new-generation ultra-portable greenhouse gas analyser base utilising Off-Axis Integrated Cavity Output Spectroscopy (OA-ICOS, UGGA 30P; Los Gatos Inc., San Jose, CA, USA). The static chambers were aluminium with a truncated pyramid shape and had two gas valves and a floating system (Supporting Information Figure S2). The static chamber open surface was 1 m2 with a headspace of 240 L. The recirculation gas flow rate was 0.783 ± 0.015 L/min (mean ± SD), and 1 Hz of frequency was recorded for both gases. To determine gas flux (quintuplicate measurements taken on 1 day per month), the valves of the static chamber were opened to equilibrate the pressure for approximately 2 min. Then, the static chamber was connected to the gas analyser in recirculation mode (Supporting Information Figure S2) for approximately 3–10 min. CH4 and CO2 fluxes (FCH4 or FCO2, mg m−2 hr−1) were determined from the linear slope of gas concentration against the time of measurement (ΔC/Δt; ppmv/hr). The area covered by the chamber (A) and the volume (V) of its headspace was considered for the flux calculation as follows: \[ F_{\text{CH}_4 \text{ or } \text{CO}_2} = \frac{\Delta C}{\Delta t} \times \frac{V}{A} \] This static chamber method used in this experiment covered the total flux (diffusive and ebullitive); the graphical analysis of the concentration increases over time allowed to distinguish between diffusive or ebullitive fluxes alone or mixed. Moreover, the high resolution (1 Hz) of the gas analyser allowed the observation of bubble events (here only for CH4; CO2 was not detectable in all bubbles trapped). When bubbles were released into the chamber, the CH4 concentration in the gas analyser increased abruptly until the gas was completely mixed inside the chamber headspace (Figure 2). Therefore, when no linear regression trend was observed to determine the flux, we used the initial and end points to determine the sum of diffusive and ebullitive CH4 fluxes, as discussed by Goodrich, Varner, Frolking, Duncan, and Crill (2011), Zhao et al. (2015) and Grasset, Abril, Guillard, Delolme, and Bornette (2016). We acknowledge that our sampling procedure may not accurately measure diel gas emissions, as previous studies have found large variations in diel CH4 and CO2 fluxes (Liu et al., 2016; Natchimuthu, Selvam, & Bastviken, 2014; Natchimuthu et al., 2016). However, as discussed by Wik, Thornton, Bastviken, Uhlbaeck, and Crill (2016), the variation seemed to be smaller than the variability among individual sampling days (for CH4). 2.6 | Data handling and statistical analysis We divided our data analysis according to the season into three main periods: (a) active stratification, from August 2014 to October 2014 and from June 2015 to July 2015; (b) mixing period from December 2014 to May 2015 (which also included the slight spring turnover); and (c) fall turnover event in November 2014. From those seasonal data analysis, we compared CH4 and CO2 dynamics in basins. First, the normality of data distribution was explored using the Shapiro–Wilk test. In all other cases (Figure 2d), flux was considered to be zero (\( R^2 < 0.7 \)). Meanwhile, CH\(_4\) fluxes with evidence of ebullition (steep increase in concentration over a long period of time) were analysed by removing data peaks or by dividing the initial and final values from each measurement by the time of the measurement (Figure 2b,c) because there is no established way to use a linear regression method to estimate gas flux in such ebullition events. 3 | RESULTS 3.1 | Temporal variation in T, O\(_2\) and pH Temporal differences among T, O\(_2\) and pH profiles between the NE and SW basins (Figure 3; Supporting Information Figure S3) were observed. Thermal stratification was found in both basins until early November 2014 and from May 2015 to the end of the study period in July 2015. In between these periods, the basins exhibited slight inverse stratification (Figure 3; Supporting Information Figure S3). Thin ice covers (ca. 3 cm thick) were formed over both basins in February 2015, and small ice patches were present during the sampling periods in March 2015 in the SW basin. Turnover events occurred in late fall and early spring (Figure 3; Supporting Information Figure S3). For further analysis, we focused on active stratification, mixing and fall turnover periods. The highest and lowest water temperatures were found in August 2014 (NE: 24°C; SW: 21°C) and January 2015 (NE: 3°C; SW: 2°C), respectively. During the summer of 2015, the weather was slightly colder than that of the previous year, with a difference in the maximum average air temperature of 5°C registered in July 2014 (27.9 ± 6.6°C, mean ± SD) compared to July 2015 (22.9 ± 4.8°C, mean ± SD; Local Stechlin Germany National Weather Service, DWD, www.dwd.de). Parts of the water layers turned anoxic during stratification periods in both basins, and during February 2015 and March 2015, only the SW basin exhibited an anoxic water zone (Supporting Information Figure S3). In 2015, the water column of the SW basin was mixed later than the NE basin. This disparity in water column dynamics was consistent with the O\(_2\) profiles from May 2015, when in the NE basin the hypolimnetic water was anoxic up to 3 m depth, while in the SW basin, a small anoxic layer of only a few centimetres depth was present (Supporting Information Figure S3). Finally, the most pronounced differences were in pH values between the basins, with higher values in the NE basin (pH 5.0–6.5) than in the SW basin (pH 3.9–5.1) throughout the year (Supporting Information Figure S3). 3.2 | Seasonal dissolved CH\(_4\) and CO\(_2\) concentrations Vertical concentration profiles of dissolved CH\(_4\) and CO\(_2\) in the water column were determined in both basins over the whole year (Figure 4). During the first and second stratification period, the mean dissolved CH\(_4\) concentration across both basins was 0.76 ± 1.68 mg CH\(_4\)/L (mean ± \( SD_y \), pooled basins average), while during the mixing period this value dropped to 0.001 ± 0.007 mg CH\(_4\)/L (mean ± \( SD_y \), pooled basins average). During the fall turnover, more than 99% of the CH\(_4\) previously stored in the stratification period was rapidly removed at a rate of 91 g C/day (\( R^2 = 0.88; p < 0.018 \)) and 113 g C/day (\( R^2 = 0.88; p < 0.019 \)) from the NE and SW basins, respectively (Figure 5a). After the fall turnover, the concentration of CH\(_4\) in the water column was low (<0.008 mg CH\(_4\)/L; maximum from both basins), with the water column well oxygenated until May 2015 (Supporting Information Figure S3). In under-ice stratification in winter (for approximately 25 days in February 2015), CH\(_4\) concentration in both basins remained low (<0.008 mg CH\(_4\)/L; maximum from both basins) and negligible amounts were stored. After the onset of the 2015, summer stratification, dissolved CH\(_4\) was stored in the water column at a rate of 21 g C/day (\( R^2 = 0.85; p < 0.027 \)) and 16 g C/day (\( R^2 = 0.86; p < 0.023 \)) in the NE and SW basins, respectively (Figure 5). Patterns of dissolved CO\(_2\) concentration in the water column differed from those of dissolved CH\(_4\) (Figure 4). Mean dissolved CO\(_2\) concentrations across both basins were estimated as 5.40 ± 3.73 mg CO\(_2\)/L (mean ± \( SD_y \); pooled basins average) during mixing period, and 11.63 ± 7.66 mg CO\(_2\)/L (mean ± \( SD_y \); pooled basins average) during the two stratification periods. During the fall turnover, CO\(_2\) concentration in the water column increased significantly (FT, \( p < 0.05 \)), with the highest concentration found in deeper water (NE: 18.84 ± 4.23 mg CO\(_2\)/L; SW: 16.77 ± 2.13 mg CO\(_2\)/L; mean ± \( SD_y \)), suggesting a higher supply of CO\(_2\) to the water column from the sediments. Between February 2015 and March 2015, CO\(_2\) concentration increased again in the water column (Figure 4; NE: 7.78 ± 5.54 mg CO\(_2\)/L; SW: 7.22 ± 1.98 mg CO\(_2\)/L; mean ± \( SD_y \)). Following the fall turnover, the additional CO\(_2\) was removed from the water columns of both basins. The next substantial increase in CO\(_2\) occurred in June 2015, which was again removed in July 2015. The loss of CO\(_2\) may have been a result of re-equilibration of the inorganic species, driven by increased photosynthesis and pushing all the water column to increase the pH from June 2015 to July 2015, which featured the highest pH values in both basins (Supporting Information Figure S3). Given the high variability of monthly dissolved CO₂ concentrations, we were unable to determine a yearly pattern. However, dissolved CO₂ in the fall turnover period was removed at a rate of 636 g C/day and 374 g C/day in the NE and SW basins, respectively, calculated from the difference in total mass between November 2014 and December 2014 (Figure 5b). During the spring turnover, CO₂ removal corresponded to 321 and 286 g C/day, calculated from the net difference in total masses between March 2015 and April 2015 in the NE basin and between February 2015 and April 2015 in the SW basin, respectively (Figure 5). 3.3 | CH₄ and CO₂ emissions CH₄ fluxes were highly variable ranging from 0.16 to 156.28 mg m⁻² day⁻¹ (Supporting Information Figure S4, median values). We could not measure CH₄ and CO₂ fluxes during February, because of ice cover. Peak CH₄ emissions occurred during the fall turnover in both basins. Thereafter, CH₄ emissions remained at a low level until the onset of summer stratification when the hypolimnion turned anoxic (Supporting Information Figure S4). These results coincided with dissolved CH₄ concentrations observed in the same season and water temperature; large gas fluxes were observed during periods when high dissolved CH₄ concentrations were found in the water column (Figure 5 and Supporting Information Figure S5). Mean monthly CH₄ emissions (including diffusion and ebullition) from the SW basin were 1.2-fold to 45-fold higher than those from the NE basin as a result of more evident ebullition (Supporting Information Figure S4) and higher dissolved CH₄ concentrations in surface waters (Figure 4) during both summer periods. In both basins, CH₄ ebullition was observed together with higher emission rates (Supporting Information Figure S4). For both basins, CH₄ ebullition was two orders of magnitude higher compared to months without evident CH₄ ebullition (FT, \( p < 0.05 \)). Mean monthly CO₂ fluxes were highly variable ranging from 11 to 2,222 mg m⁻² day⁻¹, with monthly differences of up to two orders of magnitude (Supporting Information Figure S4, median values). Similar to the CH₄ emissions pattern, maximum CO₂ emissions occurred during the fall turnover (for both basins). In the NE basin, high emissions were detected during the spring turnover; the emissions were up to eightfold higher than those in the SW basin. Later CO₂ emissions in the NE basin remained low during spring and summer of 2015, but CO₂ emissions increased during the subsequent months in the SW basin. The basins exhibit remarkable changes in emissions throughout the year. Since the installation of the separation curtains, stable stratification during summers and two turnover events per year have been registered (Casper et al., 2003; Hehmann et al., 2001). Fall turnover is the major source of CH₄ and CO₂ emissions to the atmosphere in both basins. Similar tendencies were described in small, sheltered boreal humic lakes in southern Finland and in a small mesotrophic dimictic lake in southern Germany; in both lakes, major CH₄ emissions were observed during the fall turnover, and no significant amounts of CH₄ were emitted during the spring turnover (Encinas Fernández, Peeters, & Hofmann, 2014; Kankaala, Huotari, Peltomaa, Saloranta, & Ojala, 2006; Kankaala et al., 2007; López Bellido et al., 2013). Studies in Finnish lakes attributed these low emissions during the spring turnover to short or incomplete mixing of water masses, which in turn is a result of the high absorption of solar radiation by the coloured fraction of DOC in the first few metres of water (Kankaala et al., 2007). However, in our case the spring turnover was complete, as FIGURE 5 Temporal variation in total carbon mass of (a) CH4 (kg C) and (b) CO2 (kg C) in the NE basin (blue) and SW basin (orange) from August 2014 to July 2015. Connected dots indicate the carbon emitted as CH4 and CO2 across the total area of each basin in each month (Table 1) estimated from gas fluxes and basin area (Supporting Information Figure S4); error bars indicate the propagated error from gas flux measurements (Supporting Information Figure S4). Grey line represents mean temperature in the water column (pooled basins average). Coloured bars indicate the carbon content of CH4 and CO2 in the water column. Error bars indicate the propagated error from the measurements of total concentration. Dashed lines indicate fall and spring turnover events [Colour figure can be viewed at wileyonlinelibrary.com] shown by T profiles and by the considerable CO2 emissions from the NE basin; therefore, our data suggest that no significant amounts of CH4 were stored in the water column during the winter inverse stratification due to temperature-limited methanogenesis (Schulz et al., 1997), possible methane oxidation in the water column (Martinez-Cruz, Sepulveda-Jauregui, Walter Anthony, & Thalasso, 2015; Ricao Canelhas, Denfeld, Weyhenmeyer, Bastviken, & Bertilsson, 2016), and the relatively short ice-covered period compared with that of high northern lakes (Sepulveda-Jauregui, Anthony, Martinez-Cruz, Greene, & Thalasso, 2015; Vonk et al., 2015). Encinas Fernández et al. (2014) attributed these low CH4 emissions during the spring turnover to continuous oxic conditions in the hypolimnia following the fall turnover, similar to the results of this study. Additionally, the low spring emissions could be the result of lower temperatures and reduced supply of bio-labile DOC mitigating the methanogenic activity during the short winter stratification. Overall, more systematic studies in different types of lakes are required to improve the temporal CH4 and CO2 emission estimations (Natchimuthu, Wallin, Klemetsson, & Bastviken, 2017; Natchimuthu et al., 2016). DOC availability can trigger CH4 emission through its influence on methanogenesis. A lower DOC supply, as in the NE basin, may therefore be reflected in an attenuation of the two typical effects of DOC in lake ecosystems: (a) DOC is used by the aerobic, heterotrophic microbiome, which rapidly consume the O2 in the water column and surficial sediments, developing anoxic conditions for anaerobic carbon degradation (Adler, Eckert, & Sivan, 2011; Borrel et al., 2011), and (b) DOC enhances anaerobic respiration, including methanogenesis (Casper, 1992b; Heslop et al., 2015; Walter Anthony, Anthony, Grosse, & Chanton, 2012; Walter Anthony et al., 2016). Anoxic hypolimnia may further lead to major CH4 emissions as a result of the decomposition of more labile sources of DOC by syntrophic methanogenesis processes (i.e., by primary decomposers, fermenters and methanogens), which are restricted when O2 is present close to sediments (Chen et al., 2017). In addition, methanogenesis is strongly dependent on temperature, showing a more pronounced change than aerobic CH4 oxidation under temperature variations (Nguyen, Crill, & Bastviken, 2010; Sepulveda-Jauregui et al., 2018; Yvon-Durocher et al., 2014). Warmer temperatures may then promote the production of CH4 in sediments, leading to oversaturation in pore water and thus forcing ebullition. While CH4 ebullition was evident in most of the warm months (excluding June 2015 and July 2015 in the NE basin), it was not detected during the cold months. However, we acknowledge that our ebullition evidence is a gross observation, as the pathway has been reported in several lakes in cold months (Walter, Zimov, Chanton, Verbyla, & Chapin, 2006; Wik, Crill, Bastviken, Danielsson, & Norbäck, 2011). In our study, we exclusively sampled on 1 day each month, which is not sufficient to accurately estimate this emission pathway. In the future, higher temporal resolution of sampling (by diurnal sampling, sampling several days per month and spatial analysis) is required to reduce uncertainties in CH₄ ebullition from aquatic ecosystems, as previously recommended by Wik, Thornton, et al. (2016). However, other methods used in the literature contain large uncertainties; DelSontro et al. (2011) indicated that the acoustic technology has large coefficients of variation that exceed 100%, while the classic randomised bubble trap method is highly biased and underestimates results (Walter Anthony & Anthony, 2013). Newer gas analysers and the combination with established techniques may help to determine CH₄ diffusion and ebullition in freshwater ecosystems. Zhao et al. (2015) suggested such a method as a tool for assessing diffusion and ebullition, while Grasset et al. (2016) was one of the first studies to include ebullition data from these newer gas analysers. In the context of CO₂, Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle can be classified as an acidic lake, in which CO₂ is the major inorganic carbon species (Cole & Prairie, 2009) and where the availability of allochthonous and autochthonous inorganic carbon is in some ecosystems a very important driver of CO₂ emissions to the atmosphere (Tank et al., 2018; Tranvik et al., 2009; Weyhenmeyer et al., 2015). During turnover events, with the exception of spring in the SW basin, peaks of CO₂ fluxes were detected jointly with high CO₂ stored in the water column. The surplus CO₂ for both basins likely did not completely originate from surficial (0–20 cm, data not shown) sediments (1.0 ± 0.5 g C/m², mean ± SD_y, pooled basins average), as stored quantities were one order of magnitude lower than the mass of CO₂ emitted (13.0 ± 4.6 g C/m², mean ± SD_y, pooled basins average) and dissolved in the water column (9.3 ± 4.3 g C/m², mean ± SD_y, pooled basins average). This suggests inputs of CO₂ directly from external sources of inorganic carbon and indirectly from mineralisation of internal or external DOC (Brothers et al., 2014; Engel et al., 2018; Maberly et al., 2013; Tank et al., 2018; Tranvik et al., 2009; Weyhenmeyer et al., 2015). The reduction in DOC in the NE basin potentially accounted for the 41% reduction in total annual CO₂ emissions. Moreover, CH₄ emissions decreased to a similar extent (53%), but cannot, as previously discussed, be adequately explained by the reduced availability of DOC to the pelagic community. Ducharme-Riel, Vachon, Del Giorgio, and Prairie (2015) remarked on the complexity of lake dynamics since interaction between physical and biological factors regulates CO₂ dynamics. Sources of CO₂ and contributions by different sources need to be elucidated (Drake et al., 2018; Engel et al., 2018; Tank et al., 2018). It is important to note that we could not observe any CO₂ ebullition with the new gas analyser used in this study, but we acknowledge that our device was not sensitive enough to confirm CO₂ in bubbles for several reasons: (a) CO₂ is highly soluble in water, and therefore, bubbles trapped in sediments might have had low CO₂ concentration; (b) the remaining CO₂ concentration in gas bubbles could have been re-dissolved through the water column before bubbles were emitted to the atmosphere (McGinnis et al., 2011); (c) there was a high CO₂ concentration inside the chamber (atmospheric concentration, ca. 380 ppm) at the initial time of sampling (to observe CO₂ bubbles it would be necessary to exceed this threshold). Similarly, the analyses of Casper et al. (2000) and Sepulveda-Jauregui et al. (2015) determined that only 1% of CO₂ was emitted by ebullition and 99% by diffusion in small shallow lakes. Together, our results may help to identify the environmental factors that regulate carbon emissions in small lakes. In freshwater systems, temperature controls the biological activity across food webs, the length of stratification periods and gas solubility. High temperatures amplified CH₄ emissions (Sepulveda-Jauregui et al., 2018), which led to markedly higher amounts of CH₄ stored and emitted from the basins in the hotter summer of 2014 with a clear correlation between CH₄ emissions and temperature. Similar responses to regional temperature have been shown in ponds, in small shallow, and medium-sized lakes (Bartosiewicz, Laurion, & Macintyre, 2015; Bartosiewicz et al., 2016; Encinas Fernández et al., 2014; Liikanen, Huttunen, Valli, & Martikainen, 2002; Miettinen et al., 2015; Natchimuthu et al., 2014; Room et al., 2014) and in enclosure experiments (Audet et al., 2017; Yvon-Durocher et al., 2017), suggesting that in predicted warming scenarios, an increase in carbon greenhouse gas emissions can be expected in lake ecosystems regardless of DOC inputs and their biogeochemical effects in the water column (e.g., in stratification, temperature regimes, pH, microbial metabolism and CO₂ dynamics). Despite the long-term division of Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle that created two very different stable ecosystems with regard to carbon supply, the CH₄ and to some extent CO₂, emissions to the atmosphere were mainly determined by DOC-independent environmental conditions, as suggested by direct correlations between gas flux and temperature and between pH and dissolved gases. However, pH is an indirect factor associated with DOC correlation with dissolved gas concentrations. Therefore, the correlation between pH and dissolved CH₄ and CO₂ in the SW basin implied that DOC can play an important role in greenhouse gas emissions (Drake et al., 2018). In the case of CH₄, previous studies on methanogenesis in sediments of this acidic bog lake showed that the pathways to form CH₄ were similar to those in pH-neutral lakes (Conrad et al., 2010). Therefore, the reduction in DOC inputs to aquatic ecosystems would benefit several ecological and environmental issues, but in the context of CH₄ and CO₂ emission to the atmosphere from small lakes, the lake size and warming are probably the key factors for determining CH₄ and CO₂ emissions (Holgerson & Raymond, 2016; Kankaala, Huotari, Tulonen, & Ojala, 2013; Room et al., 2014; Sepulveda-Jauregui et al., 2018; Yvon-Durocher et al., 2017). 4.2 | O₂ dynamics governing carbon greenhouse gas storage and emission Higher CH₄ emission periods coincided with the presence of extensive anoxic hypolimnia (in summer and fall). In contrast, low CH₄ emission periods were observed when the water column was oxygenated (in winter and early spring). We suggest that the presence of O₂ in the surficial sediment layers led to a decrease in methanogenic activity by inhibition because it is a strictly anaerobic process. Also, aerobic CH₄ oxidation likely occurred in the superficial sediment layers, further reducing the amount of CH₄ released to the water column. The reciprocal gradient between dissolved O₂ and CH₄ present during the stratification period suggested that CH₄ oxidation in the water column may have regulated diffusive CH₄ emission in stratification periods, but had little effect during mixing periods, as previously reported for lakes (Bartosiewicz et al., 2016; Casper et al., 2005; Encinas Fernández et al., 2014; Kankaala et al., 2006; Martinez-Cruz et al., 2015; Ricao Canelhas et al., 2016; Utsumi et al., 1998). The correlation analyses of dissolved gases (CH₄, CO₂ and O₂) showed that CH₄ and CO₂ are stored in anoxic layers and that they are indicators of high net heterotrophy (Borges et al., 2015; Sepulveda-Jauregui et al., 2015). The weaker correlation between CO₂ and O₂ (when compared to CH₄ and O₂) was consistent with previous reports of dissolved CO₂ patterns in acidic lakes (e.g., Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle) that are being strongly influenced by catchments rich in organic and inorganic carbon (Holgerson & Raymond, 2016; Tranvik et al., 2009; Weyhenmeyer et al., 2015). However, the reciprocal correlation between dissolved O₂ and CH₄ or CO₂ suggests that dissolved O₂ in the water column is an important indicator of CH₄ and CO₂ storage. Total carbon storage (calculated from dissolved CH₄ and CO₂ concentrations) followed dissolved O₂ changes over the seasons (Figure 7), with higher CH₄ and CO₂ emissions occurring when anoxic conditions predominated (maximum of 71 ± 13%, mean ± SD_y, pooled basins average). This may have been the result of higher microbial activity in the summer compared to colder periods of mixing; the reduction in the aerobic zone of the water column may have led to a decrease in aerobic methane oxidation activity. For more than 2 months during the winter, the water column was well oxygenated in both basins, and when temperature increased in spring, O₂ was quickly consumed in the newly established hypolimnia. Bartosiewicz et al. (2016) and Encinas Fernández et al. (2014) also found dissolved O₂ in the water column to be an indicator of CH₄ and CO₂ dynamics in summer. Moreover, Sabrekov et al. (2017) pointed out that O₂ patterns were among the major factors that controlled the dynamics of CH₄ and CO₂ in Siberian lakes, based on regional model development. Therefore, dissolved O₂ can be used as a tracer of biological activity associated with temperature and stratification changes during the seasons. Interestingly, we did not find any relationship between dissolved CH₄ or CO₂ and T or pH, when data from both basins were grouped. Instead, we found a positive correlation between pH and CO₂ and CH₄ concentrations when solely assessed in the water column of the SW basin. This correlation may indicate a higher microbial activity in all trophic levels (from primary production to heterotrophy) and not an intrinsic effect of recalcitrant DOC in the sediments (indicated by the low pH in the SW basin) on CH₄ and CO₂. Moreover, only the western basins of Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle receive inflow from an adjacent peat bog (Burkert et al., 2004; Koschel, 1995), which may supply CH₄ and CO₂ and explain the positive correlation between pH and both gases. Such external sources have been suggested as an important source of both gases for freshwater ecosystems (Garcia-Tigreros Kodovska et al., 2016; Tank et al., 2018; Weyhenmeyer et al., 2015). FIGURE 7 Per cent of carbon stored (sum of CH₄–C and CO₂–C) in the anoxic (grey) and oxic (white) water layers in the water column during the time of the study in both basins of Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle beginning in August 2014 and ending in July 2015 5 | CONCLUDING REMARKS In the artificially divided Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle, the reduction in DOC inputs over 30 years to one of the studied basins was not the factor dominating CH4 and CO2 dynamics. Instead, seasonal changes in ambient temperature, O2 and stratification periods determined the relative contribution of cumulative carbon greenhouse gas emissions. Despite significant differences in pH and DOC developed between the two basins, CH4 and CO2 emissions were in the same order of magnitude over the year. The latter result shows the knowledge gap regarding the mineralisation processes of DOC in small acidic lakes. Therefore, the effect of DOC inputs to these types of lakes, including on CH4 and CO2 emissions, is still unclear. Further studies in various types of lakes are needed in order to better identify the effects of DOC on small and shallow lakes, which are a key component in global carbon greenhouse gas emissions. STANDARD PAPER Assessment of methane and carbon dioxide emissions in two sub-basins of a small acidic bog lake artificially divided 30 years ago Armando Sepulveda-Jauregui1,2,3 | Karla Martinez-Cruz1,2 | Maximilian Lau4 | Peter Casper1 1Department of Experimental Limnology, Leibniz-Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries, Stechlin, Germany 2Department of Sciences and Natural Resources, University of Magallanes, Punta Arenas, Chile 3Center for Climate and Resilience Research (CR)2, University of Chile, Santiago, Chile 4Department of Chemical Analytics and Biogeochemistry, Leibniz-Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries, Berlin, Germany Correspondence Peter Casper, Department of Experimental Limnology, Leibniz-Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries, Stechlin, Germany. Email: pc@igb-berlin.de Funding information Leibniz-Gemeinschaft, Grant/Award Number: Aqualink/SAW 2012-IGB 4167, TemBi/SAW-2011-IGB-2; Consejo Nacional de Ciencia y Tecnología, Grant/Award Number: International Postdoctoral Fellowship/232083, PhD Fellowship/330197/233369; Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft, Grant/Award Number: Nr LA 4177/1-1 Abstract 1. Although lakes are important sources of methane (CH4) and carbon dioxide (CO2) to the atmosphere contributing to global warming, their CH4 and CO2 emissions are rarely assessed. In particular, increasing inputs of terrestrial dissolved organic carbon (DOC) may affect gas dynamics and alter seasonal changes in gas production. 2. Here, we analysed variations in CH4 and CO2 dynamics in sub-basins of an acidic bog lake, which was artificially divided into four quarters three decades ago, leading to divergence in water chemistry and biology. In the divided lake, only the south-west basin (SW) received DOC inputs from an adjacent peat bog, while the north-east basin (NE) was hydrologically disconnected. A year-long determination of CH4 and CO2 production and emission patterns in the two contrasting basins exposed the indirect mechanisms by which DOC supply exercised control on greenhouse gas dynamics in this shallow lake. 3. In both basins, dissolved CH4 was negatively correlated with dissolved oxygen (O2) through the water column, suggesting that aerobic methanotrophy is an important regulator of CH4 emissions in this lake. In contrast, the amount of CO2 stored in oxic and anoxic layers was not significantly different between the basins, suggesting that O2 is not the most important driver of dissolved CO2. 4. Estimated total CH4 and CO2 emissions were 2.1 and 1.7 times lower in the NE basin than in the SW basin, with major CH4 and CO2 emissions occurring during the fall turnover. The differences in CH4 and CO2 emissions suggest that the hydro-physical properties, namely seasonal temperature, the duration of stratification and O2 availability, are the main drivers of CH4 and CO2 emissions to the atmosphere from small shallow lakes under the influence of DOC inputs under global warming pressure. KEYWORDS carbon storage, dissolved greenhouse gases, humic substances, limnology, year-round experiment 1 | INTRODUCTION Even though lakes cover a small proportion of the global land masses (ca. 4%), they are considered a major component in the global carbon cycle (Cole et al., 2007), emitting significant amounts of methane (CH4) and carbon dioxide (CO2) to the atmosphere (Holgerson & Raymond, 2016; Saunois et al., 2016). From those ecosystems, small lakes with surface areas <1 km2 comprise the major proportion of lakes (Cael & Seekell, 2016; Verpoorter, Kutser, Seekell, & Tranvik, 2014). With respect to the amount of the Earth's surface that they cover, small lakes emit disproportionately high amounts of CH4 and CO2, and their projected contribution to global warming is still under investigation (Audet et al., 2017; Downing, 2010; Holgerson & Raymond, 2016; Wik, Varner, Walter Anthony, Macintyre, & Bastviken, 2016; Yvon-Durocher, Hulatt, Woodward, & Trimmer, 2017). Because small lakes are commonly shallow, the sediments and water column interact strongly with the air temperature (Bar-tosiewicz, Laurion, Clayer, & Maranger, 2016; Heslop et al., 2015). Therefore, carbon mineralisation from allochthonous and autochthonous sources increases in warmer seasons, resulting in higher production of CH4 and CO2 (Gudasz, Sobek, Bastviken, Koehler, & Tranvik, 2015; Schulz, Matsuyama, & Conrad, 1997; Sobek, Tranvik, & Cole, 2005). Although CH4 and CO2 productions are temperature dependent in lakes, their emission pathways are not identical. CH4 is mainly produced in anoxic sediments, with a lower amount derived from terrestrial inputs (Paytan et al., 2015; Stanley et al., 2016) and oxic layers (DelSontro, del Giorgio, & Prairie, 2017); it is released primarily by ebullition and, to a lesser extent, by diffusion (Casper, Maberly, Hall, & Finlay, 2000; DelSontro, Boutet, St-Pierre, Del Giorgio, & Prairie, 2016; Wik, Varner, et al., 2016). CO2 is produced along the water column and in sediments (biologically and abiotically), or is derived from terrestrial inputs, and is released primarily by diffusion due to its high solubility (24 times more soluble than CH4) (Battin et al., 2009; Casper et al., 2000; Engel et al., 2018; Maberly, Barker, Stott, & De Ville, 2013; Tank, Fellman, Hood, & Kritzberg, 2018; Weyhenmeyer et al., 2015). The delivery of fresh dissolved organic carbon (DOC) from the catchment is among the key drivers that have been shown to increase the magnitude of CH4 and CO2 emissions (Drake, Raymond, & Spencer, 2018), especially from small lakes (Chmiel et al., 2016; Gonzalez-Valencia et al., 2014; West, Creamer, & Jones, 2015). However, DOC can comprise different proportions of fresh (ready bio-labile) and more recalcitrant fractions, the latter being older in age, highly aromatic (and thus coloured) and regularly referred to as “humic-like” (Raeke, Lechtenfeld, Wagner, Herzsprung, & Reemtsma, 2016). Small lakes that receive large quantities of recalcitrant DOC generally feature the following: reduced metabolism, lower pH and O2 availability, altered contaminant toxicity, lowered light penetration, longer stratification periods and disfavoured food for fish and benthic communities (Brothers et al., 2014; Hessen & Tranvik, 1998; Wetzel, 2001; Williamson, Morris, Pace, & Olson, 1999). It has been regularly reported that, in small lakes with high DOC load, respiration dominates over primary production, resulting in CO2 supersaturation (Cole & Prairie, 2009; Kortelainen et al., 2006; Tranvik et al., 2009) and attenuated CH4 production (Casper, 1992a, 1992b; Casper, Chan, Furtado, & Adams, 2003). Alternatively, parts of the loaded DOC can be incorporated into higher trophic levels, photochemically degraded or absorbed to mineral surfaces (Brothers et al., 2014; Riedel, Zak, Biester, & Dittmar, 2013; Vachon, Lapierre, & del Giorgio, 2016). The cumulative effects of DOC on carbon greenhouse gas emissions from lakes are therefore highly complex and under ongoing debate (Casper et al., 2003; Kankaala, Taipale, Nykanen, & Jones, 2007; López Bellido, Tulonen, Kankaala, & Ojala, 2013; Miettinen et al., 2015; Peura et al., 2014). The current and projected increase in delivery of terrestrial carbon to freshwater ecosystems and the accompanying socio-ecological challenges (e.g., drinking water and fishery services) are some of the most pressing topics in limnology (Clark et al., 2010; Drake et al., 2018; Tank et al., 2018). One topic with several uncertainties is how the ecosystems will recover after the reduction and/or blocking of DOC inputs from the catchment. One method used for assessing this question is the use of experimental enclosures in the ecosystems; they can achieve a realistic manipulation of the ecosystem (Giling et al., 2017) to obtain insights into the functioning of lake metabolism at the ecosystem level, such as CH4 and CO2 cycling (Audet et al., 2017; Bogard et al., 2014; Casper, 1992a, 1992b; Casper et al., 2003, 2005; Davidson et al., 2015; Yvon-Durocher et al., 2017). Audet et al. (2017) and Davidson et al. (2015, 2018) found that biotic interactions influenced greenhouse gas emissions more strongly than warming effects, while Yvon-Durocher et al. (2017) showed that long-term effects of warming increased CH4 and CO2 emissions derived from the change in microorganism metabolism and ecosystem dynamics. In Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle, an acidic lake rich in DOC, CH4 and CO2 dynamics have been examined in sediments. Similar methanogenic communities and dissolved gases were found in contrasting basins (Casper, 1992a, 1992b; Casper et al., 2003, 2005). In this study, we assessed the balance between CO2 and CH4 accumulated and emitted in two contrasting basins in a long-running whole-lake experiment. In 1986, experimental Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle was first divided into two basins by a plastic curtain (Kasprzak, 1993), and later, in 1989, it was subdivided into four basins (Figure 1). The two western basins receive allochthonous DOC inputs from an adjacent peat bog (Sachse, Babenzien, Ginzel, Gelbrecht, & Steinberg, 2001), keeping the pH at 4.4. Meanwhile, the two eastern basins have remained unaffected by DOC inputs from the adjacent peat bog, favouring a pH increase up to 6.5. Besides this pH increase, biomass and biological activity across all trophic levels in the eastern basins were higher compared to those in the western basins (Hehmann, Krienitz, & Koschel, 2001). Our aim was to evaluate how long-lasting (nearly 30 years) modification of DOC input to a small lake alters its CH4 and CO2 dynamics. The experimental whole-lake enclosure allowed the manipulation of nonartificial DOC inputs for almost 30 years, which provided a unique opportunity to assess the effect of DOC reduction on carbon greenhouse gas emission in lakes. Independent from intersystem variations in climatic or land-use conditions, this work closely examined whether reduced DOC inputs could be a means for greenhouse gas mitigation in lakes. 2 | METHODS 2.1 | Study site and sampling strategy Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle is a small naturally acidic bog lake, located in a forested area in the Mecklenburg-Brandenburg Lake District in north-eastern Germany at an altitude of 59 m a.s.l. and about 100 km north of Germany's capital Berlin. The landscape, consisting of end moraine, outwash plain and glacial spillways, formed during the Weichsel glacial period (Burkert, Ginzel, Babenzien, & Koschel, 2004). At present, water supplies are provided by ground water and precipitation (Casper & Koschel, 1995). Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle was divided by plastic curtains in 1986 into two basins (east and west), and into four compartments by a second east–west separation in 1990. Initially, the division was conducted to enable whole-lake experiments in food-web manipulation (Kasprzak, 1993; Koschel, 1995). Over the decades of division, research in Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle has covered several other topics: plankton studies (Glöckner et al., 2000; Hehmann et al., 2001; Macek, Simek, & Bittl, 2001), microorganisms and microbial activity (Grossart et al., 2008; Kanaparthi, Pommerenke, Casper, & Dumont, 2013; Simek et al., 1998), basic limnology and geographical settings (Burkert et al., 2004; Kasprzak, 1993; Koschel, 1995; Richter, 1997; Succow & Jeschke, 1986), and CH4 and CO2 cycle (Casper et al., 2003; Chan, Wolf, Hepperle, & Casper, 2002; Conrad, Claus, & Casper, 2010), among others. The two most contrasting basins, namely south-west basin (SW) (characterised by a low pH of 4.4 and DOC of 37.3 mg/L) and the north-east basin (NE) (with a pH of 6.5 and DOC of 16.4 mg/L), were selected for this study (Figure 1). The main limnological characteristics of the original lake, NE and SW basins are summarised in Table 1. The catchment areas draining the eastern basins provided mainly inflow, while the catchment area adjacent to the western basins was only outflow (Figure 1). Generally, Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle is stratified during the summer stagnation period, and anoxic hypolimnia are usually found in all basins from May to September or October (Casper et al., 2003). Both basins were sampled monthly over 1 year from August 2014 to July 2015. Water samples for these analyses were collected in September 2014, January 2015 and June 2015. Sulphate was analysed using ion chromatography (electrical conductivity detector; Dionex Corp., Sunnyvale CA, USA), NO3– and SRP were analysed spectrophotometrically by flow injection analysis (FIAstar 5000, Foss Analytical, Hilleroed, Denmark), and DOC was measured using a total carbon analyser (Shimadzu TOC-Vcsh, Shimadzu, Kyoto, Japan). 2.3 | Dissolved CH4 and CO2 in the water column Monthly water samples were collected at 0.5-m depth intervals using a 2-L-Limnos sampler to measure dissolved CH4 and CO2 concentrations. We subsampled from the port of the Limnos sampler with a 60-ml syringe and gently transferred the sample into 20-ml headspace vials until the water overflowed (performed in duplicate). We then sealed the vials with silicone/PTFE stoppers and magnetic crimp caps. In the laboratory, a headspace was created by displacing water with He (99.999%; Air Liquide, Düsseldorf, Germany) using a two-way needle system. Approximately 40% of the water was replaced, and volumes of sample and headspace were calculated by weight. (2012) using the NIST database (Linstrom & Mallard, 2014). 2.4 | CH4 and CO2 storage estimation CH4 and CO2 stored in the water column were determined using the vertical profiles of CH4 and CO2 concentrations. For each month, we estimated the total mass of CH4 and CO2 stored in the basins by calculating the gas concentration and water volume of the respective layer. The volume of each layer was determined using a hypsometric curve (Supporting Information Figure S1). Linear regressions of total CH4 and CO2 content in the water columns over time were used to estimate stored/removed CH4 and CO2 through the seasons. Total masses of CH4 and CO2 removed (emitted or consumed) during the turnover were obtained from the difference in amounts of CH4 and CO2 stored in the water column before and after turnover using the slope determined in the regression analysis. 2.5 | Greenhouse gas flux measurement CH4 and CO2 fluxes were measured using the static chamber technique in a recirculation mode coupled to a new-generation ultra-portable greenhouse gas analyser base utilising Off-Axis Integrated Cavity Output Spectroscopy (OA-ICOS, UGGA 30P; Los Gatos Inc., San Jose, CA, USA). The static chambers were aluminium with a truncated pyramid shape and had two gas valves and a floating system (Supporting Information Figure S2). The static chamber open surface was 1 m2 with a headspace of 240 L. The recirculation gas flow rate was 0.783 ± 0.015 L/min (mean ± SD), and 1 Hz of frequency was recorded for both gases. To determine gas flux (quintuplicate measurements taken on 1 day per month), the valves of the static chamber were opened to equilibrate the pressure for approximately 2 min. Then, the static chamber was connected to the gas analyser in recirculation mode (Supporting Information Figure S2) for approximately 3–10 min. CH4 and CO2 fluxes (FCH4 or FCO2, mg m−2 hr−1) were determined from the linear slope of gas concentration against the time of measurement (ΔC/Δt; ppmv/hr). The area covered by the chamber (A) and the volume (V) of its headspace was considered for the flux calculation as follows: \[ F_{\text{CH}_4 \text{ or } \text{CO}_2} = \frac{\Delta C}{\Delta t} \times \frac{V}{A} \] This static chamber method used in this experiment covered the total flux (diffusive and ebullitive); the graphical analysis of the concentration increases over time allowed to distinguish between diffusive or ebullitive fluxes alone or mixed. Moreover, the high resolution (1 Hz) of the gas analyser allowed the observation of bubble events (here only for CH4; CO2 was not detectable in all bubbles trapped). When bubbles were released into the chamber, the CH4 concentration in the gas analyser increased abruptly until the gas was completely mixed inside the chamber headspace (Figure 2). Therefore, when no linear regression trend was observed to determine the flux, we used the initial and end points to determine the sum of diffusive and ebullitive CH4 fluxes, as discussed by Goodrich, Varner, Frolking, Duncan, and Crill (2011), Zhao et al. (2015) and Grasset, Abril, Guillard, Delolme, and Bornette (2016). We acknowledge that our sampling procedure may not accurately measure diel gas emissions, as previous studies have found large variations in diel CH4 and CO2 fluxes (Liu et al., 2016; Natchimuthu, Selvam, & Bastviken, 2014; Natchimuthu et al., 2016). However, as discussed by Wik, Thornton, Bastviken, Uhlbaeck, and Crill (2016), the variation seemed to be smaller than the variability among individual sampling days (for CH4). 2.6 | Data handling and statistical analysis We divided our data analysis according to the season into three main periods: (a) active stratification, from August 2014 to October 2014 and from June 2015 to July 2015; (b) mixing period from December 2014 to May 2015 (which also included the slight spring turnover); and (c) fall turnover event in November 2014. From those seasonal data analysis, we compared CH4 and CO2 dynamics in basins. First, the normality of data distribution was explored using the Shapiro–Wilk test. In all other cases (Figure 2d), flux was considered to be zero (\( R^2 < 0.7 \)). Meanwhile, CH\(_4\) fluxes with evidence of ebullition (steep increase in concentration over a long period of time) were analysed by removing data peaks or by dividing the initial and final values from each measurement by the time of the measurement (Figure 2b,c) because there is no established way to use a linear regression method to estimate gas flux in such ebullition events. 3 | RESULTS 3.1 | Temporal variation in T, O\(_2\) and pH Temporal differences among T, O\(_2\) and pH profiles between the NE and SW basins (Figure 3; Supporting Information Figure S3) were observed. Thermal stratification was found in both basins until early November 2014 and from May 2015 to the end of the study period in July 2015. In between these periods, the basins exhibited slight inverse stratification (Figure 3; Supporting Information Figure S3). Thin ice covers (ca. 3 cm thick) were formed over both basins in February 2015, and small ice patches were present during the sampling periods in March 2015 in the SW basin. Turnover events occurred in late fall and early spring (Figure 3; Supporting Information Figure S3). For further analysis, we focused on active stratification, mixing and fall turnover periods. The highest and lowest water temperatures were found in August 2014 (NE: 24°C; SW: 21°C) and January 2015 (NE: 3°C; SW: 2°C), respectively. During the summer of 2015, the weather was slightly colder than that of the previous year, with a difference in the maximum average air temperature of 5°C registered in July 2014 (27.9 ± 6.6°C, mean ± SD) compared to July 2015 (22.9 ± 4.8°C, mean ± SD; Local Stechlin Germany National Weather Service, DWD, www.dwd.de). Parts of the water layers turned anoxic during stratification periods in both basins, and during February 2015 and March 2015, only the SW basin exhibited an anoxic water zone (Supporting Information Figure S3). In 2015, the water column of the SW basin was mixed later than the NE basin. This disparity in water column dynamics was consistent with the O\(_2\) profiles from May 2015, when in the NE basin the hypolimnetic water was anoxic up to 3 m depth, while in the SW basin, a small anoxic layer of only a few centimetres depth was present (Supporting Information Figure S3). Finally, the most pronounced differences were in pH values between the basins, with higher values in the NE basin (pH 5.0–6.5) than in the SW basin (pH 3.9–5.1) throughout the year (Supporting Information Figure S3). 3.2 | Seasonal dissolved CH\(_4\) and CO\(_2\) concentrations Vertical concentration profiles of dissolved CH\(_4\) and CO\(_2\) in the water column were determined in both basins over the whole year (Figure 4). During the first and second stratification period, the mean dissolved CH\(_4\) concentration across both basins was 0.76 ± 1.68 mg CH\(_4\)/L (mean ± \( SD_y \), pooled basins average), while during the mixing period this value dropped to 0.001 ± 0.007 mg CH\(_4\)/L (mean ± \( SD_y \), pooled basins average). During the fall turnover, more than 99% of the CH\(_4\) previously stored in the stratification period was rapidly removed at a rate of 91 g C/day (\( R^2 = 0.88; p < 0.018 \)) and 113 g C/day (\( R^2 = 0.88; p < 0.019 \)) from the NE and SW basins, respectively (Figure 5a). After the fall turnover, the concentration of CH\(_4\) in the water column was low (<0.008 mg CH\(_4\)/L; maximum from both basins), with the water column well oxygenated until May 2015 (Supporting Information Figure S3). In under-ice stratification in winter (for approximately 25 days in February 2015), CH\(_4\) concentration in both basins remained low (<0.008 mg CH\(_4\)/L; maximum from both basins) and negligible amounts were stored. After the onset of the 2015, summer stratification, dissolved CH\(_4\) was stored in the water column at a rate of 21 g C/day (\( R^2 = 0.85; p < 0.027 \)) and 16 g C/day (\( R^2 = 0.86; p < 0.023 \)) in the NE and SW basins, respectively (Figure 5). Patterns of dissolved CO\(_2\) concentration in the water column differed from those of dissolved CH\(_4\) (Figure 4). Mean dissolved CO\(_2\) concentrations across both basins were estimated as 5.40 ± 3.73 mg CO\(_2\)/L (mean ± \( SD_y \); pooled basins average) during mixing period, and 11.63 ± 7.66 mg CO\(_2\)/L (mean ± \( SD_y \); pooled basins average) during the two stratification periods. During the fall turnover, CO\(_2\) concentration in the water column increased significantly (FT, \( p < 0.05 \)), with the highest concentration found in deeper water (NE: 18.84 ± 4.23 mg CO\(_2\)/L; SW: 16.77 ± 2.13 mg CO\(_2\)/L; mean ± \( SD_y \)), suggesting a higher supply of CO\(_2\) to the water column from the sediments. Between February 2015 and March 2015, CO\(_2\) concentration increased again in the water column (Figure 4; NE: 7.78 ± 5.54 mg CO\(_2\)/L; SW: 7.22 ± 1.98 mg CO\(_2\)/L; mean ± \( SD_y \)). Following the fall turnover, the additional CO\(_2\) was removed from the water columns of both basins. The next substantial increase in CO\(_2\) occurred in June 2015, which was again removed in July 2015. The loss of CO\(_2\) may have been a result of re-equilibration of the inorganic species, driven by increased photosynthesis and pushing all the water column to increase the pH from June 2015 to July 2015, which featured the highest pH values in both basins (Supporting Information Figure S3). Given the high variability of monthly dissolved CO₂ concentrations, we were unable to determine a yearly pattern. However, dissolved CO₂ in the fall turnover period was removed at a rate of 636 g C/day and 374 g C/day in the NE and SW basins, respectively, calculated from the difference in total mass between November 2014 and December 2014 (Figure 5b). During the spring turnover, CO₂ removal corresponded to 321 and 286 g C/day, calculated from the net difference in total masses between March 2015 and April 2015 in the NE basin and between February 2015 and April 2015 in the SW basin, respectively (Figure 5). 3.3 | CH₄ and CO₂ emissions CH₄ fluxes were highly variable ranging from 0.16 to 156.28 mg m⁻² day⁻¹ (Supporting Information Figure S4, median values). We could not measure CH₄ and CO₂ fluxes during February, because of ice cover. Peak CH₄ emissions occurred during the fall turnover in both basins. Thereafter, CH₄ emissions remained at a low level until the onset of summer stratification when the hypolimnion turned anoxic (Supporting Information Figure S4). These results coincided with dissolved CH₄ concentrations observed in the same season and water temperature; large gas fluxes were observed during periods when high dissolved CH₄ concentrations were found in the water column (Figure 5 and Supporting Information Figure S5). Mean monthly CH₄ emissions (including diffusion and ebullition) from the SW basin were 1.2-fold to 45-fold higher than those from the NE basin as a result of more evident ebullition (Supporting Information Figure S4) and higher dissolved CH₄ concentrations in surface waters (Figure 4) during both summer periods. In both basins, CH₄ ebullition was observed together with higher emission rates (Supporting Information Figure S4). For both basins, CH₄ ebullition was two orders of magnitude higher compared to months without evident CH₄ ebullition (FT, \( p < 0.05 \)). Mean monthly CO₂ fluxes were highly variable ranging from 11 to 2,222 mg m⁻² day⁻¹, with monthly differences of up to two orders of magnitude (Supporting Information Figure S4, median values). Similar to the CH₄ emissions pattern, maximum CO₂ emissions occurred during the fall turnover (for both basins). In the NE basin, high emissions were detected during the spring turnover; the emissions were up to eightfold higher than those in the SW basin. Later CO₂ emissions in the NE basin remained low during spring and summer of 2015, but CO₂ emissions increased during the subsequent months in the SW basin.
