In all other cases (Figure 2d), flux was considered to be zero (\( R^2 < 0.7 \)). Meanwhile, CH\(_4\) fluxes with evidence of ebullition (steep increase in concentration over a long period of time) were analysed by removing data peaks or by dividing the initial and final values from each measurement by the time of the measurement (Figure 2b,c) because there is no established way to use a linear regression method to estimate gas flux in such ebullition events. 3 | RESULTS 3.1 | Temporal variation in T, O\(_2\) and pH Temporal differences among T, O\(_2\) and pH profiles between the NE and SW basins (Figure 3; Supporting Information Figure S3) were observed. Thermal stratification was found in both basins until early November 2014 and from May 2015 to the end of the study period in July 2015. In between these periods, the basins exhibited slight inverse stratification (Figure 3; Supporting Information Figure S3). Thin ice covers (ca. 3 cm thick) were formed over both basins in February 2015, and small ice patches were present during the sampling periods in March 2015 in the SW basin. Turnover events occurred in late fall and early spring (Figure 3; Supporting Information Figure S3). For further analysis, we focused on active stratification, mixing and fall turnover periods. The highest and lowest water temperatures were found in August 2014 (NE: 24°C; SW: 21°C) and January 2015 (NE: 3°C; SW: 2°C), respectively. During the summer of 2015, the weather was slightly colder than that of the previous year, with a difference in the maximum average air temperature of 5°C registered in July 2014 (27.9 ± 6.6°C, mean ± SD) compared to July 2015 (22.9 ± 4.8°C, mean ± SD; Local Stechlin Germany National Weather Service, DWD, www.dwd.de). Parts of the water layers turned anoxic during stratification periods in both basins, and during February 2015 and March 2015, only the SW basin exhibited an anoxic water zone (Supporting Information Figure S3). In 2015, the water column of the SW basin was mixed later than the NE basin. This disparity in water column dynamics was consistent with the O\(_2\) profiles from May 2015, when in the NE basin the hypolimnetic water was anoxic up to 3 m depth, while in the SW basin, a small anoxic layer of only a few centimetres depth was present (Supporting Information Figure S3). Finally, the most pronounced differences were in pH values between the basins, with higher values in the NE basin (pH 5.0–6.5) than in the SW basin (pH 3.9–5.1) throughout the year (Supporting Information Figure S3). 3.2 | Seasonal dissolved CH\(_4\) and CO\(_2\) concentrations Vertical concentration profiles of dissolved CH\(_4\) and CO\(_2\) in the water column were determined in both basins over the whole year (Figure 4). During the first and second stratification period, the mean dissolved CH\(_4\) concentration across both basins was 0.76 ± 1.68 mg CH\(_4\)/L (mean ± \( SD_y \), pooled basins average), while during the mixing period this value dropped to 0.001 ± 0.007 mg CH\(_4\)/L (mean ± \( SD_y \), pooled basins average). During the fall turnover, more than 99% of the CH\(_4\) previously stored in the stratification period was rapidly removed at a rate of 91 g C/day (\( R^2 = 0.88; p < 0.018 \)) and 113 g C/day (\( R^2 = 0.88; p < 0.019 \)) from the NE and SW basins, respectively (Figure 5a). After the fall turnover, the concentration of CH\(_4\) in the water column was low (<0.008 mg CH\(_4\)/L; maximum from both basins), with the water column well oxygenated until May 2015 (Supporting Information Figure S3). In under-ice stratification in winter (for approximately 25 days in February 2015), CH\(_4\) concentration in both basins remained low (<0.008 mg CH\(_4\)/L; maximum from both basins) and negligible amounts were stored. After the onset of the 2015, summer stratification, dissolved CH\(_4\) was stored in the water column at a rate of 21 g C/day (\( R^2 = 0.85; p < 0.027 \)) and 16 g C/day (\( R^2 = 0.86; p < 0.023 \)) in the NE and SW basins, respectively (Figure 5). Patterns of dissolved CO\(_2\) concentration in the water column differed from those of dissolved CH\(_4\) (Figure 4). Mean dissolved CO\(_2\) concentrations across both basins were estimated as 5.40 ± 3.73 mg CO\(_2\)/L (mean ± \( SD_y \); pooled basins average) during mixing period, and 11.63 ± 7.66 mg CO\(_2\)/L (mean ± \( SD_y \); pooled basins average) during the two stratification periods. During the fall turnover, CO\(_2\) concentration in the water column increased significantly (FT, \( p < 0.05 \)), with the highest concentration found in deeper water (NE: 18.84 ± 4.23 mg CO\(_2\)/L; SW: 16.77 ± 2.13 mg CO\(_2\)/L; mean ± \( SD_y \)), suggesting a higher supply of CO\(_2\) to the water column from the sediments. Between February 2015 and March 2015, CO\(_2\) concentration increased again in the water column (Figure 4; NE: 7.78 ± 5.54 mg CO\(_2\)/L; SW: 7.22 ± 1.98 mg CO\(_2\)/L; mean ± \( SD_y \)). Following the fall turnover, the additional CO\(_2\) was removed from the water columns of both basins. The next substantial increase in CO\(_2\) occurred in June 2015, which was again removed in July 2015. The loss of CO\(_2\) may have been a result of re-equilibration of the inorganic species, driven by increased photosynthesis and pushing all the water column to increase the pH from June 2015 to July 2015, which featured the highest pH values in both basins (Supporting Information Figure S3). Given the high variability of monthly dissolved CO₂ concentrations, we were unable to determine a yearly pattern. However, dissolved CO₂ in the fall turnover period was removed at a rate of 636 g C/day and 374 g C/day in the NE and SW basins, respectively, calculated from the difference in total mass between November 2014 and December 2014 (Figure 5b). During the spring turnover, CO₂ removal corresponded to 321 and 286 g C/day, calculated from the net difference in total masses between March 2015 and April 2015 in the NE basin and between February 2015 and April 2015 in the SW basin, respectively (Figure 5). 3.3 | CH₄ and CO₂ emissions CH₄ fluxes were highly variable ranging from 0.16 to 156.28 mg m⁻² day⁻¹ (Supporting Information Figure S4, median values). We could not measure CH₄ and CO₂ fluxes during February, because of ice cover. Peak CH₄ emissions occurred during the fall turnover in both basins. Thereafter, CH₄ emissions remained at a low level until the onset of summer stratification when the hypolimnion turned anoxic (Supporting Information Figure S4). These results coincided with dissolved CH₄ concentrations observed in the same season and water temperature; large gas fluxes were observed during periods when high dissolved CH₄ concentrations were found in the water column (Figure 5 and Supporting Information Figure S5). Mean monthly CH₄ emissions (including diffusion and ebullition) from the SW basin were 1.2-fold to 45-fold higher than those from the NE basin as a result of more evident ebullition (Supporting Information Figure S4) and higher dissolved CH₄ concentrations in surface waters (Figure 4) during both summer periods. In both basins, CH₄ ebullition was observed together with higher emission rates (Supporting Information Figure S4). For both basins, CH₄ ebullition was two orders of magnitude higher compared to months without evident CH₄ ebullition (FT, \( p < 0.05 \)). Mean monthly CO₂ fluxes were highly variable ranging from 11 to 2,222 mg m⁻² day⁻¹, with monthly differences of up to two orders of magnitude (Supporting Information Figure S4, median values). Similar to the CH₄ emissions pattern, maximum CO₂ emissions occurred during the fall turnover (for both basins). In the NE basin, high emissions were detected during the spring turnover; the emissions were up to eightfold higher than those in the SW basin. Later CO₂ emissions in the NE basin remained low during spring and summer of 2015, but CO₂ emissions increased during the subsequent months in the SW basin. The basins exhibit remarkable changes in emissions throughout the year. Since the installation of the separation curtains, stable stratification during summers and two turnover events per year have been registered (Casper et al., 2003; Hehmann et al., 2001). Fall turnover is the major source of CH₄ and CO₂ emissions to the atmosphere in both basins. Similar tendencies were described in small, sheltered boreal humic lakes in southern Finland and in a small mesotrophic dimictic lake in southern Germany; in both lakes, major CH₄ emissions were observed during the fall turnover, and no significant amounts of CH₄ were emitted during the spring turnover (Encinas Fernández, Peeters, & Hofmann, 2014; Kankaala, Huotari, Peltomaa, Saloranta, & Ojala, 2006; Kankaala et al., 2007; López Bellido et al., 2013). Studies in Finnish lakes attributed these low emissions during the spring turnover to short or incomplete mixing of water masses, which in turn is a result of the high absorption of solar radiation by the coloured fraction of DOC in the first few metres of water (Kankaala et al., 2007). However, in our case the spring turnover was complete, as FIGURE 5 Temporal variation in total carbon mass of (a) CH4 (kg C) and (b) CO2 (kg C) in the NE basin (blue) and SW basin (orange) from August 2014 to July 2015. Connected dots indicate the carbon emitted as CH4 and CO2 across the total area of each basin in each month (Table 1) estimated from gas fluxes and basin area (Supporting Information Figure S4); error bars indicate the propagated error from gas flux measurements (Supporting Information Figure S4). Grey line represents mean temperature in the water column (pooled basins average). Coloured bars indicate the carbon content of CH4 and CO2 in the water column. Error bars indicate the propagated error from the measurements of total concentration. Dashed lines indicate fall and spring turnover events [Colour figure can be viewed at wileyonlinelibrary.com] shown by T profiles and by the considerable CO2 emissions from the NE basin; therefore, our data suggest that no significant amounts of CH4 were stored in the water column during the winter inverse stratification due to temperature-limited methanogenesis (Schulz et al., 1997), possible methane oxidation in the water column (Martinez-Cruz, Sepulveda-Jauregui, Walter Anthony, & Thalasso, 2015; Ricao Canelhas, Denfeld, Weyhenmeyer, Bastviken, & Bertilsson, 2016), and the relatively short ice-covered period compared with that of high northern lakes (Sepulveda-Jauregui, Anthony, Martinez-Cruz, Greene, & Thalasso, 2015; Vonk et al., 2015). Encinas Fernández et al. (2014) attributed these low CH4 emissions during the spring turnover to continuous oxic conditions in the hypolimnia following the fall turnover, similar to the results of this study. Additionally, the low spring emissions could be the result of lower temperatures and reduced supply of bio-labile DOC mitigating the methanogenic activity during the short winter stratification. Overall, more systematic studies in different types of lakes are required to improve the temporal CH4 and CO2 emission estimations (Natchimuthu, Wallin, Klemetsson, & Bastviken, 2017; Natchimuthu et al., 2016). DOC availability can trigger CH4 emission through its influence on methanogenesis. A lower DOC supply, as in the NE basin, may therefore be reflected in an attenuation of the two typical effects of DOC in lake ecosystems: (a) DOC is used by the aerobic, heterotrophic microbiome, which rapidly consume the O2 in the water column and surficial sediments, developing anoxic conditions for anaerobic carbon degradation (Adler, Eckert, & Sivan, 2011; Borrel et al., 2011), and (b) DOC enhances anaerobic respiration, including methanogenesis (Casper, 1992b; Heslop et al., 2015; Walter Anthony, Anthony, Grosse, & Chanton, 2012; Walter Anthony et al., 2016). Anoxic hypolimnia may further lead to major CH4 emissions as a result of the decomposition of more labile sources of DOC by syntrophic methanogenesis processes (i.e., by primary decomposers, fermenters and methanogens), which are restricted when O2 is present close to sediments (Chen et al., 2017). In addition, methanogenesis is strongly dependent on temperature, showing a more pronounced change than aerobic CH4 oxidation under temperature variations (Nguyen, Crill, & Bastviken, 2010; Sepulveda-Jauregui et al., 2018; Yvon-Durocher et al., 2014). Warmer temperatures may then promote the production of CH4 in sediments, leading to oversaturation in pore water and thus forcing ebullition. While CH4 ebullition was evident in most of the warm months (excluding June 2015 and July 2015 in the NE basin), it was not detected during the cold months. However, we acknowledge that our ebullition evidence is a gross observation, as the pathway has been reported in several lakes in cold months (Walter, Zimov, Chanton, Verbyla, & Chapin, 2006; Wik, Crill, Bastviken, Danielsson, & Norbäck, 2011). In our study, we exclusively sampled on 1 day each month, which is not sufficient to accurately estimate this emission pathway. In the future, higher temporal resolution of sampling (by diurnal sampling, sampling several days per month and spatial analysis) is required to reduce uncertainties in CH₄ ebullition from aquatic ecosystems, as previously recommended by Wik, Thornton, et al. (2016). However, other methods used in the literature contain large uncertainties; DelSontro et al. (2011) indicated that the acoustic technology has large coefficients of variation that exceed 100%, while the classic randomised bubble trap method is highly biased and underestimates results (Walter Anthony & Anthony, 2013). Newer gas analysers and the combination with established techniques may help to determine CH₄ diffusion and ebullition in freshwater ecosystems. Zhao et al. (2015) suggested such a method as a tool for assessing diffusion and ebullition, while Grasset et al. (2016) was one of the first studies to include ebullition data from these newer gas analysers. In the context of CO₂, Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle can be classified as an acidic lake, in which CO₂ is the major inorganic carbon species (Cole & Prairie, 2009) and where the availability of allochthonous and autochthonous inorganic carbon is in some ecosystems a very important driver of CO₂ emissions to the atmosphere (Tank et al., 2018; Tranvik et al., 2009; Weyhenmeyer et al., 2015). During turnover events, with the exception of spring in the SW basin, peaks of CO₂ fluxes were detected jointly with high CO₂ stored in the water column. The surplus CO₂ for both basins likely did not completely originate from surficial (0–20 cm, data not shown) sediments (1.0 ± 0.5 g C/m², mean ± SD_y, pooled basins average), as stored quantities were one order of magnitude lower than the mass of CO₂ emitted (13.0 ± 4.6 g C/m², mean ± SD_y, pooled basins average) and dissolved in the water column (9.3 ± 4.3 g C/m², mean ± SD_y, pooled basins average). This suggests inputs of CO₂ directly from external sources of inorganic carbon and indirectly from mineralisation of internal or external DOC (Brothers et al., 2014; Engel et al., 2018; Maberly et al., 2013; Tank et al., 2018; Tranvik et al., 2009; Weyhenmeyer et al., 2015). The reduction in DOC in the NE basin potentially accounted for the 41% reduction in total annual CO₂ emissions. Moreover, CH₄ emissions decreased to a similar extent (53%), but cannot, as previously discussed, be adequately explained by the reduced availability of DOC to the pelagic community. Ducharme-Riel, Vachon, Del Giorgio, and Prairie (2015) remarked on the complexity of lake dynamics since interaction between physical and biological factors regulates CO₂ dynamics. Sources of CO₂ and contributions by different sources need to be elucidated (Drake et al., 2018; Engel et al., 2018; Tank et al., 2018). It is important to note that we could not observe any CO₂ ebullition with the new gas analyser used in this study, but we acknowledge that our device was not sensitive enough to confirm CO₂ in bubbles for several reasons: (a) CO₂ is highly soluble in water, and therefore, bubbles trapped in sediments might have had low CO₂ concentration; (b) the remaining CO₂ concentration in gas bubbles could have been re-dissolved through the water column before bubbles were emitted to the atmosphere (McGinnis et al., 2011); (c) there was a high CO₂ concentration inside the chamber (atmospheric concentration, ca. 380 ppm) at the initial time of sampling (to observe CO₂ bubbles it would be necessary to exceed this threshold). Similarly, the analyses of Casper et al. (2000) and Sepulveda-Jauregui et al. (2015) determined that only 1% of CO₂ was emitted by ebullition and 99% by diffusion in small shallow lakes. Together, our results may help to identify the environmental factors that regulate carbon emissions in small lakes. In freshwater systems, temperature controls the biological activity across food webs, the length of stratification periods and gas solubility. High temperatures amplified CH₄ emissions (Sepulveda-Jauregui et al., 2018), which led to markedly higher amounts of CH₄ stored and emitted from the basins in the hotter summer of 2014 with a clear correlation between CH₄ emissions and temperature. Similar responses to regional temperature have been shown in ponds, in small shallow, and medium-sized lakes (Bartosiewicz, Laurion, & Macintyre, 2015; Bartosiewicz et al., 2016; Encinas Fernández et al., 2014; Liikanen, Huttunen, Valli, & Martikainen, 2002; Miettinen et al., 2015; Natchimuthu et al., 2014; Room et al., 2014) and in enclosure experiments (Audet et al., 2017; Yvon-Durocher et al., 2017), suggesting that in predicted warming scenarios, an increase in carbon greenhouse gas emissions can be expected in lake ecosystems regardless of DOC inputs and their biogeochemical effects in the water column (e.g., in stratification, temperature regimes, pH, microbial metabolism and CO₂ dynamics). Despite the long-term division of Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle that created two very different stable ecosystems with regard to carbon supply, the CH₄ and to some extent CO₂, emissions to the atmosphere were mainly determined by DOC-independent environmental conditions, as suggested by direct correlations between gas flux and temperature and between pH and dissolved gases. However, pH is an indirect factor associated with DOC correlation with dissolved gas concentrations. Therefore, the correlation between pH and dissolved CH₄ and CO₂ in the SW basin implied that DOC can play an important role in greenhouse gas emissions (Drake et al., 2018). In the case of CH₄, previous studies on methanogenesis in sediments of this acidic bog lake showed that the pathways to form CH₄ were similar to those in pH-neutral lakes (Conrad et al., 2010). Therefore, the reduction in DOC inputs to aquatic ecosystems would benefit several ecological and environmental issues, but in the context of CH₄ and CO₂ emission to the atmosphere from small lakes, the lake size and warming are probably the key factors for determining CH₄ and CO₂ emissions (Holgerson & Raymond, 2016; Kankaala, Huotari, Tulonen, & Ojala, 2013; Room et al., 2014; Sepulveda-Jauregui et al., 2018; Yvon-Durocher et al., 2017). 4.2 | O₂ dynamics governing carbon greenhouse gas storage and emission Higher CH₄ emission periods coincided with the presence of extensive anoxic hypolimnia (in summer and fall). In contrast, low CH₄ emission periods were observed when the water column was oxygenated (in winter and early spring). We suggest that the presence of O₂ in the surficial sediment layers led to a decrease in methanogenic activity by inhibition because it is a strictly anaerobic process. Also, aerobic CH₄ oxidation likely occurred in the superficial sediment layers, further reducing the amount of CH₄ released to the water column. The reciprocal gradient between dissolved O₂ and CH₄ present during the stratification period suggested that CH₄ oxidation in the water column may have regulated diffusive CH₄ emission in stratification periods, but had little effect during mixing periods, as previously reported for lakes (Bartosiewicz et al., 2016; Casper et al., 2005; Encinas Fernández et al., 2014; Kankaala et al., 2006; Martinez-Cruz et al., 2015; Ricao Canelhas et al., 2016; Utsumi et al., 1998). The correlation analyses of dissolved gases (CH₄, CO₂ and O₂) showed that CH₄ and CO₂ are stored in anoxic layers and that they are indicators of high net heterotrophy (Borges et al., 2015; Sepulveda-Jauregui et al., 2015). The weaker correlation between CO₂ and O₂ (when compared to CH₄ and O₂) was consistent with previous reports of dissolved CO₂ patterns in acidic lakes (e.g., Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle) that are being strongly influenced by catchments rich in organic and inorganic carbon (Holgerson & Raymond, 2016; Tranvik et al., 2009; Weyhenmeyer et al., 2015). However, the reciprocal correlation between dissolved O₂ and CH₄ or CO₂ suggests that dissolved O₂ in the water column is an important indicator of CH₄ and CO₂ storage. Total carbon storage (calculated from dissolved CH₄ and CO₂ concentrations) followed dissolved O₂ changes over the seasons (Figure 7), with higher CH₄ and CO₂ emissions occurring when anoxic conditions predominated (maximum of 71 ± 13%, mean ± SD_y, pooled basins average). This may have been the result of higher microbial activity in the summer compared to colder periods of mixing; the reduction in the aerobic zone of the water column may have led to a decrease in aerobic methane oxidation activity. For more than 2 months during the winter, the water column was well oxygenated in both basins, and when temperature increased in spring, O₂ was quickly consumed in the newly established hypolimnia. Bartosiewicz et al. (2016) and Encinas Fernández et al. (2014) also found dissolved O₂ in the water column to be an indicator of CH₄ and CO₂ dynamics in summer. Moreover, Sabrekov et al. (2017) pointed out that O₂ patterns were among the major factors that controlled the dynamics of CH₄ and CO₂ in Siberian lakes, based on regional model development. Therefore, dissolved O₂ can be used as a tracer of biological activity associated with temperature and stratification changes during the seasons. Interestingly, we did not find any relationship between dissolved CH₄ or CO₂ and T or pH, when data from both basins were grouped. Instead, we found a positive correlation between pH and CO₂ and CH₄ concentrations when solely assessed in the water column of the SW basin. This correlation may indicate a higher microbial activity in all trophic levels (from primary production to heterotrophy) and not an intrinsic effect of recalcitrant DOC in the sediments (indicated by the low pH in the SW basin) on CH₄ and CO₂. Moreover, only the western basins of Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle receive inflow from an adjacent peat bog (Burkert et al., 2004; Koschel, 1995), which may supply CH₄ and CO₂ and explain the positive correlation between pH and both gases. Such external sources have been suggested as an important source of both gases for freshwater ecosystems (Garcia-Tigreros Kodovska et al., 2016; Tank et al., 2018; Weyhenmeyer et al., 2015). FIGURE 7 Per cent of carbon stored (sum of CH₄–C and CO₂–C) in the anoxic (grey) and oxic (white) water layers in the water column during the time of the study in both basins of Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle beginning in August 2014 and ending in July 2015 5 | CONCLUDING REMARKS In the artificially divided Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle, the reduction in DOC inputs over 30 years to one of the studied basins was not the factor dominating CH4 and CO2 dynamics. Instead, seasonal changes in ambient temperature, O2 and stratification periods determined the relative contribution of cumulative carbon greenhouse gas emissions. Despite significant differences in pH and DOC developed between the two basins, CH4 and CO2 emissions were in the same order of magnitude over the year. The latter result shows the knowledge gap regarding the mineralisation processes of DOC in small acidic lakes. Therefore, the effect of DOC inputs to these types of lakes, including on CH4 and CO2 emissions, is still unclear. Further studies in various types of lakes are needed in order to better identify the effects of DOC on small and shallow lakes, which are a key component in global carbon greenhouse gas emissions. title: bacterial processes and biogeochemical changes in the water body of kettle holes - mainly driven by autochthonous organic matter?
author: attermeyer; katrin; grossart; hans-peter; flury; sabine; premke; katrin
context:
Bacterial processes and biogeochemical changes in the water body of kettle holes - mainly driven by autochthonous organic matter? Katrin Attermeyer1,2 · Hans-Peter Grossart3,4 · Sabine Flury1,5 · Katrin Premke1,6 Received: 15 February 2016 / Accepted: 27 February 2017 / Published online: 7 April 2017 © Springer International Publishing 2017 Abstract Kettle holes are small inland waters formed from glacially-created depressions often situated in agricultural landscapes. Due to their high perimeter-to-area ratio facilitating a high aquatic-terrestrial coupling, kettle holes can accumulate high concentrations of organic carbon and nutrients, fueling microbial activities and turnover rates. Thus, they represent hotspots of carbon turnover in the landscape, but their bacterial activities and controlling factors have not been well investigated. Therefore, we aimed to assess the relative importance of various environmental factors on bacterial and biogeochemical processes in the water column of kettle holes and to disentangle their variations. In the water body of ten kettle holes in north-eastern Germany, we measured several physico-chemical and biological parameters such as carbon quantity and quality, as well as bacterial protein production (BP) and community respiration (CR) in spring, early summer and autumn 2014. Particulate organic matter served as an indicator of autochthonous production and represented an important parameter to explain variations in BP and CR. This notion is supported by qualitative absorbance indices of dissolved molecules in water samples and C:N ratios of the sediments, which demonstrate high fractions of autochthonous organic matter (OM) in the studied kettle holes. In contrast, dissolved chemical parameters were less important for bacterial activities although they revealed strong differences throughout the growing season. Pelagic bacterial activities and dynamics might thus be regulated by autochthonous OM in kettle holes implying a control of important biogeochemical processes by internal primary production rather than facilitated exchange with the terrestrial surrounding due to a high perimeter-to-area ratio. Keywords Bacterial production · Carbon turnover · Growth efficiency · Ponds · Respiration · DOC quality · LC-OCD Introduction Small depressional wetlands, referred to here as kettle holes, are abundant elements in the hummocky, post-glacial landscape in Northern Europe, Northern America, and Siberia. They evolved from topographic depressions formed during the ice retreat after the Pleistocene about 10,000–12,000 years ago by delayed melting of remnant ice blocks. The depression size ranges from 0.0001 to 0.03 km² and they can be either permanently filled with water, completely dry or experience wet and dry cycles of different time periods. In north-eastern Germany, kettle holes are widely distributed and hence important landscape components. With a density of up to 4,000 per km\(^2\) they are mainly situated in agricultural landscapes (Kalettka et al. 2001; Lischeid and Kalettka 2012). Kettle hole types have been classified according to different hydro-geomorphic characteristics reflecting their high heterogeneity (Kalettka and Rudat 2006). They differ widely with respect to groundwater inflow, surface runoff, internal carbon (C) assimilation and mineralization, macrophyte abundance, and land-use of the respective catchments. As a result, kettle holes fulfill important hydrological and ecological functions affecting the water balance of the surrounding landscape (Hayashi et al. 2003; Gerke et al. 2010). Generally, they are very sensitive to changing hydrological conditions and undergo pronounced wet-dry cycles. Today, small aquatic systems such as kettle holes are widely recognized as hotspots of C turnover in the landscape (Waiser and Robarts 2004; Cole et al. 2007; Tranvik et al. 2009; Aufdenkampe et al. 2011; Premke et al. 2016). Initial studies of C cycling in small ponds or impoundments show that these systems accumulate high biomasses and can constitute a major and currently underestimated C sink (Cole et al. 1988; Downing et al. 2008). Other studies, however, show that kettle holes also can be significant sources of important greenhouse gases such as N\(_2\)O, CH\(_4\) and CO\(_2\), which is further exacerbated by eutrophication (Merbach et al. 2002). One study conducted in two wetlands in the prairie region of the North American Great Plains, points towards an important role of bacteria in the metabolism of these systems (Waiser and Robarts 2004). Yet, most of the research on microbial C cycling has been conducted in small, shallow lakes and artificial, small standing inland waters with much less known about the microbiology and biogeochemistry of kettle holes. Kettle holes generally contain high concentrations of C and nutrients such as nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) (e.g. Lischeid and Kalettka 2012). On the one hand, high N and P concentrations can facilitate high primary production rates (Schindler 1978), and nutrient additions in combination with food web manipulations have been shown to turn net-heterotrophic lakes into net-autotrophic systems (Cole et al. 2000). On the other hand, it is also known that the net metabolic balance in lakes varies continuously along a gradient of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) concentration: as DOC increases, primary production may decrease and lake metabolism becomes progressively more heterotrophic (Tranvik 1988; Prairie et al. 2002; Jansson et al. 2007). This pattern is driven mainly by a change in the ratio of primary production to total respiration supported by an increase in allochthonous DOC. This suggests that allochthonous DOC plays an important regulatory role in lake metabolism through its influence on microbial metabolism (Jansson et al. 2000). In this study, we investigated ten kettle holes in the north-eastern part of Germany representing a gradient in DOC concentrations and a broad diversity of kettle hole types. We aimed to assess the relative importance of allochthonous vs. autochthonous C for bacterial and biogeochemical processes in the water body. We hypothesized that allochthonous DOC is the major driver for bacterial activities in the water body of kettle holes and is more important than autochthonous C. In spring, early summer and autumn 2014, we measured various physico-chemical parameters such as nutrients (N and P), C quantity and quality (Liquid Chromatography with Organic Carbon Detection, absorbance), and bacterial protein production and community respiration in the water body of the kettle holes to evaluate the factors driving bacterial activities in kettle hole water bodies. Methods Study site All kettle holes are located in the Quillow catchment in the temperate north-eastern part of Germany, approximately 80 km north-east of Berlin. A detailed description of the area can be found in Kleeberg et al. (2016). Ten kettle holes were selected (Table 1) based on a gradient in DOC concentrations. The 10 kettle holes in this study vary in size from 0.57 to 4.29 \( \times \) 10\(^{-3}\) km\(^2\). All kettle holes exhibited macrophytes, but the dominant vegetation type differed. They were mostly vegetated by *Typha* spp., *Carex* spp., *Phragmites australis* or *Phalaris arundinacea* (Table 1). Despite variation in the dominant vegetation type, eight kettle holes were surrounded by arable land and two by grassland. All kettle holes were permanently flooded during the sampling campaign, except one of the smallest (identification number 3, see Table 1) which dried out in summer. Thus, the dataset was reduced to nine for early summer and autumn. Sampling The kettle holes were sampled three times during the growing season in 2014: in spring (February, 25th and 27th), early summer (June, 24th and 26th), and autumn (October, 28th and 30th). Temperature, pH and oxygen (O\(_2\)) concentrations were determined on site, using electronic probes (DurOx and SenTix for February and June as well as the Multi3410 probe for the October campaign; WTW, Weilheim, Germany). Size, global positioning system (GPS) coordinates, dominant vegetation from Kalettka and Rudat (2006) and dissolved organic carbon (DOC) concentrations from the three samplings in February (Feb), June (Jun) and October (Oct) in the center of each kettle hole with a water sampler (LIM-NOS, Turku, Finland) for chemical analyses as well as for determination of bacterial cell numbers and production. The samples were transported to the laboratory under dark conditions and close to in situ temperatures and processed within 5 h after sampling. One sample per kettle hole was collected based on the assumption that it is representative for the entire kettle hole (Mukhopadhyay et al. 2004). Additionally, three polypropylene incubation cores length 30 cm; width 5.2 cm; volume 0.5 L per kettle hole were filled with water for CR measurements. Chemical analysis Total organic carbon (TOC), total dissolved organic carbon (DOC), total dissolved nitrogen (TDN; all in mgL−1), and total dissolved phosphorus (TDP; in μgL−1) were analyzed according to standard chemical procedures (Strickland and Parsons 1968; Wetzel and Likens 1991). The dissolved fraction was analyzed after filtering the sample through a 0.2 μm cellulose acetate filter (Whatman, Dassel, Germany) pre-rinsed with 500 mL double distilled water to avoid contamination of the samples. Concentrations of organic C were determined with a C analyzer (Shimadzu, 3 TOC-V CPH, Duisburg, Germany) as non-purgeable C after acidification with 2 mol L−1 HCl. The carbon dioxide generated by catalytic high-temperature oxidation (850 °C) was measured online by infrared absorption. POC was then calculated from TOC minus DOC as all TOC measurements were substantially higher than DOC. Samples for TDP were incubated with 5% (w/v) K2S2O8 for 30 min at 134 °C in a steam autoclave prior to analysis. Phosphorus concentrations were measured photometrically (FIA compact analyzer MLE, Dresden, Germany) using the molybdenum-blue method (Koroleff 1976). Dissolved nitrogen was oxidized with Oxisolv® (Merck, Darmstadt, Germany) at 120 °C for 45 min in an autoclave and measured with a Foss FIAstar 5010 analyzer (Rellingen, Germany). C:N and C:P molar ratios were calculated from DOC vs. TDN and TDP, respectively. Particulate organic matter (POM; in mg L−1) was determined by filtering a known amount of water through a combusted GF/C filter (nominal pore size 1.2 μm; Whatman, Dassel, Germany) and subsequent freeze-drying. The dry weight difference of the empty and ‘sample’ filter per filtered water volume was considered POM. Absorbance measurements for DOC were done on a Hitachi U2900 UV/Vis spectrophotometer using a 1 cm quartz cuvette. Absorbance spectra were measured from 190 to 800 nm at 0.5 nm increments and instrument noise was assessed measuring double distilled water as a blank. To investigate the chromophoric dissolved organic matter properties, optical indices such as the A250:A365 ratio and specific UV absorbance (SUVA) at 254 and 285 nm were determined. The A250:A365 ratio (also called E2:E3 ratio) was calculated using absorption coefficients at the appropriate wavelengths and indicates changes in the relative molecule size of DOM (Peuravuori and Pihlaja 1997). SUVA254 and SUVA285 were calculated by dividing absorbance of 254 and 285 nm (in m−1) by DOC concentration (in mg L−1). SUVA254 is considered a proxy for aromaticity (Weishaar et al. 2003) and SUVA285 a proxy for fulvic acid concentrations in the water (Giancoli Barreto et al. 2003). Furthermore, DOC was characterized by size exclusion chromatography with online C and nitrogen detection (Liquid Chromatography-Organic Carbon Detection–Organic Nitrogen Detection; LC-OCD–OND; Huber et al. 2011). The DOC of the filtered samples passes through a size-exclusion column packed with resin (Toyopearl HW 50S, volume of 11 250×20 mm). Phosphate buffer (0.029 mol L^{-1}, pH 6.5) was used as eluent at a flow rate of 1.1 mL min^{-1}. DOC was detected with infrared (IR) absorbance of CO_2 after ultraviolet (UV) oxidation of DOC at 185 nm in a cylindrical UV thin-film reactor (Graentzel-reactor). DOC can then be summarized in three fractions: high molecular weight substances (HMWS, e.g. polysaccharides), humic or humic-like substances (HS) comprising building blocks, and low molecular weight substances (LMWS) including both low molecular weight acids and low molecular weight neutral substances. Building blocks are a specific fraction that reflect breakdown products of humic substances with a lower molecular weight and follow humic substances in the chromatogram (Huber et al. 2011). The individual fractions and their molecular weights were identified based on fulvic and humic acid standards from the International Humic Substances Society and analyzed with a suitable software program (FIFFIKUS; DOC-Labor Huber, Karlsruhe, Germany). Bacterial cell number and production Total bacterial cell number was determined by epifluorescence microscopy after staining with SYBR Gold (Invitrogen, Darmstadt, Germany; Shibata et al. 2006). Glutaraldehyde fixed samples (0.9% final concentration) were filtered onto a 0.2 µm polycarbonate filter (Whatman, Dassel, Germany) and embedded in Citifluor (CITIFLUOR AF1, Science Services, München, Germany) with a SYBR Gold staining solution diluted to 1:1000 (Molecular Probes, Eugene, Oregon, USA). For each filter, 500–1000 bacterial cells were counted with an epifluorescence microscope at 1000× magnification (Zeiss, Axio Imager. Z1, Jena, Germany). Bacterial protein production (BP) was determined via incorporation of L-^{14}C-leucine into the protein fraction using the protocol of Simon and Azam (1989). 5 mL of the water were incubated with L-^{14}C-leucine (Hartmann Analytic, Braunschweig, Germany, specific activity 306 mCi mmol^{-1}) at a final concentration of 120 nmol L^{-1}. Three replicates and one blank were measured for each kettle hole. A detailed description of the procedure is given in Attermeyer et al. (2013). Net disintegrations per minute were converted to pmol leucine L^{-1} d^{-1} according to Simon and Azam (1989), and an isotope dilution factor of 2 was applied (Kirchman 1993). BP for water samples is given as µg C L^{-1} d^{-1}. Community respiration Community respiration (CR) was determined by measuring O_2 depletion over time with a needle-type O_2 microsensor (Optode, PreSens, Regensburg, Germany) after mixing the water column. Briefly, the O_2 sensor was inserted through a septum in the gastight container and O_2 depletion was measured at regular intervals (every 6–12 h) over time. The total incubation time was generally 24 h at in situ temperatures in the dark. If initial O_2 concentrations were close to suboxic conditions (e.g. in June, ~2 mg L^{-1}), the incubation time was reduced to avoid anoxic conditions which are known to slow down bacterial activities. The amount of consumed O_2 was converted to µg C L^{-1} d^{-1} by using a conversion factor of 1 (Berggren et al. 2012). For details see Attermeyer et al. (2013). We assumed that the majority of O_2 consumption was caused by bacterial respiration as they have been shown to make up to more than 90% of the biomass of the pelagic community (Daniel et al. 2005). Bacterial growth efficiency (BGE) describing the proportion of C entering the bacterial pool that is incorporated into biomass was thus calculated based on BP and CR (BGE=BP/(BP+CR)). As respiration of non-bacteria microorganisms is included, we recognize a slight underestimation of real growth efficiencies due to a higher total community respiration. Sediment analysis Two kettle holes (number 5 and 10 in Table 1) were additionally sampled on a monthly basis from February 2013 to March 2014 for analysis of sedimentary C:N ratios and stable C isotope ratios (δ^{13}C) of organic matter (Meyers 1994). For the analysis, four sediment cores (6 cm diameter) per kettle hole were retrieved using a push corer (UWITEC, Austria). The dried and homogenized sediments were analyzed for C and N via a Vario EL (Elementar Analysesysteme, Germany) according to the company’s recommendations (Elementar Application material, AB-C-250101-D-01/AB-C-250101-E-01). Stable C isotope signature (δ^{13}C) was measured on an elemental analyzer (Flash HT, Thermo-Finnigan) connected to a Con-flow IV (Thermo-Scientific) after treating the dried sediment with HCl vapor for 48 h. In-house standards and certified standards (sucrose; IAEA-CH-6 and L-glutamic acid; USGS40) were used for calibration. Isotopic values are expressed in delta notation (in ‰ units), relative to Vienna Pee Dee Belemnite. Precision of analysis was within 0.1‰. Statistics Differences between samplings (in February, June, and October) for all measured variables were tested with the non-parametric Kruskal Wallis test (Kruskal and Wallis 1952) as data were not normally distributed. Single comparisons between February vs. June, February vs. October, and June vs. October were done in post-hoc comparisons after Mann Whitney U with a corrected p after Bonferroni Holm (Mann and Whitney 1947). The univariate statistical analyses were done in IBM SPSS Statistics 22 (IBM Corporation, Armonk, NY, USA). To identify major drivers (independent (X) variables) for BP and CR (dependent (Y) variables) in kettle holes, we used multivariate linear regression by means of partial least squares projections (PLS regression; Eriksson et al. 2001). PLS regression relates two data matrices, X and Y, to each other by a linear multivariate model (Höskuldsson 1988; Wold et al. 2001). This is a robust method that can deal with non-normally distributed data, missing values, co-correlation of X variables and a large dataset of independent (X) variables. To improve the model performance, we confirmed a nearly symmetrical distribution of data (skewness <2) and showed a constant “error variance” (Minimum/Maximum ratio >0.1) as described in Sobek et al. (2007). If the data did not fulfill these conditions they were log- or log(X+1)-transformed. Before running the PLS regression, data were mean-centered and scaled to unit variance. The results of the PLS regression are displayed as loading plots which show the importance of the independent variables in explaining the dependent variable (BP and CR). All environmental variables included in the two models are described in Table 3. Correlations of the variables can be extracted from the spatial distribution in the loading plot: positively correlated when situated close to each other and negatively correlated when distant from each other. The model was evaluated on the basis of the R2Y and Q2 values. R2Y reveals the explained variance of X by Y (goodness of fit) and Q2 the predicted variation of the model. The closer both values, the better and more robust is the model. Furthermore, a permutation test was run to assess how much of the explained variance could be attributed to random chance. Y values were permutated (100 times) and a PLS model was created for each permutated Y variable separately. The difference between the intercept of R2Y and Q2 regressions derived from 100 permutated datasets. The original R2Y and Q2 provided an estimate of the background correlation due to chance for the Y variable. Small background correlations indicated a stable model (Eriksson et al. 2001). PLS regression was performed in Statistica12 (Statsoft, Hamburg, Germany) and model validation was done in SIMCA 14 (Umetrics, Umeå, Sweden). Results Physico-chemical analysis Water temperatures were lowest in February (4.1–5.8 °C), highest in June (14.1–18.8 °C) and intermediate in October (5.4–7.8). Oxygen (O2) concentrations were lowest in early summer when some kettle holes showed suboxic to anoxic conditions (see Supp. 1), but pH exhibited no clear trend with higher or lower values throughout the sampling period (7.9 ± 1; mean ± standard deviation). POM was highest, but also most variable in June ranging from 3.0 to 58.6 mg L−1. DOC concentrations covered a huge range from 9.7 up to 42.3 mg L−1 (Fig. 1c) and varied extensively between different kettle holes and sampling dates. From February to June, DOC increased in almost all kettle holes, on average by 76%. This trend changed in October when DOC dropped back to values more similar to February (Fig. 1c). TDN increased during the growing season from February to October and ranged between 0.7 and 7.5 mg L−1 across all sampling dates and kettle holes (Fig. 1d). The trend differed for TDP which showed generally higher values in June as compared to October (range from 18 to 1674 µg L−1 over all sampling dates and kettle holes; Fig. 1e). The highest variations of TDP in all kettle holes occurred in June when the highest value was measured. All measured nutrients (DOC, TDN, and TDP) were significantly different between the three sampling dates (Table 4) indicating a generally high temporal variability in kettle hole nutrient dynamics. The DOC quality parameters were significantly different at the three sampling dates. The separate models were more robust than a combined model and separation allowed us to improve conclusions explaining variables for BP and CR. The BP model extracted one significant component from the data matrix that explained 37% of the variance in BP. The loadings plot showed that POC and POM were the two most important variables for explaining the observed variance in BP (Fig. 3a). Both, POC and POM, positively correlated with BP. Other physico-chemical parameters including two qualitative parameters (O2, temperature, TDP, C:P and A250:A365) were also highly influential. Model predictability and the permutation test revealed that the model is valid (Q2 = 0.12; background correlation in R2Y = 0.21). The CR model extracted two significant components that explained together 64% of the variance in CR (Fig. 3b). The loadings plot also found POC and POM as highly influential factors together with cell numbers which was confirmed by high VIP numbers. Other factors that were important for BP were only moderately influential for CR. Model predictability was lower for the CR model (cumulative Q2 for both components = -0.28), but the background correlation was at the same level (R2Y = 0.20) as for the BP model. Although more robust models have higher model predictability (Q2) and lower background correlation, we think that our models still deliver information about the most important factors explaining BP and CR in kettle holes. Discussion Interestingly, the POM pool which is tightly linked with the autochthonous OM in the kettle holes was the most important component to explain the observed variations in pelagic BP and CR. In contrast to the traditional view that kettle holes are tightly connected to their terrestrial surrounding, our PLS models for CR and BP thus suggest a minor role of allochthonous OM and a major role of autochthonous OM in regulating bacterial activities in kettle holes—at least during the growing season. Environmental drivers of bacterial activities in the water body of kettle holes Pelagic BP and CR were mainly driven by the particulate organic matter pool (POM) which was the most influential factor as revealed by PLS (Fig. 3). Compared to other aquatic systems, POM concentrations in kettle hole water bodies are on the high end of observed concentrations. For example, POC usually contributes about 10% of the total Fig. 2 Boxplots of microbial activities: a Bacterial production (unit \( \mu \)g C L\(^{-1}\)d\(^{-1}\)), b Microbial respiration (unit \( \mu \)g C L\(^{-1}\)d\(^{-1}\)), and c bacterial growth efficiency in kettle holes in February (Feb), June (Jun), and October (Oct). Boxplots indicate the medians, the 25th and 75th percentiles (boxes), the 5th and 95th percentiles (whiskers) and the mean values (black squares) OC and does not exceed 0.2 mg C L\(^{-1}\) in oligotrophic and 1 ± 2 mg C L\(^{-1}\) in eutrophic environments (Thurman 1985; Wetzel 1984). In most aquatic systems, substrate composition or availability represents the major factors explaining bulk bacterial production (Sigee 2005; Torremorell et al. 2014). In our study, nutrient dynamics and temperature are additional controlling factors of BP (Fig. 3). In contrast, CR was affected by temperature only moderately and nutrient effects were negligible. This suggests an uncoupling of CR from environmental parameters that greatly control bacterial and algal biomass production (Hall and Cotner 2007). In many aquatic systems, however, POM in the water body—at least during the growing season—can be regarded as a proxy for algal biomass (Hodell and Schelske 1998; Hessen et al. 2003; Gu et al. 2006). In a related study conducted in two of our selected kettle holes (here labeled as #5 and #10), sedimentation of organic C was positively correlated with Chlorophyll \( a \) concentrations in the water body further supporting the close and positive relationship between algal biomass and POM also in our kettle holes (Kleeberg et al. 2016). Additionally, TDP and C:P ratio highly influenced BP in our study. Since phytoplankton biomass is strongly dependent on total P in lakes (Guildford and Hecky 2000), TDP concentrations may indirectly influence BP in the kettle holes via changes in phytoplankton dynamics. Black circles display highly influential variables (>1 VIP), grey circles display moderately influential (1–0.7 VIP) and blank circles display less influential variables (<0.7 VIP). The dependent variables are displayed as stars allochthonous OC (Kritzberg et al. 2006) and autochthonous OC generally supports higher biomass production (Karlsson et al. 2015) in aquatic systems. Our results also suggest that bacterial activities are highly-dependent on availability of algal and macrophyte OM though also kettle holes potentially receive high loads of allochthonous OM from erosion (Downing et al. 2008) as was observed in our autumn dataset by an increase in aromaticity (Fig. 1). Bacterial C processing in the water body of kettle holes Mean BGE in the kettle holes was 0.31 ± 0.17, similar to the commonly measured mean of 0.3 (del Giorgio and Cole 1998). The measured bacterial activities in our kettle holes are also within the range of eutrophic temperate aquatic systems (Cole et al. 1988; del Giorgio and; Cole 1998), e.g. BP is similar to eutrophic and hypertrophic lakes (see Table 2). However, when comparing our results to studies from temperate regions, BP rates were slightly lower. Tropical, hypertrophic systems, however, typically have higher BP maxima, approximately twice as high as those measured in our kettle holes. In other studies of temperate lakes and prairie wetlands in Canada (Nixdorf and Jander 2003; Waiser and Robarts 2004), a seasonal trend in bacterial activities with higher summer values was detected, similar to our study. The high BP and BGE in early summer are likely caused by high temperatures and a sufficient supply of organic matter from algae and macrophytes in early summer that could be efficiently channeled into bacterial biomass production. Very likely, the high organic matter input in early summer increased the quality of bioavailable DOC which might be due to a release of exudates by autochthonous production (Sell and Overbeck 1992). This has been also observed in similar systems in Canada (Waiser and Robarts 2004). The high bacterial production in early summer may also increase the availability of bacterial biomass for zooplankton or macroinvertebrates (Søndergaard et al. 2005), which in turn may raise grazing pressure on bacterioplankton in kettle holes. Since many kettle holes lack fishes, a high grazing pressure on bacteria can be expected in these systems (Rautio and Vincent 2006). Effects of temporal differences in water chemistry on microbial activities Almost all dissolved water parameters (O₂, pH, DOC, %LMWS, HMWS:LMWS, TDN, TDP, and absorbance indices) significantly differed between the sampling dates in February, June and October (Table 4), whereby DOC varied most with an increase of 76% from February to June. A high intra-annual variability in nutrients in small aquatic systems is characteristic for numerous kettle holes in north-eastern Germany (Lischeid and Kalettka 2012), shallow, artificial ponds in southeastern England (Bennion and Smith 2000), and also for some tropical ponds (Mukhopadhyay et al. 2004). After the first observed increase from February to June, DOC no longer increased between June and October. This observation might suggest increased DOC degradation by internal microbial processes, which is supported by relatively high BP and BGE in all kettle holes in early summer and autumn (similar to Nixdorf and Jander 2003; Waiser and Robarts 2004; see Table 2) with around 184 ± 136 µg C L⁻¹ d⁻¹ and 129 ± 127 µg C L⁻¹ d⁻¹, respectively. BGE was around 37 ± 13% in early summer and 38 ± 19% in autumn. This is higher than the mean BGE determined by del Giorgio and Cole (1998) with around 30% for natural aquatic systems. An alternative explanation for this notion could be related to external factors such as catchment dynamics and photochemical degradation. Waiser (2006), for example, suggests hydrological characteristics as the most important factors affecting DOC concentrations in closed basin prairie wetlands. Unfortunately, we have no data on kettle hole hydrology and cannot exclude that DOC concentrations are altered by exchange with the surrounding terrestrial landscape. SUVA254 of our kettle holes was generally less than 3 L mg⁻¹ m⁻¹ indicating the prevalence of water soluble and less aromatic DOC (Peuravuori and Pihlaja 1997; Volk et al. 1997). In addition, SUVA285 rarely exceeded 1 L mg⁻¹ m⁻¹ in all of our investigated kettle holes (Fig. 1f, g) indicating a dominance of aliphatic substances probably originating from autochthonous primary production (Rostan and Cellot 1995). In general, autochthonous DOC tends to be less colored than terrestrially derived DOC (i.e., low absorbance indices) (Laurion et al. 2000). Low SUVA254/285 values might also point to photo-degradation of the DOC pool, decreasing aromaticity and color (Teixeira et al. 2013). However, low aromaticity and color throughout the seasons and no obvious decrease in SUVA254/285 and molecular size in June compared to February and October could indicate a minor importance of photo-degradative effects on DOC availability. In February, we measured a rather low BGE which may reflect lower OM bioavailability for the bacterial community due to a lack of newly produced autochthonous OM. Lower temperatures at this time of the year might also have limited BGE. During the growing season, however, new production by phytoplankton and macrophytes due to, for example, exudation, increases DOC molecular sizes. Nevertheless, in autumn a higher input of terrestrial OM following rain events and/or leaf litter fall may have increased LMWS concentrations in the water column (Fig. 1i). As a result, allochthonous inputs might play a minor role in shaping the dissolved OM pool in kettle holes during the growing season. Although we cannot exclude that heavy rain events or other “hot moments” might have increased terrestrial OM inputs, our data indicate that autochthonous C dominated C sources and that only a limited C input occurred from the catchment during our sampling campaigns. Additional support for the high autochthony of kettle holes stems from sediment C:N and d^{13}C data (Fig. 4) that suggest two of our studied kettle holes (number 5 and 10 in Table 1) have an autochthonous dominated fraction. Also, stable isotope analysis of POM from kettle holes 5 and 10 (ranging from −30.8 to −39.7‰) further suggests that the sedimenting OM is of primarily autochthonous origin. This notion is supported by findings of Downing et al. (2008) indicating that high rates of primary production in eutrophic impoundments contribute a substantial fraction to OC burial. In conclusion, contrary to our hypothesis, autochthonous production (POM and POC) may be the major driver for bacterial activities in the water column of kettle holes in the agricultural landscape. Variations in bacterial activities were best explained by the particulate organic matter pool that apparently plays a more important role for aquatic C turnover in kettle holes than in other aquatic systems. Our results highlight the importance of autochthonous sources for bacterial C turnover and biogeochemical processes in the water body of kettle holes and suggest that allochthonous C sources play a minor role in sustaining bacterial activities during the growing season. Thus, allochthonous OC introduced from terrestrial surroundings might be more prone to sedimentation where it can be microbially remineralized or buried. Yet, in kettle holes, further studies on their ecosystem function and role as hotspots for C turnover or C sequestration need to be performed to better evaluate the particular role of kettle holes for C cycling in a landscape perspective. title: bacterial processes and biogeochemical changes in the water body of kettle holes - mainly driven by autochthonous organic matter?
author: attermeyer; katrin; grossart; hans-peter; flury; sabine; premke; katrin
context:
Bacterial processes and biogeochemical changes in the water body of kettle holes - mainly driven by autochthonous organic matter? Katrin Attermeyer1,2 · Hans-Peter Grossart3,4 · Sabine Flury1,5 · Katrin Premke1,6 Received: 15 February 2016 / Accepted: 27 February 2017 / Published online: 7 April 2017 © Springer International Publishing 2017 Abstract Kettle holes are small inland waters formed from glacially-created depressions often situated in agricultural landscapes. Due to their high perimeter-to-area ratio facilitating a high aquatic-terrestrial coupling, kettle holes can accumulate high concentrations of organic carbon and nutrients, fueling microbial activities and turnover rates. Thus, they represent hotspots of carbon turnover in the landscape, but their bacterial activities and controlling factors have not been well investigated. Therefore, we aimed to assess the relative importance of various environmental factors on bacterial and biogeochemical processes in the water column of kettle holes and to disentangle their variations. In the water body of ten kettle holes in north-eastern Germany, we measured several physico-chemical and biological parameters such as carbon quantity and quality, as well as bacterial protein production (BP) and community respiration (CR) in spring, early summer and autumn 2014. Particulate organic matter served as an indicator of autochthonous production and represented an important parameter to explain variations in BP and CR. This notion is supported by qualitative absorbance indices of dissolved molecules in water samples and C:N ratios of the sediments, which demonstrate high fractions of autochthonous organic matter (OM) in the studied kettle holes. In contrast, dissolved chemical parameters were less important for bacterial activities although they revealed strong differences throughout the growing season. Pelagic bacterial activities and dynamics might thus be regulated by autochthonous OM in kettle holes implying a control of important biogeochemical processes by internal primary production rather than facilitated exchange with the terrestrial surrounding due to a high perimeter-to-area ratio. Keywords Bacterial production · Carbon turnover · Growth efficiency · Ponds · Respiration · DOC quality · LC-OCD Introduction Small depressional wetlands, referred to here as kettle holes, are abundant elements in the hummocky, post-glacial landscape in Northern Europe, Northern America, and Siberia. They evolved from topographic depressions formed during the ice retreat after the Pleistocene about 10,000–12,000 years ago by delayed melting of remnant ice blocks. The depression size ranges from 0.0001 to 0.03 km² and they can be either permanently filled with water, completely dry or experience wet and dry cycles of different time periods. In north-eastern Germany, kettle holes are widely distributed and hence important landscape components. With a density of up to 4,000 per km\(^2\) they are mainly situated in agricultural landscapes (Kalettka et al. 2001; Lischeid and Kalettka 2012). Kettle hole types have been classified according to different hydro-geomorphic characteristics reflecting their high heterogeneity (Kalettka and Rudat 2006). They differ widely with respect to groundwater inflow, surface runoff, internal carbon (C) assimilation and mineralization, macrophyte abundance, and land-use of the respective catchments. As a result, kettle holes fulfill important hydrological and ecological functions affecting the water balance of the surrounding landscape (Hayashi et al. 2003; Gerke et al. 2010). Generally, they are very sensitive to changing hydrological conditions and undergo pronounced wet-dry cycles. Today, small aquatic systems such as kettle holes are widely recognized as hotspots of C turnover in the landscape (Waiser and Robarts 2004; Cole et al. 2007; Tranvik et al. 2009; Aufdenkampe et al. 2011; Premke et al. 2016). Initial studies of C cycling in small ponds or impoundments show that these systems accumulate high biomasses and can constitute a major and currently underestimated C sink (Cole et al. 1988; Downing et al. 2008). Other studies, however, show that kettle holes also can be significant sources of important greenhouse gases such as N\(_2\)O, CH\(_4\) and CO\(_2\), which is further exacerbated by eutrophication (Merbach et al. 2002). One study conducted in two wetlands in the prairie region of the North American Great Plains, points towards an important role of bacteria in the metabolism of these systems (Waiser and Robarts 2004). Yet, most of the research on microbial C cycling has been conducted in small, shallow lakes and artificial, small standing inland waters with much less known about the microbiology and biogeochemistry of kettle holes. Kettle holes generally contain high concentrations of C and nutrients such as nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) (e.g. Lischeid and Kalettka 2012). On the one hand, high N and P concentrations can facilitate high primary production rates (Schindler 1978), and nutrient additions in combination with food web manipulations have been shown to turn net-heterotrophic lakes into net-autotrophic systems (Cole et al. 2000). On the other hand, it is also known that the net metabolic balance in lakes varies continuously along a gradient of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) concentration: as DOC increases, primary production may decrease and lake metabolism becomes progressively more heterotrophic (Tranvik 1988; Prairie et al. 2002; Jansson et al. 2007). This pattern is driven mainly by a change in the ratio of primary production to total respiration supported by an increase in allochthonous DOC. This suggests that allochthonous DOC plays an important regulatory role in lake metabolism through its influence on microbial metabolism (Jansson et al. 2000). In this study, we investigated ten kettle holes in the north-eastern part of Germany representing a gradient in DOC concentrations and a broad diversity of kettle hole types. We aimed to assess the relative importance of allochthonous vs. autochthonous C for bacterial and biogeochemical processes in the water body. We hypothesized that allochthonous DOC is the major driver for bacterial activities in the water body of kettle holes and is more important than autochthonous C. In spring, early summer and autumn 2014, we measured various physico-chemical parameters such as nutrients (N and P), C quantity and quality (Liquid Chromatography with Organic Carbon Detection, absorbance), and bacterial protein production and community respiration in the water body of the kettle holes to evaluate the factors driving bacterial activities in kettle hole water bodies. Methods Study site All kettle holes are located in the Quillow catchment in the temperate north-eastern part of Germany, approximately 80 km north-east of Berlin. A detailed description of the area can be found in Kleeberg et al. (2016). Ten kettle holes were selected (Table 1) based on a gradient in DOC concentrations. The 10 kettle holes in this study vary in size from 0.57 to 4.29 \( \times \) 10\(^{-3}\) km\(^2\). All kettle holes exhibited macrophytes, but the dominant vegetation type differed. They were mostly vegetated by *Typha* spp., *Carex* spp., *Phragmites australis* or *Phalaris arundinacea* (Table 1). Despite variation in the dominant vegetation type, eight kettle holes were surrounded by arable land and two by grassland. All kettle holes were permanently flooded during the sampling campaign, except one of the smallest (identification number 3, see Table 1) which dried out in summer. Thus, the dataset was reduced to nine for early summer and autumn. Sampling The kettle holes were sampled three times during the growing season in 2014: in spring (February, 25th and 27th), early summer (June, 24th and 26th), and autumn (October, 28th and 30th). Temperature, pH and oxygen (O\(_2\)) concentrations were determined on site, using electronic probes (DurOx and SenTix for February and June as well as the Multi3410 probe for the October campaign; WTW, Weilheim, Germany). Size, global positioning system (GPS) coordinates, dominant vegetation from Kalettka and Rudat (2006) and dissolved organic carbon (DOC) concentrations from the three samplings in February (Feb), June (Jun) and October (Oct) in the center of each kettle hole with a water sampler (LIM-NOS, Turku, Finland) for chemical analyses as well as for determination of bacterial cell numbers and production. The samples were transported to the laboratory under dark conditions and close to in situ temperatures and processed within 5 h after sampling. One sample per kettle hole was collected based on the assumption that it is representative for the entire kettle hole (Mukhopadhyay et al. 2004). Additionally, three polypropylene incubation cores length 30 cm; width 5.2 cm; volume 0.5 L per kettle hole were filled with water for CR measurements. Chemical analysis Total organic carbon (TOC), total dissolved organic carbon (DOC), total dissolved nitrogen (TDN; all in mgL−1), and total dissolved phosphorus (TDP; in μgL−1) were analyzed according to standard chemical procedures (Strickland and Parsons 1968; Wetzel and Likens 1991). The dissolved fraction was analyzed after filtering the sample through a 0.2 μm cellulose acetate filter (Whatman, Dassel, Germany) pre-rinsed with 500 mL double distilled water to avoid contamination of the samples. Concentrations of organic C were determined with a C analyzer (Shimadzu, 3 TOC-V CPH, Duisburg, Germany) as non-purgeable C after acidification with 2 mol L−1 HCl. The carbon dioxide generated by catalytic high-temperature oxidation (850 °C) was measured online by infrared absorption. POC was then calculated from TOC minus DOC as all TOC measurements were substantially higher than DOC. Samples for TDP were incubated with 5% (w/v) K2S2O8 for 30 min at 134 °C in a steam autoclave prior to analysis. Phosphorus concentrations were measured photometrically (FIA compact analyzer MLE, Dresden, Germany) using the molybdenum-blue method (Koroleff 1976). Dissolved nitrogen was oxidized with Oxisolv® (Merck, Darmstadt, Germany) at 120 °C for 45 min in an autoclave and measured with a Foss FIAstar 5010 analyzer (Rellingen, Germany). C:N and C:P molar ratios were calculated from DOC vs. TDN and TDP, respectively. Particulate organic matter (POM; in mg L−1) was determined by filtering a known amount of water through a combusted GF/C filter (nominal pore size 1.2 μm; Whatman, Dassel, Germany) and subsequent freeze-drying. The dry weight difference of the empty and ‘sample’ filter per filtered water volume was considered POM. Absorbance measurements for DOC were done on a Hitachi U2900 UV/Vis spectrophotometer using a 1 cm quartz cuvette. Absorbance spectra were measured from 190 to 800 nm at 0.5 nm increments and instrument noise was assessed measuring double distilled water as a blank. To investigate the chromophoric dissolved organic matter properties, optical indices such as the A250:A365 ratio and specific UV absorbance (SUVA) at 254 and 285 nm were determined. The A250:A365 ratio (also called E2:E3 ratio) was calculated using absorption coefficients at the appropriate wavelengths and indicates changes in the relative molecule size of DOM (Peuravuori and Pihlaja 1997). SUVA254 and SUVA285 were calculated by dividing absorbance of 254 and 285 nm (in m−1) by DOC concentration (in mg L−1). SUVA254 is considered a proxy for aromaticity (Weishaar et al. 2003) and SUVA285 a proxy for fulvic acid concentrations in the water (Giancoli Barreto et al. 2003). Furthermore, DOC was characterized by size exclusion chromatography with online C and nitrogen detection (Liquid Chromatography-Organic Carbon Detection–Organic Nitrogen Detection; LC-OCD–OND; Huber et al. 2011). The DOC of the filtered samples passes through a size-exclusion column packed with resin (Toyopearl HW 50S, volume of 11 250×20 mm). Phosphate buffer (0.029 mol L^{-1}, pH 6.5) was used as eluent at a flow rate of 1.1 mL min^{-1}. DOC was detected with infrared (IR) absorbance of CO_2 after ultraviolet (UV) oxidation of DOC at 185 nm in a cylindrical UV thin-film reactor (Graentzel-reactor). DOC can then be summarized in three fractions: high molecular weight substances (HMWS, e.g. polysaccharides), humic or humic-like substances (HS) comprising building blocks, and low molecular weight substances (LMWS) including both low molecular weight acids and low molecular weight neutral substances. Building blocks are a specific fraction that reflect breakdown products of humic substances with a lower molecular weight and follow humic substances in the chromatogram (Huber et al. 2011). The individual fractions and their molecular weights were identified based on fulvic and humic acid standards from the International Humic Substances Society and analyzed with a suitable software program (FIFFIKUS; DOC-Labor Huber, Karlsruhe, Germany). Bacterial cell number and production Total bacterial cell number was determined by epifluorescence microscopy after staining with SYBR Gold (Invitrogen, Darmstadt, Germany; Shibata et al. 2006). Glutaraldehyde fixed samples (0.9% final concentration) were filtered onto a 0.2 µm polycarbonate filter (Whatman, Dassel, Germany) and embedded in Citifluor (CITIFLUOR AF1, Science Services, München, Germany) with a SYBR Gold staining solution diluted to 1:1000 (Molecular Probes, Eugene, Oregon, USA). For each filter, 500–1000 bacterial cells were counted with an epifluorescence microscope at 1000× magnification (Zeiss, Axio Imager. Z1, Jena, Germany). Bacterial protein production (BP) was determined via incorporation of L-^{14}C-leucine into the protein fraction using the protocol of Simon and Azam (1989). 5 mL of the water were incubated with L-^{14}C-leucine (Hartmann Analytic, Braunschweig, Germany, specific activity 306 mCi mmol^{-1}) at a final concentration of 120 nmol L^{-1}. Three replicates and one blank were measured for each kettle hole. A detailed description of the procedure is given in Attermeyer et al. (2013). Net disintegrations per minute were converted to pmol leucine L^{-1} d^{-1} according to Simon and Azam (1989), and an isotope dilution factor of 2 was applied (Kirchman 1993). BP for water samples is given as µg C L^{-1} d^{-1}. Community respiration Community respiration (CR) was determined by measuring O_2 depletion over time with a needle-type O_2 microsensor (Optode, PreSens, Regensburg, Germany) after mixing the water column. Briefly, the O_2 sensor was inserted through a septum in the gastight container and O_2 depletion was measured at regular intervals (every 6–12 h) over time. The total incubation time was generally 24 h at in situ temperatures in the dark. If initial O_2 concentrations were close to suboxic conditions (e.g. in June, ~2 mg L^{-1}), the incubation time was reduced to avoid anoxic conditions which are known to slow down bacterial activities. The amount of consumed O_2 was converted to µg C L^{-1} d^{-1} by using a conversion factor of 1 (Berggren et al. 2012). For details see Attermeyer et al. (2013). We assumed that the majority of O_2 consumption was caused by bacterial respiration as they have been shown to make up to more than 90% of the biomass of the pelagic community (Daniel et al. 2005). Bacterial growth efficiency (BGE) describing the proportion of C entering the bacterial pool that is incorporated into biomass was thus calculated based on BP and CR (BGE=BP/(BP+CR)). As respiration of non-bacteria microorganisms is included, we recognize a slight underestimation of real growth efficiencies due to a higher total community respiration. Sediment analysis Two kettle holes (number 5 and 10 in Table 1) were additionally sampled on a monthly basis from February 2013 to March 2014 for analysis of sedimentary C:N ratios and stable C isotope ratios (δ^{13}C) of organic matter (Meyers 1994). For the analysis, four sediment cores (6 cm diameter) per kettle hole were retrieved using a push corer (UWITEC, Austria). The dried and homogenized sediments were analyzed for C and N via a Vario EL (Elementar Analysesysteme, Germany) according to the company’s recommendations (Elementar Application material, AB-C-250101-D-01/AB-C-250101-E-01). Stable C isotope signature (δ^{13}C) was measured on an elemental analyzer (Flash HT, Thermo-Finnigan) connected to a Con-flow IV (Thermo-Scientific) after treating the dried sediment with HCl vapor for 48 h. In-house standards and certified standards (sucrose; IAEA-CH-6 and L-glutamic acid; USGS40) were used for calibration. Isotopic values are expressed in delta notation (in ‰ units), relative to Vienna Pee Dee Belemnite. Precision of analysis was within 0.1‰. Literature data compilation To compare pelagic BP in kettle holes with current literature, we compiled data from other aquatic systems in boreal, temperate and tropical regions of mainly eutrophic to hypertrophic water bodies in which BP was measured with radiolabeled substances (either thymidine or leucine; Table 2). Statistics Differences between samplings (in February, June, and October) for all measured variables were tested with the non-parametric Kruskal Wallis test (Kruskal and Wallis 1952) as data were not normally distributed. Single comparisons between February vs. June, February vs. October, and June vs. October were done in post-hoc comparisons after Mann Whitney U with a corrected p after Bonferroni Holm (Mann and Whitney 1947). The univariate statistical analyses were done in IBM SPSS Statistics 22 (IBM Corporation, Armonk, NY, USA). To identify major drivers (independent (X) variables) for BP and CR (dependent (Y) variables) in kettle holes, we used multivariate linear regression by means of partial least squares projections (PLS regression; Eriksson et al. 2001). PLS regression relates two data matrices, X and Y, to each other by a linear multivariate model (Höskuldsson 1988; Wold et al. 2001). This is a robust method that can deal with non-normally distributed data, missing values, co-correlation of X variables and a large dataset of independent (X) variables. To improve the model performance, we confirmed a nearly symmetrical distribution of data (skewness <2) and showed a constant “error variance” (Minimum/Maximum ratio >0.1) as described in Sobek et al. (2007). If the data did not fulfill these conditions they were log- or log(X+1)-transformed. Before running the PLS regression, data were mean-centered and scaled to unit variance. The results of the PLS regression are displayed as loading plots which show the importance of the independent variables in explaining the dependent variable (BP and CR). All environmental variables included in the two models are described in Table 3. Correlations of the variables can be extracted from the spatial distribution in the loading plot: positively correlated when situated close to each other and negatively correlated when distant from each other. The model was evaluated on the basis of the R2Y and Q2 values. R2Y reveals the explained variance of X by Y (goodness of fit) and Q2 the predicted variation of the model. The closer both values, the better and more robust is the model. Furthermore, a permutation test was run to assess how much of the explained variance could be attributed to random chance. Y values were permutated (100 times) and a PLS model was created for each permutated Y variable separately. The difference between the intercept of R2Y and Q2 regressions derived from 100 permutated datasets. The original R2Y and Q2 provided an estimate of the background correlation due to chance for the Y variable. Small background correlations indicated a stable model (Eriksson et al. 2001). PLS regression was performed in Statistica12 (Statsoft, Hamburg, Germany) and model validation was done in SIMCA 14 (Umetrics, Umeå, Sweden). Results Physico-chemical analysis Water temperatures were lowest in February (4.1–5.8 °C), highest in June (14.1–18.8 °C) and intermediate in October (5.4–7.8). Oxygen (O2) concentrations were lowest in early summer when some kettle holes showed suboxic to anoxic conditions (see Supp. 1), but pH exhibited no clear trend with higher or lower values throughout the sampling period (7.9 ± 1; mean ± standard deviation). POM was highest, but also most variable in June ranging from 3.0 to 58.6 mg L−1. DOC concentrations covered a huge range from 9.7 up to 42.3 mg L−1 (Fig. 1c) and varied extensively between different kettle holes and sampling dates. From February to June, DOC increased in almost all kettle holes, on average by 76%. This trend changed in October when DOC dropped back to values more similar to February (Fig. 1c). TDN increased during the growing season from February to October and ranged between 0.7 and 7.5 mg L−1 across all sampling dates and kettle holes (Fig. 1d). The trend differed for TDP which showed generally higher values in June as compared to October (range from 18 to 1674 µg L−1 over all sampling dates and kettle holes; Fig. 1e). The highest variations of TDP in all kettle holes occurred in June when the highest value was measured. All measured nutrients (DOC, TDN, and TDP) were significantly different between the three sampling dates (Table 4) indicating a generally high temporal variability in kettle hole nutrient dynamics. The DOC quality parameters were significantly different at the three sampling dates.
