Size, global positioning system (GPS) coordinates, dominant vegetation from Kalettka and Rudat (2006) and dissolved organic carbon (DOC) concentrations from the three samplings in February (Feb), June (Jun) and October (Oct) in the center of each kettle hole with a water sampler (LIM-NOS, Turku, Finland) for chemical analyses as well as for determination of bacterial cell numbers and production. The samples were transported to the laboratory under dark conditions and close to in situ temperatures and processed within 5 h after sampling. One sample per kettle hole was collected based on the assumption that it is representative for the entire kettle hole (Mukhopadhyay et al. 2004). Additionally, three polypropylene incubation cores length 30 cm; width 5.2 cm; volume 0.5 L per kettle hole were filled with water for CR measurements. Chemical analysis Total organic carbon (TOC), total dissolved organic carbon (DOC), total dissolved nitrogen (TDN; all in mgL−1), and total dissolved phosphorus (TDP; in μgL−1) were analyzed according to standard chemical procedures (Strickland and Parsons 1968; Wetzel and Likens 1991). The dissolved fraction was analyzed after filtering the sample through a 0.2 μm cellulose acetate filter (Whatman, Dassel, Germany) pre-rinsed with 500 mL double distilled water to avoid contamination of the samples. Concentrations of organic C were determined with a C analyzer (Shimadzu, 3 TOC-V CPH, Duisburg, Germany) as non-purgeable C after acidification with 2 mol L−1 HCl. The carbon dioxide generated by catalytic high-temperature oxidation (850 °C) was measured online by infrared absorption. POC was then calculated from TOC minus DOC as all TOC measurements were substantially higher than DOC. Samples for TDP were incubated with 5% (w/v) K2S2O8 for 30 min at 134 °C in a steam autoclave prior to analysis. Phosphorus concentrations were measured photometrically (FIA compact analyzer MLE, Dresden, Germany) using the molybdenum-blue method (Koroleff 1976). Dissolved nitrogen was oxidized with Oxisolv® (Merck, Darmstadt, Germany) at 120 °C for 45 min in an autoclave and measured with a Foss FIAstar 5010 analyzer (Rellingen, Germany). C:N and C:P molar ratios were calculated from DOC vs. TDN and TDP, respectively. Particulate organic matter (POM; in mg L−1) was determined by filtering a known amount of water through a combusted GF/C filter (nominal pore size 1.2 μm; Whatman, Dassel, Germany) and subsequent freeze-drying. The dry weight difference of the empty and ‘sample’ filter per filtered water volume was considered POM. Absorbance measurements for DOC were done on a Hitachi U2900 UV/Vis spectrophotometer using a 1 cm quartz cuvette. Absorbance spectra were measured from 190 to 800 nm at 0.5 nm increments and instrument noise was assessed measuring double distilled water as a blank. To investigate the chromophoric dissolved organic matter properties, optical indices such as the A250:A365 ratio and specific UV absorbance (SUVA) at 254 and 285 nm were determined. The A250:A365 ratio (also called E2:E3 ratio) was calculated using absorption coefficients at the appropriate wavelengths and indicates changes in the relative molecule size of DOM (Peuravuori and Pihlaja 1997). SUVA254 and SUVA285 were calculated by dividing absorbance of 254 and 285 nm (in m−1) by DOC concentration (in mg L−1). SUVA254 is considered a proxy for aromaticity (Weishaar et al. 2003) and SUVA285 a proxy for fulvic acid concentrations in the water (Giancoli Barreto et al. 2003). Furthermore, DOC was characterized by size exclusion chromatography with online C and nitrogen detection (Liquid Chromatography-Organic Carbon Detection–Organic Nitrogen Detection; LC-OCD–OND; Huber et al. 2011). The DOC of the filtered samples passes through a size-exclusion column packed with resin (Toyopearl HW 50S, volume of 11 250×20 mm). Phosphate buffer (0.029 mol L^{-1}, pH 6.5) was used as eluent at a flow rate of 1.1 mL min^{-1}. DOC was detected with infrared (IR) absorbance of CO_2 after ultraviolet (UV) oxidation of DOC at 185 nm in a cylindrical UV thin-film reactor (Graentzel-reactor). DOC can then be summarized in three fractions: high molecular weight substances (HMWS, e.g. polysaccharides), humic or humic-like substances (HS) comprising building blocks, and low molecular weight substances (LMWS) including both low molecular weight acids and low molecular weight neutral substances. Building blocks are a specific fraction that reflect breakdown products of humic substances with a lower molecular weight and follow humic substances in the chromatogram (Huber et al. 2011). The individual fractions and their molecular weights were identified based on fulvic and humic acid standards from the International Humic Substances Society and analyzed with a suitable software program (FIFFIKUS; DOC-Labor Huber, Karlsruhe, Germany). Bacterial cell number and production Total bacterial cell number was determined by epifluorescence microscopy after staining with SYBR Gold (Invitrogen, Darmstadt, Germany; Shibata et al. 2006). Glutaraldehyde fixed samples (0.9% final concentration) were filtered onto a 0.2 µm polycarbonate filter (Whatman, Dassel, Germany) and embedded in Citifluor (CITIFLUOR AF1, Science Services, München, Germany) with a SYBR Gold staining solution diluted to 1:1000 (Molecular Probes, Eugene, Oregon, USA). For each filter, 500–1000 bacterial cells were counted with an epifluorescence microscope at 1000× magnification (Zeiss, Axio Imager. Z1, Jena, Germany). Bacterial protein production (BP) was determined via incorporation of L-^{14}C-leucine into the protein fraction using the protocol of Simon and Azam (1989). 5 mL of the water were incubated with L-^{14}C-leucine (Hartmann Analytic, Braunschweig, Germany, specific activity 306 mCi mmol^{-1}) at a final concentration of 120 nmol L^{-1}. Three replicates and one blank were measured for each kettle hole. A detailed description of the procedure is given in Attermeyer et al. (2013). Net disintegrations per minute were converted to pmol leucine L^{-1} d^{-1} according to Simon and Azam (1989), and an isotope dilution factor of 2 was applied (Kirchman 1993). BP for water samples is given as µg C L^{-1} d^{-1}. Community respiration Community respiration (CR) was determined by measuring O_2 depletion over time with a needle-type O_2 microsensor (Optode, PreSens, Regensburg, Germany) after mixing the water column. Briefly, the O_2 sensor was inserted through a septum in the gastight container and O_2 depletion was measured at regular intervals (every 6–12 h) over time. The total incubation time was generally 24 h at in situ temperatures in the dark. If initial O_2 concentrations were close to suboxic conditions (e.g. in June, ~2 mg L^{-1}), the incubation time was reduced to avoid anoxic conditions which are known to slow down bacterial activities. The amount of consumed O_2 was converted to µg C L^{-1} d^{-1} by using a conversion factor of 1 (Berggren et al. 2012). For details see Attermeyer et al. (2013). We assumed that the majority of O_2 consumption was caused by bacterial respiration as they have been shown to make up to more than 90% of the biomass of the pelagic community (Daniel et al. 2005). Bacterial growth efficiency (BGE) describing the proportion of C entering the bacterial pool that is incorporated into biomass was thus calculated based on BP and CR (BGE=BP/(BP+CR)). As respiration of non-bacteria microorganisms is included, we recognize a slight underestimation of real growth efficiencies due to a higher total community respiration. Sediment analysis Two kettle holes (number 5 and 10 in Table 1) were additionally sampled on a monthly basis from February 2013 to March 2014 for analysis of sedimentary C:N ratios and stable C isotope ratios (δ^{13}C) of organic matter (Meyers 1994). For the analysis, four sediment cores (6 cm diameter) per kettle hole were retrieved using a push corer (UWITEC, Austria). The dried and homogenized sediments were analyzed for C and N via a Vario EL (Elementar Analysesysteme, Germany) according to the company’s recommendations (Elementar Application material, AB-C-250101-D-01/AB-C-250101-E-01). Stable C isotope signature (δ^{13}C) was measured on an elemental analyzer (Flash HT, Thermo-Finnigan) connected to a Con-flow IV (Thermo-Scientific) after treating the dried sediment with HCl vapor for 48 h. In-house standards and certified standards (sucrose; IAEA-CH-6 and L-glutamic acid; USGS40) were used for calibration. Isotopic values are expressed in delta notation (in ‰ units), relative to Vienna Pee Dee Belemnite. Precision of analysis was within 0.1‰. Statistics Differences between samplings (in February, June, and October) for all measured variables were tested with the non-parametric Kruskal Wallis test (Kruskal and Wallis 1952) as data were not normally distributed. Single comparisons between February vs. June, February vs. October, and June vs. October were done in post-hoc comparisons after Mann Whitney U with a corrected p after Bonferroni Holm (Mann and Whitney 1947). The univariate statistical analyses were done in IBM SPSS Statistics 22 (IBM Corporation, Armonk, NY, USA). To identify major drivers (independent (X) variables) for BP and CR (dependent (Y) variables) in kettle holes, we used multivariate linear regression by means of partial least squares projections (PLS regression; Eriksson et al. 2001). PLS regression relates two data matrices, X and Y, to each other by a linear multivariate model (Höskuldsson 1988; Wold et al. 2001). This is a robust method that can deal with non-normally distributed data, missing values, co-correlation of X variables and a large dataset of independent (X) variables. To improve the model performance, we confirmed a nearly symmetrical distribution of data (skewness <2) and showed a constant “error variance” (Minimum/Maximum ratio >0.1) as described in Sobek et al. (2007). If the data did not fulfill these conditions they were log- or log(X+1)-transformed. Before running the PLS regression, data were mean-centered and scaled to unit variance. The results of the PLS regression are displayed as loading plots which show the importance of the independent variables in explaining the dependent variable (BP and CR). All environmental variables included in the two models are described in Table 3. Correlations of the variables can be extracted from the spatial distribution in the loading plot: positively correlated when situated close to each other and negatively correlated when distant from each other. The model was evaluated on the basis of the R2Y and Q2 values. R2Y reveals the explained variance of X by Y (goodness of fit) and Q2 the predicted variation of the model. The closer both values, the better and more robust is the model. Furthermore, a permutation test was run to assess how much of the explained variance could be attributed to random chance. Y values were permutated (100 times) and a PLS model was created for each permutated Y variable separately. The difference between the intercept of R2Y and Q2 regressions derived from 100 permutated datasets. The original R2Y and Q2 provided an estimate of the background correlation due to chance for the Y variable. Small background correlations indicated a stable model (Eriksson et al. 2001). PLS regression was performed in Statistica12 (Statsoft, Hamburg, Germany) and model validation was done in SIMCA 14 (Umetrics, Umeå, Sweden). Results Physico-chemical analysis Water temperatures were lowest in February (4.1–5.8 °C), highest in June (14.1–18.8 °C) and intermediate in October (5.4–7.8). Oxygen (O2) concentrations were lowest in early summer when some kettle holes showed suboxic to anoxic conditions (see Supp. 1), but pH exhibited no clear trend with higher or lower values throughout the sampling period (7.9 ± 1; mean ± standard deviation). POM was highest, but also most variable in June ranging from 3.0 to 58.6 mg L−1. DOC concentrations covered a huge range from 9.7 up to 42.3 mg L−1 (Fig. 1c) and varied extensively between different kettle holes and sampling dates. From February to June, DOC increased in almost all kettle holes, on average by 76%. This trend changed in October when DOC dropped back to values more similar to February (Fig. 1c). TDN increased during the growing season from February to October and ranged between 0.7 and 7.5 mg L−1 across all sampling dates and kettle holes (Fig. 1d). The trend differed for TDP which showed generally higher values in June as compared to October (range from 18 to 1674 µg L−1 over all sampling dates and kettle holes; Fig. 1e). The highest variations of TDP in all kettle holes occurred in June when the highest value was measured. All measured nutrients (DOC, TDN, and TDP) were significantly different between the three sampling dates (Table 4) indicating a generally high temporal variability in kettle hole nutrient dynamics. The DOC quality parameters were significantly different at the three sampling dates. The separate models were more robust than a combined model and separation allowed us to improve conclusions explaining variables for BP and CR. The BP model extracted one significant component from the data matrix that explained 37% of the variance in BP. The loadings plot showed that POC and POM were the two most important variables for explaining the observed variance in BP (Fig. 3a). Both, POC and POM, positively correlated with BP. Other physico-chemical parameters including two qualitative parameters (O2, temperature, TDP, C:P and A250:A365) were also highly influential. Model predictability and the permutation test revealed that the model is valid (Q2 = 0.12; background correlation in R2Y = 0.21). The CR model extracted two significant components that explained together 64% of the variance in CR (Fig. 3b). The loadings plot also found POC and POM as highly influential factors together with cell numbers which was confirmed by high VIP numbers. Other factors that were important for BP were only moderately influential for CR. Model predictability was lower for the CR model (cumulative Q2 for both components = -0.28), but the background correlation was at the same level (R2Y = 0.20) as for the BP model. Although more robust models have higher model predictability (Q2) and lower background correlation, we think that our models still deliver information about the most important factors explaining BP and CR in kettle holes. Discussion Interestingly, the POM pool which is tightly linked with the autochthonous OM in the kettle holes was the most important component to explain the observed variations in pelagic BP and CR. In contrast to the traditional view that kettle holes are tightly connected to their terrestrial surrounding, our PLS models for CR and BP thus suggest a minor role of allochthonous OM and a major role of autochthonous OM in regulating bacterial activities in kettle holes—at least during the growing season. Environmental drivers of bacterial activities in the water body of kettle holes Pelagic BP and CR were mainly driven by the particulate organic matter pool (POM) which was the most influential factor as revealed by PLS (Fig. 3). Compared to other aquatic systems, POM concentrations in kettle hole water bodies are on the high end of observed concentrations. For example, POC usually contributes about 10% of the total Fig. 2 Boxplots of microbial activities: a Bacterial production (unit \( \mu \)g C L\(^{-1}\)d\(^{-1}\)), b Microbial respiration (unit \( \mu \)g C L\(^{-1}\)d\(^{-1}\)), and c bacterial growth efficiency in kettle holes in February (Feb), June (Jun), and October (Oct). Boxplots indicate the medians, the 25th and 75th percentiles (boxes), the 5th and 95th percentiles (whiskers) and the mean values (black squares) OC and does not exceed 0.2 mg C L\(^{-1}\) in oligotrophic and 1 ± 2 mg C L\(^{-1}\) in eutrophic environments (Thurman 1985; Wetzel 1984). In most aquatic systems, substrate composition or availability represents the major factors explaining bulk bacterial production (Sigee 2005; Torremorell et al. 2014). In our study, nutrient dynamics and temperature are additional controlling factors of BP (Fig. 3). In contrast, CR was affected by temperature only moderately and nutrient effects were negligible. This suggests an uncoupling of CR from environmental parameters that greatly control bacterial and algal biomass production (Hall and Cotner 2007). In many aquatic systems, however, POM in the water body—at least during the growing season—can be regarded as a proxy for algal biomass (Hodell and Schelske 1998; Hessen et al. 2003; Gu et al. 2006). In a related study conducted in two of our selected kettle holes (here labeled as #5 and #10), sedimentation of organic C was positively correlated with Chlorophyll \( a \) concentrations in the water body further supporting the close and positive relationship between algal biomass and POM also in our kettle holes (Kleeberg et al. 2016). Additionally, TDP and C:P ratio highly influenced BP in our study. Since phytoplankton biomass is strongly dependent on total P in lakes (Guildford and Hecky 2000), TDP concentrations may indirectly influence BP in the kettle holes via changes in phytoplankton dynamics. Our results also suggest that bacterial activities are highly-dependent on availability of algal and macrophyte OM though also kettle holes potentially receive high loads of allochthonous OM from erosion (Downing et al. 2008) as was observed in our autumn dataset by an increase in aromaticity (Fig. 1). Bacterial C processing in the water body of kettle holes Mean BGE in the kettle holes was 0.31 ± 0.17, similar to the commonly measured mean of 0.3 (del Giorgio and Cole 1998). The measured bacterial activities in our kettle holes are also within the range of eutrophic temperate aquatic systems (Cole et al. 1988; del Giorgio and; Cole 1998), e.g. BP is similar to eutrophic and hypertrophic lakes (see Table 2). However, when comparing our results to studies from temperate regions, BP rates were slightly lower. Tropical, hypertrophic systems, however, typically have higher BP maxima, approximately twice as high as those measured in our kettle holes. In other studies of temperate lakes and prairie wetlands in Canada (Nixdorf and Jander 2003; Waiser and Robarts 2004), a seasonal trend in bacterial activities with higher summer values was detected, similar to our study. The high BP and BGE in early summer are likely caused by high temperatures and a sufficient supply of organic matter from algae and macrophytes in early summer that could be efficiently channeled into bacterial biomass production. Very likely, the high organic matter input in early summer increased the quality of bioavailable DOC which might be due to a release of exudates by autochthonous production (Sell and Overbeck 1992). This has been also observed in similar systems in Canada (Waiser and Robarts 2004). The high bacterial production in early summer may also increase the availability of bacterial biomass for zooplankton or macroinvertebrates (Søndergaard et al. 2005), which in turn may raise grazing pressure on bacterioplankton in kettle holes. Since many kettle holes lack fishes, a high grazing pressure on bacteria can be expected in these systems (Rautio and Vincent 2006). Effects of temporal differences in water chemistry on microbial activities Almost all dissolved water parameters (O₂, pH, DOC, %LMWS, HMWS:LMWS, TDN, TDP, and absorbance indices) significantly differed between the sampling dates in February, June and October (Table 4), whereby DOC varied most with an increase of 76% from February to June. A high intra-annual variability in nutrients in small aquatic systems is characteristic for numerous kettle holes in north-eastern Germany (Lischeid and Kalettka 2012), shallow, artificial ponds in southeastern England (Bennion and Smith 2000), and also for some tropical ponds (Mukhopadhyay et al. 2004). After the first observed increase from February to June, DOC no longer increased between June and October. This observation might suggest increased DOC degradation by internal microbial processes, which is supported by relatively high BP and BGE in all kettle holes in early summer and autumn (similar to Nixdorf and Jander 2003; Waiser and Robarts 2004; see Table 2) with around 184 ± 136 µg C L⁻¹ d⁻¹ and 129 ± 127 µg C L⁻¹ d⁻¹, respectively. BGE was around 37 ± 13% in early summer and 38 ± 19% in autumn. This is higher than the mean BGE determined by del Giorgio and Cole (1998) with around 30% for natural aquatic systems. An alternative explanation for this notion could be related to external factors such as catchment dynamics and photochemical degradation. Waiser (2006), for example, suggests hydrological characteristics as the most important factors affecting DOC concentrations in closed basin prairie wetlands. Unfortunately, we have no data on kettle hole hydrology and cannot exclude that DOC concentrations are altered by exchange with the surrounding terrestrial landscape. SUVA254 of our kettle holes was generally less than 3 L mg⁻¹ m⁻¹ indicating the prevalence of water soluble and less aromatic DOC (Peuravuori and Pihlaja 1997; Volk et al. 1997). In addition, SUVA285 rarely exceeded 1 L mg⁻¹ m⁻¹ in all of our investigated kettle holes (Fig. 1f, g) indicating a dominance of aliphatic substances probably originating from autochthonous primary production (Rostan and Cellot 1995). In general, autochthonous DOC tends to be less colored than terrestrially derived DOC (i.e., low absorbance indices) (Laurion et al. 2000). Low SUVA254/285 values might also point to photo-degradation of the DOC pool, decreasing aromaticity and color (Teixeira et al. 2013). However, low aromaticity and color throughout the seasons and no obvious decrease in SUVA254/285 and molecular size in June compared to February and October could indicate a minor importance of photo-degradative effects on DOC availability. In February, we measured a rather low BGE which may reflect lower OM bioavailability for the bacterial community due to a lack of newly produced autochthonous OM. Lower temperatures at this time of the year might also have limited BGE. During the growing season, however, new production by phytoplankton and macrophytes due to, for example, exudation, increases DOC molecular sizes. Nevertheless, in autumn a higher input of terrestrial OM following rain events and/or leaf litter fall may have increased LMWS concentrations in the water column (Fig. 1i). As a result, allochthonous inputs might play a minor role in shaping the dissolved OM pool in kettle holes during the growing season. Although we cannot exclude that heavy rain events or other “hot moments” might have increased terrestrial OM inputs, our data indicate that autochthonous C dominated C sources and that only a limited C input occurred from the catchment during our sampling campaigns. Additional support for the high autochthony of kettle holes stems from sediment C:N and d^{13}C data (Fig. 4) that suggest two of our studied kettle holes (number 5 and 10 in Table 1) have an autochthonous dominated fraction. Also, stable isotope analysis of POM from kettle holes 5 and 10 (ranging from −30.8 to −39.7‰) further suggests that the sedimenting OM is of primarily autochthonous origin. This notion is supported by findings of Downing et al. (2008) indicating that high rates of primary production in eutrophic impoundments contribute a substantial fraction to OC burial. In conclusion, contrary to our hypothesis, autochthonous production (POM and POC) may be the major driver for bacterial activities in the water column of kettle holes in the agricultural landscape. Variations in bacterial activities were best explained by the particulate organic matter pool that apparently plays a more important role for aquatic C turnover in kettle holes than in other aquatic systems. Our results highlight the importance of autochthonous sources for bacterial C turnover and biogeochemical processes in the water body of kettle holes and suggest that allochthonous C sources play a minor role in sustaining bacterial activities during the growing season. Thus, allochthonous OC introduced from terrestrial surroundings might be more prone to sedimentation where it can be microbially remineralized or buried. Yet, in kettle holes, further studies on their ecosystem function and role as hotspots for C turnover or C sequestration need to be performed to better evaluate the particular role of kettle holes for C cycling in a landscape perspective. title: bacterial processes and biogeochemical changes in the water body of kettle holes - mainly driven by autochthonous organic matter?
author: attermeyer; katrin; grossart; hans-peter; flury; sabine; premke; katrin
context:
Bacterial processes and biogeochemical changes in the water body of kettle holes - mainly driven by autochthonous organic matter? Katrin Attermeyer1,2 · Hans-Peter Grossart3,4 · Sabine Flury1,5 · Katrin Premke1,6 Received: 15 February 2016 / Accepted: 27 February 2017 / Published online: 7 April 2017 © Springer International Publishing 2017 Abstract Kettle holes are small inland waters formed from glacially-created depressions often situated in agricultural landscapes. Due to their high perimeter-to-area ratio facilitating a high aquatic-terrestrial coupling, kettle holes can accumulate high concentrations of organic carbon and nutrients, fueling microbial activities and turnover rates. Thus, they represent hotspots of carbon turnover in the landscape, but their bacterial activities and controlling factors have not been well investigated. Therefore, we aimed to assess the relative importance of various environmental factors on bacterial and biogeochemical processes in the water column of kettle holes and to disentangle their variations. In the water body of ten kettle holes in north-eastern Germany, we measured several physico-chemical and biological parameters such as carbon quantity and quality, as well as bacterial protein production (BP) and community respiration (CR) in spring, early summer and autumn 2014. Particulate organic matter served as an indicator of autochthonous production and represented an important parameter to explain variations in BP and CR. This notion is supported by qualitative absorbance indices of dissolved molecules in water samples and C:N ratios of the sediments, which demonstrate high fractions of autochthonous organic matter (OM) in the studied kettle holes. In contrast, dissolved chemical parameters were less important for bacterial activities although they revealed strong differences throughout the growing season. Pelagic bacterial activities and dynamics might thus be regulated by autochthonous OM in kettle holes implying a control of important biogeochemical processes by internal primary production rather than facilitated exchange with the terrestrial surrounding due to a high perimeter-to-area ratio. Keywords Bacterial production · Carbon turnover · Growth efficiency · Ponds · Respiration · DOC quality · LC-OCD Introduction Small depressional wetlands, referred to here as kettle holes, are abundant elements in the hummocky, post-glacial landscape in Northern Europe, Northern America, and Siberia. They evolved from topographic depressions formed during the ice retreat after the Pleistocene about 10,000–12,000 years ago by delayed melting of remnant ice blocks. The depression size ranges from 0.0001 to 0.03 km² and they can be either permanently filled with water, completely dry or experience wet and dry cycles of different time periods. In north-eastern Germany, kettle holes are widely distributed and hence important landscape components. With a density of up to 4,000 per km\(^2\) they are mainly situated in agricultural landscapes (Kalettka et al. 2001; Lischeid and Kalettka 2012). Kettle hole types have been classified according to different hydro-geomorphic characteristics reflecting their high heterogeneity (Kalettka and Rudat 2006). They differ widely with respect to groundwater inflow, surface runoff, internal carbon (C) assimilation and mineralization, macrophyte abundance, and land-use of the respective catchments. As a result, kettle holes fulfill important hydrological and ecological functions affecting the water balance of the surrounding landscape (Hayashi et al. 2003; Gerke et al. 2010). Generally, they are very sensitive to changing hydrological conditions and undergo pronounced wet-dry cycles. Today, small aquatic systems such as kettle holes are widely recognized as hotspots of C turnover in the landscape (Waiser and Robarts 2004; Cole et al. 2007; Tranvik et al. 2009; Aufdenkampe et al. 2011; Premke et al. 2016). Initial studies of C cycling in small ponds or impoundments show that these systems accumulate high biomasses and can constitute a major and currently underestimated C sink (Cole et al. 1988; Downing et al. 2008). Other studies, however, show that kettle holes also can be significant sources of important greenhouse gases such as N\(_2\)O, CH\(_4\) and CO\(_2\), which is further exacerbated by eutrophication (Merbach et al. 2002). One study conducted in two wetlands in the prairie region of the North American Great Plains, points towards an important role of bacteria in the metabolism of these systems (Waiser and Robarts 2004). Yet, most of the research on microbial C cycling has been conducted in small, shallow lakes and artificial, small standing inland waters with much less known about the microbiology and biogeochemistry of kettle holes. Kettle holes generally contain high concentrations of C and nutrients such as nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) (e.g. Lischeid and Kalettka 2012). On the one hand, high N and P concentrations can facilitate high primary production rates (Schindler 1978), and nutrient additions in combination with food web manipulations have been shown to turn net-heterotrophic lakes into net-autotrophic systems (Cole et al. 2000). On the other hand, it is also known that the net metabolic balance in lakes varies continuously along a gradient of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) concentration: as DOC increases, primary production may decrease and lake metabolism becomes progressively more heterotrophic (Tranvik 1988; Prairie et al. 2002; Jansson et al. 2007). This pattern is driven mainly by a change in the ratio of primary production to total respiration supported by an increase in allochthonous DOC. This suggests that allochthonous DOC plays an important regulatory role in lake metabolism through its influence on microbial metabolism (Jansson et al. 2000). In this study, we investigated ten kettle holes in the north-eastern part of Germany representing a gradient in DOC concentrations and a broad diversity of kettle hole types. We aimed to assess the relative importance of allochthonous vs. autochthonous C for bacterial and biogeochemical processes in the water body. We hypothesized that allochthonous DOC is the major driver for bacterial activities in the water body of kettle holes and is more important than autochthonous C. In spring, early summer and autumn 2014, we measured various physico-chemical parameters such as nutrients (N and P), C quantity and quality (Liquid Chromatography with Organic Carbon Detection, absorbance), and bacterial protein production and community respiration in the water body of the kettle holes to evaluate the factors driving bacterial activities in kettle hole water bodies. Methods Study site All kettle holes are located in the Quillow catchment in the temperate north-eastern part of Germany, approximately 80 km north-east of Berlin. A detailed description of the area can be found in Kleeberg et al. (2016). Ten kettle holes were selected (Table 1) based on a gradient in DOC concentrations. The 10 kettle holes in this study vary in size from 0.57 to 4.29 \( \times \) 10\(^{-3}\) km\(^2\). All kettle holes exhibited macrophytes, but the dominant vegetation type differed. They were mostly vegetated by *Typha* spp., *Carex* spp., *Phragmites australis* or *Phalaris arundinacea* (Table 1). Despite variation in the dominant vegetation type, eight kettle holes were surrounded by arable land and two by grassland. All kettle holes were permanently flooded during the sampling campaign, except one of the smallest (identification number 3, see Table 1) which dried out in summer. Thus, the dataset was reduced to nine for early summer and autumn. Sampling The kettle holes were sampled three times during the growing season in 2014: in spring (February, 25th and 27th), early summer (June, 24th and 26th), and autumn (October, 28th and 30th). Temperature, pH and oxygen (O\(_2\)) concentrations were determined on site, using electronic probes (DurOx and SenTix for February and June as well as the Multi3410 probe for the October campaign; WTW, Weilheim, Germany). Size, global positioning system (GPS) coordinates, dominant vegetation from Kalettka and Rudat (2006) and dissolved organic carbon (DOC) concentrations from the three samplings in February (Feb), June (Jun) and October (Oct) in the center of each kettle hole with a water sampler (LIM-NOS, Turku, Finland) for chemical analyses as well as for determination of bacterial cell numbers and production. The samples were transported to the laboratory under dark conditions and close to in situ temperatures and processed within 5 h after sampling. One sample per kettle hole was collected based on the assumption that it is representative for the entire kettle hole (Mukhopadhyay et al. 2004). Additionally, three polypropylene incubation cores length 30 cm; width 5.2 cm; volume 0.5 L per kettle hole were filled with water for CR measurements. Chemical analysis Total organic carbon (TOC), total dissolved organic carbon (DOC), total dissolved nitrogen (TDN; all in mgL−1), and total dissolved phosphorus (TDP; in μgL−1) were analyzed according to standard chemical procedures (Strickland and Parsons 1968; Wetzel and Likens 1991). The dissolved fraction was analyzed after filtering the sample through a 0.2 μm cellulose acetate filter (Whatman, Dassel, Germany) pre-rinsed with 500 mL double distilled water to avoid contamination of the samples. Concentrations of organic C were determined with a C analyzer (Shimadzu, 3 TOC-V CPH, Duisburg, Germany) as non-purgeable C after acidification with 2 mol L−1 HCl. The carbon dioxide generated by catalytic high-temperature oxidation (850 °C) was measured online by infrared absorption. POC was then calculated from TOC minus DOC as all TOC measurements were substantially higher than DOC. Samples for TDP were incubated with 5% (w/v) K2S2O8 for 30 min at 134 °C in a steam autoclave prior to analysis. Phosphorus concentrations were measured photometrically (FIA compact analyzer MLE, Dresden, Germany) using the molybdenum-blue method (Koroleff 1976). Dissolved nitrogen was oxidized with Oxisolv® (Merck, Darmstadt, Germany) at 120 °C for 45 min in an autoclave and measured with a Foss FIAstar 5010 analyzer (Rellingen, Germany). C:N and C:P molar ratios were calculated from DOC vs. TDN and TDP, respectively. Particulate organic matter (POM; in mg L−1) was determined by filtering a known amount of water through a combusted GF/C filter (nominal pore size 1.2 μm; Whatman, Dassel, Germany) and subsequent freeze-drying. The dry weight difference of the empty and ‘sample’ filter per filtered water volume was considered POM. Absorbance measurements for DOC were done on a Hitachi U2900 UV/Vis spectrophotometer using a 1 cm quartz cuvette. Absorbance spectra were measured from 190 to 800 nm at 0.5 nm increments and instrument noise was assessed measuring double distilled water as a blank. To investigate the chromophoric dissolved organic matter properties, optical indices such as the A250:A365 ratio and specific UV absorbance (SUVA) at 254 and 285 nm were determined. The A250:A365 ratio (also called E2:E3 ratio) was calculated using absorption coefficients at the appropriate wavelengths and indicates changes in the relative molecule size of DOM (Peuravuori and Pihlaja 1997). SUVA254 and SUVA285 were calculated by dividing absorbance of 254 and 285 nm (in m−1) by DOC concentration (in mg L−1). SUVA254 is considered a proxy for aromaticity (Weishaar et al. 2003) and SUVA285 a proxy for fulvic acid concentrations in the water (Giancoli Barreto et al. 2003). Furthermore, DOC was characterized by size exclusion chromatography with online C and nitrogen detection (Liquid Chromatography-Organic Carbon Detection–Organic Nitrogen Detection; LC-OCD–OND; Huber et al. 2011). The DOC of the filtered samples passes through a size-exclusion column packed with resin (Toyopearl HW 50S, volume of 11 250×20 mm). Phosphate buffer (0.029 mol L^{-1}, pH 6.5) was used as eluent at a flow rate of 1.1 mL min^{-1}. DOC was detected with infrared (IR) absorbance of CO_2 after ultraviolet (UV) oxidation of DOC at 185 nm in a cylindrical UV thin-film reactor (Graentzel-reactor). DOC can then be summarized in three fractions: high molecular weight substances (HMWS, e.g. polysaccharides), humic or humic-like substances (HS) comprising building blocks, and low molecular weight substances (LMWS) including both low molecular weight acids and low molecular weight neutral substances. Building blocks are a specific fraction that reflect breakdown products of humic substances with a lower molecular weight and follow humic substances in the chromatogram (Huber et al. 2011). The individual fractions and their molecular weights were identified based on fulvic and humic acid standards from the International Humic Substances Society and analyzed with a suitable software program (FIFFIKUS; DOC-Labor Huber, Karlsruhe, Germany). Bacterial cell number and production Total bacterial cell number was determined by epifluorescence microscopy after staining with SYBR Gold (Invitrogen, Darmstadt, Germany; Shibata et al. 2006). Glutaraldehyde fixed samples (0.9% final concentration) were filtered onto a 0.2 µm polycarbonate filter (Whatman, Dassel, Germany) and embedded in Citifluor (CITIFLUOR AF1, Science Services, München, Germany) with a SYBR Gold staining solution diluted to 1:1000 (Molecular Probes, Eugene, Oregon, USA). For each filter, 500–1000 bacterial cells were counted with an epifluorescence microscope at 1000× magnification (Zeiss, Axio Imager. Z1, Jena, Germany). Bacterial protein production (BP) was determined via incorporation of L-^{14}C-leucine into the protein fraction using the protocol of Simon and Azam (1989). 5 mL of the water were incubated with L-^{14}C-leucine (Hartmann Analytic, Braunschweig, Germany, specific activity 306 mCi mmol^{-1}) at a final concentration of 120 nmol L^{-1}. Three replicates and one blank were measured for each kettle hole. A detailed description of the procedure is given in Attermeyer et al. (2013). Net disintegrations per minute were converted to pmol leucine L^{-1} d^{-1} according to Simon and Azam (1989), and an isotope dilution factor of 2 was applied (Kirchman 1993). BP for water samples is given as µg C L^{-1} d^{-1}. Community respiration Community respiration (CR) was determined by measuring O_2 depletion over time with a needle-type O_2 microsensor (Optode, PreSens, Regensburg, Germany) after mixing the water column. Briefly, the O_2 sensor was inserted through a septum in the gastight container and O_2 depletion was measured at regular intervals (every 6–12 h) over time. The total incubation time was generally 24 h at in situ temperatures in the dark. If initial O_2 concentrations were close to suboxic conditions (e.g. in June, ~2 mg L^{-1}), the incubation time was reduced to avoid anoxic conditions which are known to slow down bacterial activities. The amount of consumed O_2 was converted to µg C L^{-1} d^{-1} by using a conversion factor of 1 (Berggren et al. 2012). For details see Attermeyer et al. (2013). We assumed that the majority of O_2 consumption was caused by bacterial respiration as they have been shown to make up to more than 90% of the biomass of the pelagic community (Daniel et al. 2005). Bacterial growth efficiency (BGE) describing the proportion of C entering the bacterial pool that is incorporated into biomass was thus calculated based on BP and CR (BGE=BP/(BP+CR)). As respiration of non-bacteria microorganisms is included, we recognize a slight underestimation of real growth efficiencies due to a higher total community respiration. Sediment analysis Two kettle holes (number 5 and 10 in Table 1) were additionally sampled on a monthly basis from February 2013 to March 2014 for analysis of sedimentary C:N ratios and stable C isotope ratios (δ^{13}C) of organic matter (Meyers 1994). For the analysis, four sediment cores (6 cm diameter) per kettle hole were retrieved using a push corer (UWITEC, Austria). The dried and homogenized sediments were analyzed for C and N via a Vario EL (Elementar Analysesysteme, Germany) according to the company’s recommendations (Elementar Application material, AB-C-250101-D-01/AB-C-250101-E-01). Stable C isotope signature (δ^{13}C) was measured on an elemental analyzer (Flash HT, Thermo-Finnigan) connected to a Con-flow IV (Thermo-Scientific) after treating the dried sediment with HCl vapor for 48 h. In-house standards and certified standards (sucrose; IAEA-CH-6 and L-glutamic acid; USGS40) were used for calibration. Isotopic values are expressed in delta notation (in ‰ units), relative to Vienna Pee Dee Belemnite. Precision of analysis was within 0.1‰. Statistics Differences between samplings (in February, June, and October) for all measured variables were tested with the non-parametric Kruskal Wallis test (Kruskal and Wallis 1952) as data were not normally distributed. Single comparisons between February vs. June, February vs. October, and June vs. October were done in post-hoc comparisons after Mann Whitney U with a corrected p after Bonferroni Holm (Mann and Whitney 1947). The univariate statistical analyses were done in IBM SPSS Statistics 22 (IBM Corporation, Armonk, NY, USA). To identify major drivers (independent (X) variables) for BP and CR (dependent (Y) variables) in kettle holes, we used multivariate linear regression by means of partial least squares projections (PLS regression; Eriksson et al. 2001). PLS regression relates two data matrices, X and Y, to each other by a linear multivariate model (Höskuldsson 1988; Wold et al. 2001). This is a robust method that can deal with non-normally distributed data, missing values, co-correlation of X variables and a large dataset of independent (X) variables. To improve the model performance, we confirmed a nearly symmetrical distribution of data (skewness <2) and showed a constant “error variance” (Minimum/Maximum ratio >0.1) as described in Sobek et al. (2007). If the data did not fulfill these conditions they were log- or log(X+1)-transformed. Before running the PLS regression, data were mean-centered and scaled to unit variance. The results of the PLS regression are displayed as loading plots which show the importance of the independent variables in explaining the dependent variable (BP and CR). All environmental variables included in the two models are described in Table 3. Correlations of the variables can be extracted from the spatial distribution in the loading plot: positively correlated when situated close to each other and negatively correlated when distant from each other. The model was evaluated on the basis of the R2Y and Q2 values. R2Y reveals the explained variance of X by Y (goodness of fit) and Q2 the predicted variation of the model. The closer both values, the better and more robust is the model. Furthermore, a permutation test was run to assess how much of the explained variance could be attributed to random chance. Y values were permutated (100 times) and a PLS model was created for each permutated Y variable separately. The difference between the intercept of R2Y and Q2 regressions derived from 100 permutated datasets. The original R2Y and Q2 provided an estimate of the background correlation due to chance for the Y variable. Small background correlations indicated a stable model (Eriksson et al. 2001). PLS regression was performed in Statistica12 (Statsoft, Hamburg, Germany) and model validation was done in SIMCA 14 (Umetrics, Umeå, Sweden). Results Physico-chemical analysis Water temperatures were lowest in February (4.1–5.8 °C), highest in June (14.1–18.8 °C) and intermediate in October (5.4–7.8). Oxygen (O2) concentrations were lowest in early summer when some kettle holes showed suboxic to anoxic conditions (see Supp. 1), but pH exhibited no clear trend with higher or lower values throughout the sampling period (7.9 ± 1; mean ± standard deviation). POM was highest, but also most variable in June ranging from 3.0 to 58.6 mg L−1. DOC concentrations covered a huge range from 9.7 up to 42.3 mg L−1 (Fig. 1c) and varied extensively between different kettle holes and sampling dates. From February to June, DOC increased in almost all kettle holes, on average by 76%. This trend changed in October when DOC dropped back to values more similar to February (Fig. 1c). TDN increased during the growing season from February to October and ranged between 0.7 and 7.5 mg L−1 across all sampling dates and kettle holes (Fig. 1d). The trend differed for TDP which showed generally higher values in June as compared to October (range from 18 to 1674 µg L−1 over all sampling dates and kettle holes; Fig. 1e). The highest variations of TDP in all kettle holes occurred in June when the highest value was measured. All measured nutrients (DOC, TDN, and TDP) were significantly different between the three sampling dates (Table 4) indicating a generally high temporal variability in kettle hole nutrient dynamics. The DOC quality parameters were significantly different at the three sampling dates. The separate models were more robust than a combined model and separation allowed us to improve conclusions explaining variables for BP and CR. The BP model extracted one significant component from the data matrix that explained 37% of the variance in BP. The loadings plot showed that POC and POM were the two most important variables for explaining the observed variance in BP (Fig. 3a). Both, POC and POM, positively correlated with BP. Other physico-chemical parameters including two qualitative parameters (O2, temperature, TDP, C:P and A250:A365) were also highly influential. Model predictability and the permutation test revealed that the model is valid (Q2 = 0.12; background correlation in R2Y = 0.21). The CR model extracted two significant components that explained together 64% of the variance in CR (Fig. 3b). The loadings plot also found POC and POM as highly influential factors together with cell numbers which was confirmed by high VIP numbers. Other factors that were important for BP were only moderately influential for CR. Model predictability was lower for the CR model (cumulative Q2 for both components = -0.28), but the background correlation was at the same level (R2Y = 0.20) as for the BP model. Although more robust models have higher model predictability (Q2) and lower background correlation, we think that our models still deliver information about the most important factors explaining BP and CR in kettle holes. Discussion Interestingly, the POM pool which is tightly linked with the autochthonous OM in the kettle holes was the most important component to explain the observed variations in pelagic BP and CR. In contrast to the traditional view that kettle holes are tightly connected to their terrestrial surrounding, our PLS models for CR and BP thus suggest a minor role of allochthonous OM and a major role of autochthonous OM in regulating bacterial activities in kettle holes—at least during the growing season. Environmental drivers of bacterial activities in the water body of kettle holes Pelagic BP and CR were mainly driven by the particulate organic matter pool (POM) which was the most influential factor as revealed by PLS (Fig. 3). Compared to other aquatic systems, POM concentrations in kettle hole water bodies are on the high end of observed concentrations. For example, POC usually contributes about 10% of the total Fig. 2 Boxplots of microbial activities: a Bacterial production (unit \( \mu \)g C L\(^{-1}\)d\(^{-1}\)), b Microbial respiration (unit \( \mu \)g C L\(^{-1}\)d\(^{-1}\)), and c bacterial growth efficiency in kettle holes in February (Feb), June (Jun), and October (Oct). Boxplots indicate the medians, the 25th and 75th percentiles (boxes), the 5th and 95th percentiles (whiskers) and the mean values (black squares) OC and does not exceed 0.2 mg C L\(^{-1}\) in oligotrophic and 1 ± 2 mg C L\(^{-1}\) in eutrophic environments (Thurman 1985; Wetzel 1984). In most aquatic systems, substrate composition or availability represents the major factors explaining bulk bacterial production (Sigee 2005; Torremorell et al. 2014). In our study, nutrient dynamics and temperature are additional controlling factors of BP (Fig. 3). In contrast, CR was affected by temperature only moderately and nutrient effects were negligible. This suggests an uncoupling of CR from environmental parameters that greatly control bacterial and algal biomass production (Hall and Cotner 2007). In many aquatic systems, however, POM in the water body—at least during the growing season—can be regarded as a proxy for algal biomass (Hodell and Schelske 1998; Hessen et al. 2003; Gu et al. 2006). In a related study conducted in two of our selected kettle holes (here labeled as #5 and #10), sedimentation of organic C was positively correlated with Chlorophyll \( a \) concentrations in the water body further supporting the close and positive relationship between algal biomass and POM also in our kettle holes (Kleeberg et al. 2016). Additionally, TDP and C:P ratio highly influenced BP in our study. Since phytoplankton biomass is strongly dependent on total P in lakes (Guildford and Hecky 2000), TDP concentrations may indirectly influence BP in the kettle holes via changes in phytoplankton dynamics. Black circles display highly influential variables (>1 VIP), grey circles display moderately influential (1–0.7 VIP) and blank circles display less influential variables (<0.7 VIP). The dependent variables are displayed as stars allochthonous OC (Kritzberg et al. 2006) and autochthonous OC generally supports higher biomass production (Karlsson et al. 2015) in aquatic systems. Our results also suggest that bacterial activities are highly-dependent on availability of algal and macrophyte OM though also kettle holes potentially receive high loads of allochthonous OM from erosion (Downing et al. 2008) as was observed in our autumn dataset by an increase in aromaticity (Fig. 1). Bacterial C processing in the water body of kettle holes Mean BGE in the kettle holes was 0.31 ± 0.17, similar to the commonly measured mean of 0.3 (del Giorgio and Cole 1998). The measured bacterial activities in our kettle holes are also within the range of eutrophic temperate aquatic systems (Cole et al. 1988; del Giorgio and; Cole 1998), e.g. BP is similar to eutrophic and hypertrophic lakes (see Table 2). However, when comparing our results to studies from temperate regions, BP rates were slightly lower. Tropical, hypertrophic systems, however, typically have higher BP maxima, approximately twice as high as those measured in our kettle holes. In other studies of temperate lakes and prairie wetlands in Canada (Nixdorf and Jander 2003; Waiser and Robarts 2004), a seasonal trend in bacterial activities with higher summer values was detected, similar to our study. The high BP and BGE in early summer are likely caused by high temperatures and a sufficient supply of organic matter from algae and macrophytes in early summer that could be efficiently channeled into bacterial biomass production. Very likely, the high organic matter input in early summer increased the quality of bioavailable DOC which might be due to a release of exudates by autochthonous production (Sell and Overbeck 1992). This has been also observed in similar systems in Canada (Waiser and Robarts 2004). The high bacterial production in early summer may also increase the availability of bacterial biomass for zooplankton or macroinvertebrates (Søndergaard et al. 2005), which in turn may raise grazing pressure on bacterioplankton in kettle holes. Since many kettle holes lack fishes, a high grazing pressure on bacteria can be expected in these systems (Rautio and Vincent 2006). Effects of temporal differences in water chemistry on microbial activities Almost all dissolved water parameters (O₂, pH, DOC, %LMWS, HMWS:LMWS, TDN, TDP, and absorbance indices) significantly differed between the sampling dates in February, June and October (Table 4), whereby DOC varied most with an increase of 76% from February to June. A high intra-annual variability in nutrients in small aquatic systems is characteristic for numerous kettle holes in north-eastern Germany (Lischeid and Kalettka 2012), shallow, artificial ponds in southeastern England (Bennion and Smith 2000), and also for some tropical ponds (Mukhopadhyay et al. 2004). After the first observed increase from February to June, DOC no longer increased between June and October. This observation might suggest increased DOC degradation by internal microbial processes, which is supported by relatively high BP and BGE in all kettle holes in early summer and autumn (similar to Nixdorf and Jander 2003; Waiser and Robarts 2004; see Table 2) with around 184 ± 136 µg C L⁻¹ d⁻¹ and 129 ± 127 µg C L⁻¹ d⁻¹, respectively. BGE was around 37 ± 13% in early summer and 38 ± 19% in autumn. This is higher than the mean BGE determined by del Giorgio and Cole (1998) with around 30% for natural aquatic systems. An alternative explanation for this notion could be related to external factors such as catchment dynamics and photochemical degradation. Waiser (2006), for example, suggests hydrological characteristics as the most important factors affecting DOC concentrations in closed basin prairie wetlands. Unfortunately, we have no data on kettle hole hydrology and cannot exclude that DOC concentrations are altered by exchange with the surrounding terrestrial landscape. SUVA254 of our kettle holes was generally less than 3 L mg⁻¹ m⁻¹ indicating the prevalence of water soluble and less aromatic DOC (Peuravuori and Pihlaja 1997; Volk et al. 1997). In addition, SUVA285 rarely exceeded 1 L mg⁻¹ m⁻¹ in all of our investigated kettle holes (Fig. 1f, g) indicating a dominance of aliphatic substances probably originating from autochthonous primary production (Rostan and Cellot 1995). In general, autochthonous DOC tends to be less colored than terrestrially derived DOC (i.e., low absorbance indices) (Laurion et al. 2000). Low SUVA254/285 values might also point to photo-degradation of the DOC pool, decreasing aromaticity and color (Teixeira et al. 2013). However, low aromaticity and color throughout the seasons and no obvious decrease in SUVA254/285 and molecular size in June compared to February and October could indicate a minor importance of photo-degradative effects on DOC availability. In February, we measured a rather low BGE which may reflect lower OM bioavailability for the bacterial community due to a lack of newly produced autochthonous OM. Lower temperatures at this time of the year might also have limited BGE. During the growing season, however, new production by phytoplankton and macrophytes due to, for example, exudation, increases DOC molecular sizes. Nevertheless, in autumn a higher input of terrestrial OM following rain events and/or leaf litter fall may have increased LMWS concentrations in the water column (Fig. 1i). As a result, allochthonous inputs might play a minor role in shaping the dissolved OM pool in kettle holes during the growing season. Although we cannot exclude that heavy rain events or other “hot moments” might have increased terrestrial OM inputs, our data indicate that autochthonous C dominated C sources and that only a limited C input occurred from the catchment during our sampling campaigns. Additional support for the high autochthony of kettle holes stems from sediment C:N and d^{13}C data (Fig. 4) that suggest two of our studied kettle holes (number 5 and 10 in Table 1) have an autochthonous dominated fraction. Also, stable isotope analysis of POM from kettle holes 5 and 10 (ranging from −30.8 to −39.7‰) further suggests that the sedimenting OM is of primarily autochthonous origin. This notion is supported by findings of Downing et al. (2008) indicating that high rates of primary production in eutrophic impoundments contribute a substantial fraction to OC burial. In conclusion, contrary to our hypothesis, autochthonous production (POM and POC) may be the major driver for bacterial activities in the water column of kettle holes in the agricultural landscape. Variations in bacterial activities were best explained by the particulate organic matter pool that apparently plays a more important role for aquatic C turnover in kettle holes than in other aquatic systems. Our results highlight the importance of autochthonous sources for bacterial C turnover and biogeochemical processes in the water body of kettle holes and suggest that allochthonous C sources play a minor role in sustaining bacterial activities during the growing season. Thus, allochthonous OC introduced from terrestrial surroundings might be more prone to sedimentation where it can be microbially remineralized or buried. Yet, in kettle holes, further studies on their ecosystem function and role as hotspots for C turnover or C sequestration need to be performed to better evaluate the particular role of kettle holes for C cycling in a landscape perspective. title: biodiversity of constructed wetlands for wastewater treatment
author: hsu

Biodiversity of constructed wetlands for wastewater treatment Chorng-Bin Hsu a, Hwey-Lian Hsieh b, Lei Yang c, Sheng-Hai Wu a, Jui-Sheng Chang d, Shu-Chuan Hsiao a, Hui-Chen Su e, Chao-Hsien Yeh e, Yi-Shen Ho f, Hsing-Juh Lin a,b,* a Department of Life Sciences, National Chung Hsing University, Taichung 40227, Taiwan b Biodiversity Research Center, Academia Sinica, Taipei 11529, Taiwan c Department of Marine Environment and Engineering, National Sun Yat-sen University, Kaohsiung 80424, Taiwan d Department of Leisure Management, Yu Da University, Miaoli 36143, Taiwan e Department of Water Resources Engineering and Conservation, Feng Chia University, Taichung 40724, Taiwan f Wild Bird Society of Taipei, Taipei 10664, Taiwan A R T I C L E I N F O Article history: Received 7 October 2010 Received in revised form 15 April 2011 Accepted 6 June 2011 Available online 2 July 2011 Keywords: Free-water-surface (FWS) constructed wetlands Subtropics Richness Diversity Community A B S T R A C T Constructed wetlands are often built for wastewater treatment to mitigate the adverse effects of organic pollution in streams and rivers caused by inputs of municipal wastewater. However, there has been little analysis of biodiversity and related factors influencing the ecosystem functioning of constructed wetlands. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the biodiversity of two free-water-surface integrated constructed wetlands in subtropical Taiwan by analyzing the water quality, habitat characteristics, and biotic communities of algae, macrophytes, birds, fish, and aquatic macroinvertebrates in the treatment cells. Our results indicated that the two integrated constructed wetlands (Hsin-Hai II and Daniaopi Constructed Wetlands) achieved good performance in reducing the concentrations of total nitrogen (TN) and total phosphorus (TP), and loadings of biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) and chemical oxygen demand (COD) from municipal sewage. In total, 58 bird species, 7 fish species, and 34 aquatic macroinvertebrate taxa were recorded in the two wetlands. The results of stepwise multiple regressions showed that the richness, abundance, and diversity of birds increased with wetland area. Fish richness and abundance respectively increased with wetland area and dissolved oxygen, while the diversity decreased with increases in TP concentrations. The richness and density of aquatic macroinvertebrates increased with the cover of aquatic macrophytes, while the diversity increased with wetland area. Ordination analyses indicated that variations in the community structures of birds, fishes, and aquatic macroinvertebrates were respectively best explained by water temperature, wetland area, and species richness of fish. Our results suggest that wetland area, cover of aquatic macrophytes, and water quality were the most important factors governing the diversity in the constructed wetlands, and that the factors influencing community structures varied among different taxonomic groups. In addition to improving water quality, this study implied that the biodiversity of constructed wetlands for wastewater treatment can be enhanced through proper design and management. © 2011 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved. 1. Introduction Due to increasing population densities and impacts from human activities, pollution remains an essential issue for water quality protection and conservation of biodiversity in urban areas. There is a wide range of treatment technologies that can be used to improve the quality of wastewater to meet effluent standards. Many regions, however, do not have purification plants or lack sufficient capacity to treat all effluents due to the high costs of treatment processes (Kivaisi, 2002). The low coverage of sewage systems often results in municipal sewage and industrial wastewater being directly discharged into aquatic environments with no treatment (Jing et al., 2008). Wetlands are well known as one of the most productive ecosystems in the world (Mitsch and Gosselink, 2007). Countless species of birds, mammals, reptiles, amphibians, fishes, and invertebrates depend on the water and vegetation in wetland habitats (Zedler and Kercher, 2005; Mitsch and Gosselink, 2007; Kadlec and Wallace, 2008). Wetlands also directly and indirectly support people by providing ecosystem services such as flood abatement, food, a clean water supply, esthetic beauty, educational and recreational benefits, and carbon sinks (Zedler, 2003; Zedler and Kercher, 2005). The ability to simultaneously achieve water quality improvement and enhance biodiversity has generated increasing interest in constructing and restoring wetlands for wastewater treatment (Kivaisi, 2002). Constructed wetlands are artificial wetlands designed to intercept wastewater and remove a wide range of pollutants before discharge into natural water bodies. They mimic natural wetland ecosystems that combine physical, chemical, and biological processes to purify the water quality in more-controlled and efficient ways (Scholz et al., 2007; Kadlec and Wallace, 2008). Constructed wetlands are widely used as low-cost alternatives to conventional tertiary municipal wastewater treatment worldwide (Kivaisi, 2002; Verhoeven et al., 2006). Researchers have demonstrated that constructed wetlands are effective for the onsite management of municipal and agricultural wastewater and can remove various nutrients, including suspended solids (SS), biological oxygen demand (BOD), chemical oxygen demand (COD), nitrogen, phosphorus, trace elements, and microorganisms contained in the wastewater (Rousseau et al., 2004; Mitsch and Gosselink, 2007; Scholz et al., 2007; Kadlec and Wallace, 2008). The success of constructed wetlands is frequently assessed based on the performance of pollution reduction (Rousseau et al., 2004; Kadlec and Wallace, 2008). Constructed wetlands can also enhance various ecosystem services (Zedler and Kercher, 2005; Vymazal, 2011). Of the ecosystem services provided by wetlands, the biodiversity of constructed wetlands has attracted relatively less attention. Despite the rapid loss in wetland area and function (Zedler and Kercher, 2005), wetland biodiversity has been overlooked until recent decades (Denny, 1994). Wetland biodiversity is considered to have substantial conservation (Zedler and Kercher, 2005) and economic value (Costanza et al., 1997), and is also used as an indicator to assess ecosystem integrity (Mayer and Galatowitsch, 2001). Most studies addressing the biodiversity of constructed wetlands focused on a single taxonomic group (e.g., Fairchild et al., 2000; Spieles and Mitsch, 2000; Benyamine et al., 2004; Fleming-Singer and Horne, 2006; Jurado et al., 2010; Korfel et al., 2010). Although faunal diversity is thought to remain high in wetlands constructed for water treatment (Kadlec and Wallace, 2008), previous studies showed that high nutrient concentrations in wastewater are directly detrimental to wetland fauna (Spieles and Mitsch, 2000; Verhoeven et al., 2006) and to aquatic macrophyte communities, and, in turn, to the fauna that relies on macrophytes (Zhang et al., 2010). Although many studies have focused on the design of constructed wetlands to increase the pollutant removal efficiency (e.g., Thullen et al., 2005; Nahlil and Mitsch, 2006; Kadlec and Wallace, 2008), designing constructed wetlands it is more difficult to enhance biodiversity than to improve water quality, since there is a limited understanding of the factors that affect biodiversity (Zedler, 2003). There is an increasing trend to design multi-purpose treatment wetlands to enhance ancillary wildlife and human use benefits (Knight, 1992, 1997). An increasing number of studies have explored aquatic communities and factors influencing them in constructed wetlands (Fairchild et al., 2000; Spieles and Mitsch, 2000; Balcombe et al., 2005; Canonico et al., 2005; Fleming-Singer and Horne, 2006; Jurado et al., 2010). However, the richness and diversity of different taxonomic groups in wetlands were determined by different factors in different regions (e.g., Findlay and Houlahan, 1997; Balcombe et al., 2005; Declerck et al., 2005; Hansson et al., 2005). Therefore, it is imperative for wetland managers to examine the relationship between environmental variables and biotic communities. Hansson et al. (2005) indicated the possibility of improving the design of wetlands in terms of both biodiversity and nutrient retention. The knowledge of relationships between environmental variables and biodiversity, especially in constructed wetlands, is of great value, not only because it is important in assessing ecosystem services provided by constructed wetlands, but also because it provides an essential tool for designing and managing wetlands in order to maintain and enhance biodiversity. In Taiwan, the water quality in many streams near urban areas is severely impacted by municipal wastewater, only <15% of which enters wastewater treatment plants (Jing et al., 2008). Under governmental support, constructed wetlands were widely built along riparian zones for on-site water treatment (Taiwan EPA, 2007). There are currently about 100 wetlands installed or under construction in Taiwan. Most of these constructed wetlands are located in riparian areas between levees and the river and are used to treat urban wastewater. Monitoring data show that these wetlands achieve an acceptable wastewater treatment performance (Jing et al., 2008). However, the biodiversity of these constructed wetlands is poorly understood. We investigated the effects of a number of environmental factors that may affect the diversity and community structures of wetland birds, fishes, and aquatic macroinvertebrates in constructed wetlands for wastewater treatment. Understanding driving factors will be of benefit to managers involved in enhancing freshwater biodiversity on a large landscape scale. The objectives of this study were to (1) evaluate the biodiversity of different biotic communities, including aquatic macrophytes, birds, fishes, and aquatic macroinvertebrates among treatment cells in two free-water-surface (FWS) integrated constructed wetlands along the riparian zone of the Da-Han River in subtropical Taiwan, (2) identify major factors influencing changes in the biodiversity of the constructed wetlands, and (3) examine relationships between the biotic community structure and environmental variables. 2. Materials and methods 2.1. Study sites The Hsin-Hai II Constructed Wetland (HS2) and Daniaopi Constructed Wetland (DN) are five-cell FWS integrated wetlands, located in the riparian zone on the eastern bank of the Da-Han River in Taipei County (Fig. 1a). The HS2 and DN were respectively completed in September and November 2006. The DN covers a larger area with a higher flow rate and shorter hydraulic retention time than HS2 (Table 1). These two integrated wetlands have similar configurations, with each comprised of five treatment cells. The five sequential cells are a depositional pond, heavily vegetated pond I, open-water pond, heavily vegetated pond II, and ecological pond in the HS2 (cells HS2-1–HS2-5) (Fig. 1b and Table 2). The wastewater effluent from the ecological pond of HS2 flows directly into the Da-Han River after treatment. In the DN, the depositional pond (DN1) is followed by an open-water pond (DN2). The heavily vegetated pond I (DN3) is divided into four parallel sub-cells (DN3-A–DN3-D), each of which receives wastewater from the open-water pond and discharges outflow into the heavily vegetated pond II (DN4) and then into the ecological pond (DN5). After treatment, the wastewater effluent flows from the ecological pond (DN5) into a drainage channel and then into the Da-Han River (Fig. 1c and Table 2). We conducted water sampling and surveyed aquatic macrophytes and macroinvertebrates, fishes, and birds in the two constructed wetlands in February (winter) and June (summer) 2009, and bi-monthly from October 2009 to August 2010. Low-elevation aerial photos were also taken in February and June 2009 and January 2010. Fig. 1. (a) Locations and configurations of (b) the Hsin-Hai II Constructed Wetland (HS2) and (c) Daniaopi Constructed Wetland (DN). 2.2. Environmental variables The wetland area of each treatment cell was estimated based on aerial photographs using the software package, Image Pro 4.0 (Media Cybernetics, Silver Spring, MD). Water variables were measured in the field using portable instruments, such as water temperature (WTW LF196, Weilheim, Germany), dissolved oxygen (WTW oxi 3302), conductivity (WTW Cond 330i), and pH (WTW pH340). Water samples were taken from the outflow of each cell, immediately placed on ice in a cooler, and brought back to the laboratory for analyses of BOD, COD, nitrate (NO3⁻), nitrite (NO2⁻), total nitrogen (TN), total phosphorus (TP), suspended solids (SS), and phytoplankton chlorophyll (Chl)-a concentration following standard methods of the APHA (Clesceri et al., 1998). 2.3. Biotic samples Aquatic macrophytes were surveyed using transects across treatment cells. Six transects were set up in each treatment cell, and all aquatic macrophytes on the transects were identified to species level. To determine the cover of aquatic macrophytes, we overlaid a grid of 2.5-m plots onto an enlarged aerial photo of each treatment cell, and the cover of each species was determined by estimating the fractions of vegetation in each grid and summing up all grids. When areal photos were not available, the cover of aquatic macrophytes was estimated on each transect in the field. We used a D-net sweep (Model 7412D, BioQuip, Rancho Dominguez, CA) to collect aquatic invertebrates modified from a procedure of the USEPA (2002). During each sweep, the D-net was placed on the wetland bottom and pushed horizontally into the vegetation, if available, for a distance of 1 m to cover an area of about 0.3 m², while bouncing the net into the sediment at least twice. The distance between locations of adjacent sweeps was at least 1 m. Two sweeps were combined into one sample, and three samples (six sweeps) were taken in each treatment cell. Materials collected in the net were poured into a 0.5-mm-mesh sieve. After elutriation and removal of large debris, samples retained on the sieve were preserved in 70% ethanol. Aquatic macroinverte-

brates were identified to the lowest possible taxonomic level and counted using a stereomicroscope in the laboratory. Nematodes and zooplankton taxa including cladoceran, copepods, and ostracods were excluded from further analyses. Major classes or orders were described for those specimens for which the species could not be determined. We used a cast net (2 m in radius with a 2-cm mesh size) and shrimp traps (15 cm in diameter) to collect fish from the constructed wetlands. The cast net was deployed three times in treatment cells where the method was applicable except in cells HS2-1, HS2-2, DN1, DN2, DN3-A, and DN3-D. Ten shrimp traps were also set up in each treatment cell. Caught fish were chilled on ice and transported back to the laboratory. A bird survey was conducted by three trained persons on three consecutive days, one for each constructed wetland. Observers patrolled the shores of treatment cells on foot during the first 3 h of daylight, and species and abundances in each treatment cell of the two constructed wetlands were determined with the aid of binoculars. The habitats where the birds were observed were also recorded. 2.4. Biotic metrics We assessed the biodiversity of constructed wetlands using two common measures of richness and the Shannon–Wiener index. Species richness (the number of species) was selected to represent the richness of birds, fishes, and aquatic macrophytes, whereas taxon richness (the number of taxa) was selected for aquatic macroinvertebrates in each treatment cell of the two constructed wetlands. The Shannon–Wiener index (\( H' \)) was calculated using the following equation: \[ H' = - \sum_{i=1}^{S} p_i \ln p_i; \] where \( p_i \) is the proportion of individuals found of the ith species (taxon) or the percent coverage of the ith aquatic macrophyte species. 2.5. Statistical analysis Variables were first examined to see if they were normally distributed. DO, SS, BOD, COD, and NO\(_x^-\) (NO\(_2^-\) + NO\(_3^-\)) concentrations were log-transformed, while wetland areas and TN, TP, and phytoplankton Chl-a concentrations were square-root-transformed to improve the normality. Abundances of birds and fishes were square-root-transformed, and the density of aquatic macroinvertebrates was log(x + 1)-transformed. An arcsine-square-root transformation was used for the percent cover of aquatic macrophytes (Zar, 1996). We used multiple regressions to develop the most appropriate statistical models to predict biodiversity measures of birds, fishes, and aquatic macroinvertebrates in the constructed wetlands. Species or taxon richness, abundance (density), and Shannon diversity (\( H' \)) of biotic communities were used as dependent variables, while wetland attributes, including wetland area, water quality, and biotic metrics, were used as independent variables in a stepwise regression model (Sokal and Rohlf, 1995). Variables with a significance level of <0.05 were included in the regression models. We did not examine the diversity of aquatic macrophytes because most of the aquatic macrophyte species were artificially introduced when constructing the wetlands. Moreover, we used multivariate techniques to examine relationships of the community structures of birds, fishes, and aquatic macroinvertebrates with environmental variables. The proportion of each species was separately calculated for birds, fishes, and aquatic macroinvertebrates. Rare species (taxa) were excluded from the analyses to reduce their influence on the ordinations (ter Braak, 1995). Only taxa constituting more than 0.5% of the total abundances for birds, fishes, and aquatic macroinvertebrates were included in the multivariate analyses. Totals of 33 species of birds, 4 species of fishes, and 13 aquatic macroinvertebrate taxa were used in the analyses (Appendix A). A prior detrended correspondence analysis (DCA) was separately conducted on the bird, fish, and aquatic macroinvertebrate data to assess the gradient length of the first DCA axis. The lengths of the gradients were 3.957, 2.869, and 2.871 (in SD units) for birds, fishes, and aquatic macroinvertebrates, respectively. Therefore, the unimodal model (e.g., the canonical correspondence analysis, CCA) was more appropriate for birds, and a linear model (e.g., the redundancy analysis, RDA) was better for fishes and aquatic macroinvertebrates (ter Braak and Šmilauer, 2002). In the ordination models, wetland area, water quality, and biotic metrics were used as explanatory variables. We ran the analysis using the automatic forward-selection mode, and only variables explaining a significant proportion of the remaining variation were included (based on a Monte Carlo test with 999 permutations at \( p < 0.1 \)). Biodiversity measures were calculated using the PRIMER vers. 5 computer software (Clarke and Gorley, 2001). Multiple regression analyses were produced using the software package SAS 9.1 (SAS Institute, 2003). Ordination analyses were performed using CANOCO for Windows vers. 4.52 (ter Braak and Šmilauer, 2002). 3. Results 3.1. Environmental variables Areas of treatment cells varied within and between constructed wetlands. The depositional ponds of the two constructed wetlands were small, at <0.2 ha. Areas of other treatment cells ranged 0.55–0.83 ha in the HS2 and 0.26–1.86 ha in the DN (Fig. 2). The cover of aquatic macrophytes was the highest in heavily vegetated ponds of each constructed wetland, i.e., HS2-2, HS2-4, DN3-A, DN3-B, and DN3-D (Fig. 2). Water quality widely varied among treatment cells in each constructed wetland. DO was low, generally <6 ppm except in the ecological ponds, and showed an increasing trend along the sequential treatment cells in both constructed wetlands (Table 2). In contrast, conductivity and concentrations of TN and TP showed a decreasing trend along sequential treatment cells, suggesting reductions in the pollutant concentrations of wastewater after passing through these constructed wetlands (Table 2). Other variables, however, fluctuated along the sequential treatment cells. The overall system performance of pollutant removal based on the reduction in concentrations in the water column is shown in Table 3. Removal of BOD and COD was higher in the HS2 with respective removal rates of 58.8% and 51.1%, and the outflow concentration was reduced to <11 and 30 mg L\(^{-1}\), respectively (Tables 2, 3). Concentrations of TN and TP were substantially reduced in the DN with respective removal rates of 51.4% and 52.3%, and the outflow concentrations were 8.4 and 0.5 ppm, respectively.
