Levels of fish species richness were low in the two constructed wetlands with mean values ranging 0–1.6 in the HS2 and 1.0–2.4 in the DN (Table 5). Higher abundances and lower \( H' \) values were observed in treatment cells of the HS2 than in those of the DN (Table 5). The dominant species in the HS2 was blue gourami (Trichogaster trichopterus), which accounted for 91.3% of the total abundance. The DN was dominated by tilapia and goldfish (Carassius auratus auratus), accounting for 63.2% and 35.0% of the total abundance, respectively. The mean taxon richness of aquatic macroinvertebrates in each treatment cell ranged 7.1–10.8 in the HS2 and 7.3–15.0 in the DN (Table 5). In the HS2, densities of aquatic macroinvertebrates were higher in HS2-2 and HS2-3 with mean values of 210.0 and 248.2 individuals m\(^{-2}\), respectively. Densities in the DN were higher in DN2 and DN1 followed by DN3-B and DN3-A (Table 5). Mean \( H' \) of aquatic macroinvertebrates in each treatment cell was similar, ranging 1.20–1.73 in the HS2 and 0.85–1.67 in the DN. The dominant taxa in the HS2 were mosquitoes (Culex spp.) and non-biting midges (Chironomidae), which respectively accounted for 33.4% and 13.6% of the total abundance. Factors affecting biotic metrics in the constructed wetlands Results from stepwise multiple regressions showed that the biodiversity and abundance of different taxonomic groups were affected by different environmental variables (Table 6). Species richness, abundance, and \( H' \) of wetland birds were positively related to the wetland area, while \( H' \) was also correlated with the cover of aquatic macrophytes (Table 6). Species richness of fishes was positively related to the wetland area and negatively related to conductivity and \( H' \) of aquatic macrophytes. Fish abundance was positively related to DO, while \( H' \) was negatively related to the TP concentration (Table 6). For aquatic macroinvertebrates, taxon richness and density were positively correlated with the cover of aquatic macrophytes and negatively with COD. \( H' \) of aquatic macroinvertebrates was positively related to the wetland area, although the \( R^2 \) value was low (Table 6). Species richness, abundance, and \( H' \) of wetland birds increased with wetland area up to about 2 ha (Fig. 3). Species richness of fishes and the taxon richness of aquatic macroinvertebrates increased with wetland area and cover of aquatic macrophytes, respectively. However, relations between environmental variables and other biotic metrics of fish and aquatic macroinvertebrates were not clear. 3.4. Discussion 4.1. Performance of pollutant removal The construction of wetlands is an alternative measure to conventional water treatment, which provides a potentially more environmentally friendly and economical treatment system to mitigate the negative effects of domestic wastewater and urban runoff (Scholz et al., 2007). Our study showed that the two constructed wetlands were effective in nutrient removal, although the performances varied between the constructed wetlands and also among nutrients. Wetland design, water quality, hydraulics, soil chem- istry, microbial communities, macroinvertebrates, and vegetation each may greatly affect the performance of constructed wetlands. The main removal mechanisms of BOD and COD include microbial degradation and settling of colloidal particles (Vymazal et al., 1998). Nitrogen is primarily removed through microbial nitrification and denitrification in most constructed wetlands (Vymazal et al., 1998). Phosphorus removal in constructed wetlands occurs from absorption and precipitation by soil particles (Vymazal, 2010). The amount of nutrients such as phosphorus removed by plant uptake generally accounts for a small fraction of total nutrients removed in constructed wetlands (Vymazal et al., 1998), and may be released back into the water after plants decay (Vymazal, 2010). Small and deep wetlands increase phosphorus retention by increasing particle sedimentation, while large surface areas may maximize nitrogen removal (Hansson et al., 2005; Kadlec and Wallace, 2008). The removal rates in this study were similar compared to nearby constructed wetlands (Fan et al., 2009). 4.2. Biodiversity of constructed wetlands Along with treating wastewater, there is an increasing trend in designing constructed wetlands to restore degraded habitats for wildlife. However, different ecological functions of wetland systems are thought to be conflicting. High nutrient loadings that surpass a critical level may cause dramatic shifts in species composition and ecosystem functioning (Verhoeven et al., 2006). Some potential problems, including bioaccumulation of toxic materials, transmission of disease, and environmental hazards, might result from the use of wetlands for wastewater treatment (Knight, 1992). Benyamine et al. (2004) indicated that the typical single-objective focus of scientific studies has led to contradictions in recommendations for the design and management of constructed wetlands for multiple uses. Nevertheless, this study combined with others (e.g., Knight, 1997; Fleming-Singer and Horne, 2006) suggest that constructed wetlands can provide attractive habitats for various kinds of wildlife. Meanwhile, after reviewing the North American Treatment Wetland (NADB) Database, Knight et al. (2001) indicated that there were no detrimental effects on wildlife caused by the pollution-cleansing function of treatment wetlands. Due to a lack of data in nearby freshwater habitats, the contribution of constructed wetlands to landscape biodiversity could not be determined in this study. Nevertheless, in addition to water quality improvement, this study suggests that the biodiversity of constructed wetlands for wastewater treatment can be enhanced through proper design and management. This study further demonstrated that the biodiversity of different taxonomic groups in constructed wetlands is governed by various factors. 4.3. Factors affecting wetland biodiversity Our results suggest a positive relationship between the area of a constructed wetland and the biodiversity and abundance of birds, which is in accordance with other studies on wetlands (Zedler, 2003; Hansson et al., 2005). In addition to wetland area, bird biodiversity was found to be affected by adjacent and regional land uses, such as road density and connectedness (Whited et al., 2000). Ordination results suggested that bird communities were mainly determined by seasonal patterns, as well as food availability and nesting requirements for brood rearing. Bird species such as the Dusky Thrush, Teal, and Yellow Wagtail were winter visitors (Shiu et al., 2005), and, therefore, were negatively correlated with water temperature. Members of the Ardeidae such as Little Egrets and Black-crowned Night Herons, and the Recurvirostridae like Black-winged Stilts were found to be associated with the species richness and abundance of fishes (Fig. 4). A number of studies indicated that they feed on a wide variety of prey types but mainly on fish (Fasola, 1994; Kazantzidis and Goutner, 2005). The association of White-breasted Waterhen (Amaurornis phoenicurus) with aquatic macrophytes can be attributed to nest-site selection for brood rearing (Gopakumar and Kaimal, 2008). Aquatic invertebrates are primary food resources for many wintering waterbirds. Wallau et al. (2010) indicated that the Common Moorhen feeds on pieces of aquatic macrophytes and removes macrophytes to search for invertebrates which utilize macrophytes as habitats. The Cattle Egret was found to rely heavily on various invertebrates as their main food sources (Lombardini et al., 2001), and its number was positively correlated with the density of aquatic macroinvertebrates (Fig. 4). Teal and Spot-billed Duck (Anatidae) may also compete with fish for the same food resources (invertebrates) and are thus found in lower densities at wetlands with fish compared to those without fish (e.g., Eriksson, 1979). Our study showed that fish biodiversity was low in these young (<5 years) constructed wetlands. Hansson et al. (2005) also found similar results and indicated that natural wetlands aged more than 100 years showed considerably higher fish species richness than young constructed wetlands. In constructed wetlands, possible sources of the fish are limited to those from nearby streams during floods and mercy releases, and, therefore, the biodiversity of fish is unlikely to increase over a short time period. This study showed that a wetland’s area is also important in determining the species richness of fishes. All treatment cells in our study were <2 ha (Fig. 2). Søndergaard et al. (2005) found that fish species richness was low, typically 1–3 species, in Danish ponds and lakes with areas of <1 ha, and gradually increased with lake size. Scheffer et al. (2006) proposed that fish are rare in small, isolated lakes, probably as a result of a higher likelihood of fish kills combined with their low colonizing ability. Moreover, fish biodiversity appeared to be most affected by the water quality in constructed wetlands. Fish species found in constructed wetlands appeared to be tolerant of high nutrient levels and low DO conditions. Blue gourami is an obligate air-breathing fish (Burggren, 1979), which means that it can adapt to changing DO levels in constructed wetlands. The dominant blue gourami and tilapia in constructed wetlands are exotics, but not the goldfish. Tilapia (Cichlidae) are among the most widely distributed exotic fishes in the world (Canonico et al., 2005). Studies found that they are able to respond to environmental changes by rapidly altering their life history characteristic and trophic levels (Bowen and Allanson, 1982), which may benefit their invasion into new environments (Holway and Suarez, 1999). The exotic species introduced to these wetlands either on purpose or accidentally may also threaten populations of native species. Our results suggest close relationships of the richness and density of aquatic macroinvertebrates with the coverage of aquatic macrophytes. The abundance and diversity of aquatic invertebrates were found to be associated with the vegetated area of wetlands (Gee et al., 1997). The presence of aquatic macrophytes might affect the distributions of aquatic macroinvertebrates and thus their biodiversity in several ways. Submerged vegetation in aquatic ecosystems forms complex structures, which may be used as habitats (Gee et al., 1997) or as refuges to reduce the foraging efficiency of predators (Diehl, 1992). Because there is more space for food attachment and collection, aquatic macrophytes provide additional resources such as epiphytes to the macroinvertebrate community, especially for grazers and thus may indirectly favor detritivores and predators (Diehl, 1992). Positive relationships between the abundance of aquatic macroinvertebrates and cover of aquatic macrophytes were reported elsewhere (de Szalay and Resh, 2000). In constructed wetlands, excessive nutrient loadings, high toxic pollutant levels, and anaerobic conditions often prevent aquatic macroinvertebrates from using wetlands as habitats (e.g., Spieles and Mitsch, 2000; Verhoeven et al., 2006). Hence, our results indicated a negative relationship of COD with the taxon richness and density of aquatic macroinvertebrates. Decreases in richness and density of aquatic macroinvertebrates were shown to be related to changes in water quality in various aquatic ecosystems (e.g., Spieles and Mitsch, 2000; Jurado et al., 2010). The community structure of aquatic macroinvertebrates in constructed wetlands was influenced by the presence of predators and suitable habitats. Fish are often the top predators in wetland ecosystems and can impact aquatic macroinvertebrates in terms of species richness, density, diversity, and community structure (Diehl, 1992). Ordination analyses indicated that the major dipteran taxa in these constructed wetlands, such as non-biting midges (Chironomidae), mosquitoes (Culicidae), and brine flies (Ephydridae), were negatively associated with the species richness of fish and dissolved oxygen. Most of the fish species in our study sites rely on aquatic invertebrates as their main food sources. The diet of the blue gourami mainly consists of aquatic invertebrates and algae-based foods (Syarifuddin and Kramer, 1996). Although goldfish predominantly eat non-animal food, studies showed that they also feed on a wide range of food resources, including various zooplankton and aquatic insects (e.g., Peterson et al., 2005). Numerous studies demonstrated that the presence of fish may reduce the density and biomass of certain taxa of aquatic invertebrates (e.g., Fairchild et al., 2000) and change the community structure of aquatic invertebrates in wetlands (Tarr et al., 2005). Moreover, many species of these dipteran families are tolerant of low DO and polluted water (Courtney et al., 1996). Relationships of damselflies (Coenagrionidae), giant water bugs (Belostomatidae), and leaf beetles (Chrysomelidae) with the cover of aquatic macrophytes suggest that the vegetation is used as food and perch sites (Cloarec, 1990; Gibbons et al., 2002; Fernandez and Hilker, 2007). The amount of unexplained variation in our models suggests that some other unmeasured variables play certain roles in regulating communities in these constructed wetlands. Keddy and Fraser (2000) suggested that variations in water depth were the most important factor governing communities in shoreline wetlands. Increases in habitat heterogeneity or complexity (Hansson et al., 2005) and age (Fairchild et al., 2000) may increase the biodiversity of wetlands. In addition, the richness of aquatic invertebrates increases with the hydroperiod, i.e., the length of time that a wetland holds water (Tarr et al., 2005). In highly connected wetlands, aquatic invertebrate richness may also increase through dispersal from areas with different environmental conditions (e.g., Cottenie and De Meester, 2003). These factors could be constructed and manipulated through proper design and management of constructed wetlands, and can therefore be used to increase biodiversity. 4.4. Implications for the design and management of constructed wetlands Previous studies examined the impacts of environmental factors on biodiversity across various taxonomic groups in lentic ecosystems (e.g., Findlay and Houlahan, 1997; Balcombe et al., 2005; Declerck et al., 2005; Hansson et al., 2005). Results from those studies as well as ours reveal that the factors influencing biodiversity differed among faunal groups in constructed wetlands. In order to maximize biodiversity in constructed wetlands, the factors involved in each taxonomic group should be taken into consideration in wetland design and management from a holistic view. According to our results, wetland area and cover of aquatic macrophytes appeared to be the two most important factors affecting biodiversity in the constructed wetlands. A wetland constructed with the aim of improving water quality and enhancing biodiversity should have a large surface area and a high cover of aquatic macrophytes. Findlay and Houlahan (1997) found that species richness of all taxa in their study, including birds, mammals, herptiles and plants, increased with wetland area. Whatever other considerations may be taken into the wetland design, from a biodiversity conservation perspective, bigger is indeed better, although the maximum richness of some taxa might be encountered at a certain area (e.g., 4–5 ha for birds, Hansson et al., 2005). Changes in macrophyte composition and cover are among the most important ecological successions in constructed wetlands (Mitsch et al., 2005). Although high macrophyte cover may increase taxa richness and density of aquatic macroinvertebrates, problems can arise as a result of the presence of dense vegetation in wetlands such as consumption of DO and contribution to nutrient loadings as plants decompose (Sartoris et al., 2000). For wastewater treatment, a high cover of aquatic macrophytes was designed as one of the important factors facilitating N retention (Thiere et al., 2011). For wildlife management, a 50:50 ratio of open water to emergent vegetation, i.e., hemi-marshes, was recommended to attract wildlife (Murkin et al., 1997). de Szalay and Resh (2000) indicated that the cover of aquatic macrophytes increased the abundances of some dipteran taxa, which might cause serious nuisance problems in wetlands. Our results also show that taxa responded differently to changes in the cover of aquatic macrophytes (Fig. 6). Since the vegetation has both positive and negative effects on the performance of constructed wetland for wastewater treatment, a proper vegetation balance is needed for optimal treatment performance through vegetation management (Thullen et al., 2005). It is widely accepted that created wetlands, whether for wastewater treatment or not, may never express the full range of ecological variability found in natural wetlands (Brooks et al., 2005). However, as water quality improves due to sequential purification along the treatment cells, the last ponds in a constructed wetland may be capable of supporting biodiversity similar to that of natural wetlands (Jurado et al., 2010). 5. Conclusions Although characterized by high nutrient loadings, constructed wetlands for wastewater treatment are able to support various wildlife and enhance biodiversity. This study indicated that the factors influencing biodiversity differed among faunal groups in constructed wetlands. The richness, abundance, and diversity of birds increased with the wetland area. Fish richness and abundance respectively increased with wetland area and dissolved oxygen, while the diversity decreased with increases in TP concentration. The richness and density of aquatic macroinvertebrates increased with the cover of aquatic macrophytes, while the diversity increased with wetland area. Therefore, a wetland constructed with the aims of improving water quality and enhancing biodiversity should have a large surface area and a high cover of aquatic macrophytes. Our results imply that ecosystem functioning of constructed wetlands, used primarily for wastewater treatment or created for new wetland areas, can be managed to enhance biodiversity.
